At its peak about twenty-eight thousand Georgians worked at the plant — many of them women. Marietta grew from eight thousand six hundred sixty-seven people in nineteen forty to twenty thousand six hundred eighty-seven by the end of the decade. Lockheed builds planes on the site today.
georgia/ga-20th.ab7ba678d143: Brunswick shipyard. J. A. Jones: ninety-nine ships in about two years. The J. A. Jones shipyard in Brunswick built ninety-nine Liberty ships in about two years. Workers poured in from farms, and the town boomed.
georgia/ga-20th.82c50718363e: Camp Gordon, Chamblee. Training ground of the eighty-second “All-American” Division. Opened in July nineteen seventeen northeast of Atlanta. It trained the eighty-second “All-American” Division — almost half of it Georgians. Today the site is an airport, DeKalb-Peachtree.
georgia/ga-20th.540e0c037f0e: Souther Field, Americus. Almost two thousand military pilots trained here. A World War One flight school northeast of Americus. It trained almost two thousand military pilots.
georgia/ga-20th.d33cc2d8a3ff: Thomasville. Where the boll weevil was first found in Georgia. The boll weevil crossed from Mexico into Texas in the eighteen nineties and spread east. It was first found in Georgia at Thomasville in nineteen fifteen. Georgia’s crop fell from about two point eight million bales in nineteen fourteen to about six hundred thousand in nineteen twenty-three.
georgia/ga-20th.de53a7982af2: Camp Wheeler, Macon. Home of the thirty-first “Dixie” Division. The thirty-first “Dixie” Division trained here; more than twelve thousand Georgians served in it. The camp reopened for training in World War Two.
georgia/ga-20th.ba84bdff6d57: Techwood Homes, Atlanta. The first federal public housing project in the US. Built with New Deal money near Georgia Tech; FDR dedicated it in nineteen thirty-five and families moved in in nineteen thirty-six. It replaced crowded slums with brick apartments — but was for white families only; University Homes nearby was built for Black families.
georgia/ga-20th.3789ce2e524f: Warm Springs. Where FDR swam, planned and died. FDR first came in nineteen twenty-four, hoping the eighty-eight degrees Fahrenheit spring water would help his polio. He built the Little White House in nineteen thirty-two. He died here on April twelfth, nineteen forty-five, while an artist was painting the “Unfinished Portrait.”
georgia/ga-20th.c74b6810b405: Savannah shipyard. Southeastern Shipbuilding: eighty-eight ships. Southeastern Shipbuilding near Savannah built eighty-eight ships. It employed more than fifteen thousand people. Liberty ships carried food, fuel and weapons across the oceans to the Allies.
georgia/ga-20th.303d14460a0d: Don't mix up: In nineteen eighteen disease was as big a danger as the enemy: the flu swept through crowded training camps.
georgia/ga-20th.7999225e9ac1: Athens, UGA. About two thousand Navy combat pilots trained here. The US Navy trained about two thousand combat pilots at the University of Georgia. Colleges across the state helped train soldiers and sailors.
georgia/ga-20th.4eb4fb1da534: Camp Hancock, Augusta. Infantry camp and one of the Army’s first airfields. Home of the twenty-eighth “Keystone” Division. It was the Army’s second military airfield. In October nineteen eighteen the flu hit hard: about three thousand cases and the camp was quarantined.
georgia/ga-20th.1768089222fb: Fort Benning, Columbus. The world’s largest infantry school in World War Two. Founded as Camp Benning in nineteen eighteen. In World War Two it was the largest infantry training school in the world; paratroopers trained here too. Renamed Fort Moore in twenty twenty-three, it became Fort Benning again in twenty twenty-five — base names can change!

georgia/ga-civilrights.c41688e98432: Atlanta. Auburn Avenue, SCLC, SNCC — and “too busy to hate”. Martin Luther King Jr. was born at five oh one Auburn Avenue in nineteen twenty-nine and preached at Ebenezer Baptist Church with his father. The SCLC was founded here in nineteen fifty-seven; SNCC made Atlanta its headquarters in October nineteen sixty. College students began the Atlanta Student Movement in nineteen sixty with “An Appeal for Human Rights” and lunch-counter sit-ins. Atlanta’s public schools began to desegregate peacefully on August thirtieth, nineteen sixty-one. Mayor Ivan Allen Jr. testified for the civil rights bill in Congress in nineteen sixty-three — rare for a white Southern mayor.
georgia/ga-civilrights.a8233cc7f1d2: Columbus. One voter’s lawsuit opens the ballot box. Dr. Thomas Brewer recruited Primus King to try to vote in the July fourth, nineteen forty-four, Democratic primary. King was turned away. His lawsuit, King versus Chapman, struck down Georgia’s whites-only primary in nineteen forty-five; the ruling was upheld in nineteen forty-six. In one-party Georgia the Democratic primary decided who won, so this opened real voting power. Black voter registration jumped to about one hundred twenty-five thousand within months.
georgia/ga-civilrights.02113b476db8: Don’t mix up: The white primary ended in nineteen forty-six, but the county unit system still kept city voters weak until nineteen sixty-two.

georgia/ga-civilwar.782b29b8c57f: Milledgeville. Secession — and a mock repeal. The secession convention met here in January eighteen sixty-one and voted two hundred eight to eighty-nine to leave the Union. On November twenty-third, eighteen sixty-four, Sherman’s left wing took the capital; Union officers held a mock session in the statehouse and “repealed” secession.
georgia/ga-civilwar.dcda68146128: Fort Pulaski. The blockade tightens. A brick fort guarding the mouth of the Savannah River, with brick walls about seven and a half feet thick. Union rifled cannon on Tybee Island, one to two miles away, broke through the walls in about thirty hours. After it fell, Savannah was almost closed to blockade runners for the rest of the war.
georgia/ga-civilwar.483f43cfaa53: Fort McAllister. The door to the sea opens. An earthwork fort guarding the Ogeechee River south of Savannah. Union troops stormed it in about fifteen minutes, opening contact with the Union navy and its supplies.
georgia/ga-civilwar.2f435feea003: Dalton and Resaca. The Atlanta Campaign begins. Sherman’s roughly one hundred thousand men faced Joseph E. Johnston’s roughly sixty thousand near Dalton. Instead of attacking head-on, Sherman kept swinging around Johnston’s flank, forcing him to retreat south. Both armies followed the Western and Atlantic Railroad — the lifeline to Atlanta.
georgia/ga-civilwar.39a00b63a2e8: Savannah. A “Christmas gift” for Lincoln. Confederate troops left Savannah, and Sherman’s army marched in without a battle. Thousands of freedom seekers had followed the army across Georgia. In January eighteen sixty-five Sherman issued Field Order Number fifteen, setting aside coastal land for freed families.
georgia/ga-civilwar.a25148228b67: Atlanta. Its fall helped re-elect Lincoln. In July eighteen sixty-four John Bell Hood replaced Johnston and attacked at Peachtree Creek on July twentieth and the Battle of Atlanta on July twenty-second. After Sherman cut the last railroad at Jonesboro, Hood left the city; Union troops entered on September second, eighteen sixty-four. Sherman wired Washington: “Atlanta is ours, and fairly won.” The good news helped Lincoln win the November election. In November Sherman’s troops burned the city’s railroads, depots and factories before marching east.
georgia/ga-civilwar.31faae48679c: Andersonville. The deadliest prison camp of the war. Built in Sumter County, far from the fighting, to hold Union prisoners. About forty-five thousand men were held here; nearly thirteen thousand died, mostly of disease, poor food, bad water and exposure. The camp commander, Henry Wirz, was tried and executed after the war. Today it is home to the National Prisoner of War Museum, honoring all American POWs.
georgia/ga-civilwar.e8b286b9263d: Chickamauga. The largest battle in Georgia. Confederate General Braxton Bragg attacked Union General William Rosecrans along Chickamauga Creek. A gap in the Union line let Confederates break through on September twentieth; General George Thomas held firm and became the “Rock of Chickamauga.” About thirty-four thousand six hundred total casualties — second only to Gettysburg. A Confederate victory, but the Union kept Chattanooga, the gateway to Georgia.
georgia/ga-civilwar.12f1e7c96a35: Memory hint: eighteen sixty-three Chickamauga, C-side wins, eighteen sixty-four Atlanta falls, September, March to the Sea, November to December, Savannah, a Christmas gift.
georgia/ga-civilwar.e795f2d9a58c: Kennesaw Mountain. Sherman’s one big frontal attack. Confederates dug in on the mountain. Sherman attacked head-on and lost about three thousand men to about one thousand Confederates. He went back to flanking moves, and Johnston retreated again. Nearby Big Shanty, today’s Kennesaw, is where Union raiders stole the locomotive “General” in the Great Locomotive Chase, April eighteen sixty-two.

georgia/ga-geography.4ad467ffcbaa: Brasstown Bald. Four thousand seven hundred eighty-four feet, one thousand four hundred fifty-eight meters — the roof of Georgia. On a clear day you can see four states from the tower on top: Georgia, Tennessee, North Carolina and South Carolina.
georgia/ga-geography.bf5c448140b6: Don’t mix up: Atlanta is in the Piedmont, not in the mountains — it is about one thousand fifty feet high, but on rolling hills.
georgia/ga-geography.6043985121e4: Blue Ridge. Georgia’s tallest mountains. Location: the northeast corner. Brasstown Bald is the highest point in Georgia, at four thousand seven hundred eighty-four feet or one thousand four hundred fifty-eight meters; the Appalachian Trail starts at Springer Mountain. Climate: the coolest region, with some snow in winter and the most rain in the state — up to about seventy to eighty inches a year. Agriculture: apples in Ellijay, cattle, poultry and hardwood forests on steep slopes. Economy: tourism and timber — and the eighteen twenty-nine gold rush at Dahlonega. Tourism includes hiking, rafting and Tallulah Gorge.
georgia/ga-geography.d3ffe896aa78: Chattahoochee River. Atlanta’s water supply and part of the Alabama border. About four hundred thirty miles from the Blue Ridge to the Florida line. Lake Lanier stores its water for metro Atlanta; Columbus grew at its Fall Line falls; it forms much of the Georgia-Alabama border.
georgia/ga-geography.7bfdfb8a6f54: Piedmont. Rolling hills and red clay. Location: from the mountains down to the Fall Line — about a third of Georgia. “Piedmont” means “foot of the mountains.” Climate: hot summers, mild winters, about fifty inches of rain. Rolling hills of red clay, colored by iron, and granite such as Stone Mountain. Agriculture: poultry, Gainesville calls itself the “Poultry Capital of the World”, cattle, dairy, timber; it was cotton country in the eighteen hundreds. Economy: the most people and jobs — Atlanta, Athens and the busy Hartsfield-Jackson airport; business, transportation, government and universities.
georgia/ga-geography.9340b8623abf: Tallulah Gorge. A gorge almost one thousand feet deep. The Tallulah River cut this gorge about two miles long. In nineteen seventy Karl Wallenda walked across it on a tightrope.
georgia/ga-geography.a3fc81d1674b: Valley and Ridge. Ridges and fertile valleys side by side. Location: the northwest, between the Appalachian Plateau and the Blue Ridge. Long ridges such as Taylor Ridge run southwest to northeast with valleys between. Climate: mild — cooler than the south, with about fifty to fifty-five inches of rain. Agriculture: grain, hay, cattle, poultry and dairy in the limestone valleys. Economy: manufacturing — Dalton is called the “Carpet Capital of the World”; Rome grew where two rivers meet to form the Coosa.
georgia/ga-geography.682c0701484e: Appalachian Mountains, Springer Mountain. The southern end of a one thousand five hundred-mile mountain chain. The Appalachians cover the Blue Ridge, Valley and Ridge and Appalachian Plateau. Mountains block easy travel, so north Georgia was settled later — and its rain feeds rivers for the whole state.

georgia/ga-government.b9e5c71e3f30: The Governor. Carries out and enforces the laws. Governor: at least thirty, a US citizen for fifteen years and a Georgia resident for six years. A four-year term, at most two terms in a row. The lieutenant governor has the same qualifications, presides over the Senate and becomes governor if the office is empty. The governor writes the budget proposal, sets the revenue estimate, signs or vetoes bills and can veto single spending items. Other statewide elected officers include the secretary of state, attorney general, state school superintendent and agriculture commissioner. State agencies do the daily work: Department of Education, Department of Transportation, GDOT, Department of Driver Services, your license, Department of Natural Resources, state parks, Department of Juvenile Justice.
georgia/ga-government.22c69b29c466: General Assembly. Makes the laws and passes the budget. Two chambers: the Senate, fifty-six senators, and the House of Representatives, one hundred eighty representatives. All serve two-year terms. Qualifications: senators at least twenty-five, representatives at least twenty-one; US citizens; Georgia residents for two years and district residents for one year. Meets every year from the second Monday in January for forty legislative days — usually into late March or early April. Leaders: the lieutenant governor presides over the Senate; the House elects its own Speaker. Committees study every bill first — most bills never leave committee. Committees include Education, Appropriations, Judiciary… Spending and tax bills must start in the House.
georgia/ga-government.6d819ca357a1: The Courts. Interprets the laws and administers justice. Supreme Court: nine justices — the highest court; it decides questions about the constitution and reviews the most serious cases. Court of Appeals: fifteen judges who check trial courts for legal mistakes. Trial courts: superior, felonies, divorce, land. State. Juvenile. Probate, wills, marriage licenses. And magistrate, warrants, small claims. Judges are chosen in nonpartisan elections — no party label on the ballot. When a seat opens early, the governor appoints a judge. Dual purpose: interpret what the laws mean, and administer justice by deciding cases fairly.

georgia/ga-modern.42924533ff56: Downtown Atlanta. Where the nineteen ninety-six Games and two mayors reshaped a city. Maynard Jackson and Andrew Young helped turn Atlanta into an international city. Maynard Jackson was mayor from nineteen seventy-four, and Andrew Young from nineteen eighty-two to nineteen ninety. Centennial Olympic Park, built for nineteen ninety-six on run-down land, is now ringed by attractions such as the Georgia Aquarium, the World of Coca-Cola and the National Center for Civil and Human Rights — tourism in action. The Carter Center, founded by Jimmy and Rosalynn Carter in nineteen eighty-two, is a few miles east.

georgia/ga-native.287fdc2db913: Sapelo Island shell rings. Huge rings of oyster and clam shells, some about three hundred feet across, built roughly four thousand years ago. Archaeologists think people gathered here for feasts — and maybe lived around the rings.
georgia/ga-native.4d67616d69e8: Stallings Island, near Augusta. A small island in the Savannah River covered with shells left by Archaic people. Pottery made here about four thousand five hundred years ago, tempered with Spanish moss or palmetto fibers, is among the oldest in North America.
georgia/ga-native.8741ec7063ee: Etowah Mounds, Cartersville. A fifty-four-acre town with six mounds, a plaza and a defensive ditch and palisade; several thousand people lived here. The sixty-three-foot mound probably held the chief’s or priest’s house. Famous finds include a pair of painted marble statues and copper plates showing bird-like dancers. Many historians think this was Itaba, a town de Soto passed in August fifteen forty.
georgia/ga-native.4f79774289d1: Yamacraw, Savannah. A small Creek band led by Tomochichi lived on Yamacraw Bluff. In seventeen thirty-three Tomochichi agreed to let Oglethorpe’s colonists settle here — the founding of Savannah.
georgia/ga-native.bf2cfe91aad9: Santa Catalina de Guale, Saint Catherines Island. The chief Spanish mission among the Guale people on the Georgia coast. Burned in the Guale revolt of fifteen ninety-seven, rebuilt by Franciscans in sixteen oh five, abandoned after raids in sixteen eighty. Archaeologists rediscovered the lost mission in the nineteen eighties.
georgia/ga-native.200c8e9cec92: Ichisi, near Macon. De Soto’s army reached the chiefdom of Ichisi in late March fifteen forty; its center is thought to be the Lamar mound site at Macon. From here he pushed northeast to Ocute on the Oconee River.
georgia/ga-native.3c89d378d78b: Kolomoki Mounds. Georgia State Parks calls it the oldest and largest Woodland site in the southeastern US. Mound A is fifty-seven feet high — the largest Woodland platform mound in eastern North America. Smaller burial mounds held people buried with pottery and other offerings.
georgia/ga-native.8b397bb63c28: Rock Eagle effigy mound. A giant bird shape made of white quartz rocks: about one hundred two feet from head to tail and one hundred twenty feet from wingtip to wingtip. No one knows exactly when or why it was built — it is best seen from the tower beside it.
georgia/ga-native.33cbb6b18aa7: Coosa, Little Egypt site. The main town of Coosa, a chiefdom whose power stretched hundreds of miles into Tennessee and Alabama. De Soto arrived on July sixteenth, fifteen forty, and took the chief hostage to force help. The site now lies under Carters Lake.
georgia/ga-native.4394eda199fc: Ocmulgee Mounds, Macon. A Clovis point found here shows Paleo hunters passed through more than twelve thousand years ago. About A D nine hundred Mississippian farmers built a town here; the Great Temple Mound stands fifty-five feet tall. The Earth Lodge, a round council chamber, has an original floor radiocarbon-dated to about A D ten fifteen — with seats for about fifty people.

georgia/ga-reconstruction.d592f0127922: Atlanta. Railroad hub, “capital of the New South”. The eighteen sixty-seven to eighteen sixty-eight convention met here and moved the capital from Milledgeville to Atlanta. Home of the International Cotton Exposition, eighteen eighty-one, and the Cotton States Exposition, eighteen ninety-five. Black colleges grew here: Atlanta University, Morehouse, Spelman, Clark. W. E. B. Du Bois taught at Atlanta University, eighteen ninety-seven to nineteen ten. Site of the nineteen oh six race massacre and the nineteen thirteen Leo Frank trial.
georgia/ga-reconstruction.0a9fd557e81d: Memory hint: nineteen thirteen trial, nineteen fifteen commutation, nineteen fifteen lynching, nineteen eighty-six pardon.
georgia/ga-reconstruction.e3ce91ee4484: Memory hint: Atlanta rose from the ashes: rails. Capital, eighteen sixty-eight. Expositions, eighteen eighty-one, eighteen ninety-five.
georgia/ga-reconstruction.6c802ccffe2e: Don’t mix up: The eighteen eighty-one exposition was the International Cotton Exposition; Booker T. Washington spoke at the eighteen ninety-five Cotton States Exposition.
georgia/ga-reconstruction.00ec72141133: Don’t mix up: The nineteen eighty-six pardon did not rule on guilt; it said Georgia failed to protect Frank and give him justice.
georgia/ga-reconstruction.e7d2dbdbd7bb: Marietta. Antisemitism and mob violence. Mary Phagan, the thirteen-year-old murder victim, was from Marietta. In August nineteen fifteen a mob took Leo Frank from the Milledgeville prison and lynched him near Marietta. Months later the Ku Klux Klan was refounded on nearby Stone Mountain; Jewish Georgians felt the danger for years.

georgia/ga-removal.2e1edfb834ac: June to September eighteen thirty-eight. Camps near Fort Cass, Charleston, Tennessee. Families wait through a hot, dry summer in crowded camps, and disease spreads. John Ross wins permission for the Cherokee to manage their own removal, so most groups wait until fall to leave. A few groups go by river in June, blue dashed line.
georgia/ga-removal.25962b73fcc5: Indian Springs, eighteen twenty-five. Washington, eighteen twenty-six to eighteen twenty-seven. In eighteen twenty-five William McIntosh signed away the last Creek land in Georgia; Creek law enforcers executed him. The eighteen twenty-six Treaty of Washington replaced his treaty, and a final eighteen twenty-seven agreement took the last strip. Given out in the eighteen twenty-seven lottery. No Creek land was left in Georgia.
georgia/ga-removal.6ccc0243523e: October eighteen thirty-eight. Nashville, Tennessee. About a dozen groups of roughly one thousand people each set out on the northern route, with wagons, on horseback and on foot.
georgia/ga-removal.1962f603b59f: Treaty of the Creek Agency, eighteen eighteen. The Creek ceded land near the heads of the Ocmulgee and Apalachee rivers. It became Gwinnett and Walton counties. Given out in the eighteen twenty lottery.
georgia/ga-removal.ed6193ae1bc9: Cherokee treaties of eighteen seventeen and eighteen nineteen. The Cherokee ceded land in the northeast mountains. It became Habersham, Hall and Rabun counties. Given out in the eighteen twenty lottery.
georgia/ga-removal.c52b89dc2c2b: January to March eighteen thirty-nine. Indian Territory, Tahlequah, Oklahoma. The last groups arrive in March eighteen thirty-nine. The Cherokee begin rebuilding their nation, with Tahlequah as its capital.
georgia/ga-removal.ceb7341bccbc: January to February eighteen thirty-nine. Springfield, Missouri. The groups push west across the Missouri Ozarks in the middle of winter.
georgia/ga-removal.73c69d69a5b2: December eighteen thirty-eight to January eighteen thirty-nine. The Mississippi River crossing. Ice on the Mississippi stops the crossing. Thousands wait for weeks in freezing weather in southern Illinois, and many die.
georgia/ga-removal.2fb3a235c393: May eighteen thirty-eight. New Echota, Georgia, Fort Wool. Soldiers go from farm to farm gathering Cherokee families, often with no time to pack. Families are held in stockades such as Fort Wool, here at the former Cherokee capital.
georgia/ga-removal.313ebc0f5692: Treaties of Augusta, seventeen eighty-three. New York, seventeen ninety. In seventeen eighty-three a few Creek leaders signed away land up to the Oconee River; most Creek rejected it and years of fighting followed. In seventeen ninety Creek leader Alexander McGillivray accepted the Oconee line in the Treaty of New York. The Cherokee also gave up land in the northeast in seventeen eighty-three, Franklin County. Georgia gave this land out as headrights.
georgia/ga-removal.19b528aaddd9: Treaty of Fort Jackson, eighteen fourteen. After the Creek War, eighteen thirteen to eighteen fourteen, General Andrew Jackson forced the Creek Nation to give up about twenty-three million acres in Alabama and south Georgia. Even Creek who had fought on the US side lost land. Georgia gave the land out in the eighteen twenty lottery.
georgia/ga-removal.d6b75cfc1326: November eighteen thirty-eight. Hopkinsville, Kentucky. Cherokee leaders White Path and Fly Smith died near here. A park marks their graves today.
georgia/ga-removal.03fdea10df1f: Late eighteen thirty-eight. Golconda, Illinois — the Ohio River. The groups cross the Ohio River by ferry.
georgia/ga-removal.4c6f4923b271: Treaties of Fort Wilkinson, eighteen oh two, and Washington, eighteen oh five. The Creek ceded land between the Oconee and Ocmulgee rivers. Georgia gave it out in its first land lottery, eighteen oh five. Milledgeville, the next capital, was laid out here in eighteen oh three.
georgia/ga-removal.3b2049571118: Treaty of Augusta, seventeen sixty-three. After the French and Indian War, Creek and Cherokee leaders met British officials at Augusta. They ceded land between the Savannah and Ogeechee rivers and a coastal strip south to the Saint Marys River. Settlers poured into the new backcountry.
georgia/ga-removal.604ac8f124fc: Treaty of Augusta, seventeen seventy-three, “New Purchase”. Cherokee and Creek leaders gave up about two million acres north of the Little River. The land paid off debts that Native hunters owed to British traders. It became Wilkes County — the Kettle Creek country of the Revolution.
georgia/ga-removal.cda2604b8c09: Treaty of New Echota, eighteen thirty-five. Georgia surveyed the Cherokee Nation and gave it away in the eighteen thirty-two land and gold lotteries — while Cherokee families still lived there. In eighteen thirty-five a small “Treaty Party” signed it away without the consent of the elected Cherokee government. In eighteen thirty-eight the US Army forced the Cherokee out: the Trail of Tears.
georgia/ga-removal.2f4be526347c: Agreement with Tomochichi and the Lower Creek, seventeen thirty-three. Tomochichi, leader of the Yamacraw, welcomed James Oglethorpe at Yamacraw Bluff. Lower Creek leaders agreed to English settlement on the coast between the Savannah and Altamaha rivers. The Trustees, and later the King, granted this land to colonists.

georgia/ga-revolution.57d9256d7683: Athens. The first state-chartered public university. The legislature chartered the University of Georgia on January twenty-seventh, seventeen eighty-five. Abraham Baldwin, who wrote the charter, was its first president. Classes began in eighteen oh one at Franklin College on six hundred thirty-three acres given by John Milledge. The town was named Athens after the ancient Greek center of learning.
georgia/ga-revolution.7f561de4c06a: Brier Creek. A Patriot defeat after Kettle Creek. Just weeks after Kettle Creek, British troops surprised a Patriot army camped at Brier Creek. Hundreds of Patriots were killed, captured or drowned trying to escape across the creek and swamps. The defeat let the British keep their hold on most of Georgia through seventeen seventy-nine.
georgia/ga-revolution.7ea727d69214: Kettle Creek. Georgia’s great Patriot victory. About seven hundred Loyalists under Colonel John Boyd were marching to join the British at Augusta. About four hundred Patriot militia under Andrew Pickens, John Dooly and Elijah Clarke surprised their camp in Wilkes County. Boyd was mortally wounded; casualties were about twenty-one Patriots and one hundred fifteen Loyalists, estimates. Austin Dabney, a free Black artilleryman, was badly wounded here and later honored by the state.
georgia/ga-revolution.e4d469654a7d: Don’t mix up: UGA was chartered in seventeen eighty-five but didn’t hold classes until eighteen oh one.
georgia/ga-revolution.ee11a0d3d19d: Savannah. Liberty Boys, a British capture and a failed siege. Liberty Boys met at Tondee’s Tavern in seventeen seventy-four to seventeen seventy-five to protest British laws. The Declaration of Independence was read aloud here on August tenth, seventeen seventy-six. British troops captured Savannah on December twenty-ninth, seventeen seventy-eight, and held it until July seventeen eighty-two. On October ninth, seventeen seventy-nine, a French-American attack on the British lines failed; Casimir Pulaski was mortally wounded.
georgia/ga-revolution.fbc8eb1a8465: Philadelphia. The first paper mill in North America opened near here in sixteen ninety — almost one thousand six hundred years after Cai Lun. In seventeen seventy-six the Declaration of Independence was signed here and printed with movable type.
georgia/ga-revolution.cee6067e6d0f: Augusta. Changed hands again and again. The British occupied Augusta in early seventeen seventy-nine, left, and returned in seventeen eighty. Elijah Clarke attacked it in September seventeen eighty but had to retreat. On June fifth, seventeen eighty-one, Patriots under Pickens, Clarke and Henry Lee forced the British to surrender Augusta. Georgia’s government met here from seventeen eighty-six until the capital moved to Louisville in seventeen ninety-six.
georgia/ga-revolution.5b4fd3c4455b: Midway and Sunbury. Georgia’s most eager Patriots. Saint John’s Parish sent Dr. Lyman Hall to the Continental Congress in seventeen seventy-five, before the rest of Georgia joined. Lyman Hall and Button Gwinnett both had ties to this parish. At Fort Morris in Sunbury, November seventeen seventy-eight, Colonel John McIntosh answered a British demand to surrender: “Come and take it!” Liberty County, created in seventeen seventy-seven, got its name from the parish’s Patriot spirit.
georgia/ga-revolution.1aa2a2bd0586: Milledgeville. The capital keeps moving west. Laid out as the new capital in eighteen oh three on land recently ceded by the Creek. Named for Governor John Milledge. The legislature first met here in eighteen oh seven; it stayed the capital until eighteen sixty-eight, when Atlanta took over.
georgia/ga-revolution.f4f06b32e2e2: Louisville. A town built to be the capital. Planned as a new capital closer to the center of the settled land. Named for King Louis the Sixteenth of France, who had helped the Americans win the war. In seventeen ninety-six the papers of the Yazoo land sale were burned here in public.

math/angles.f603a0b4da57: Do the same inside a right angle. Now the two parts always add to ninety degrees. Two angles that add to ninety degrees are called complementary.
math/angles.db5517fb7189: One angle is enough! Here one angle is one hundred fifteen degrees. Its vertical angle is also one hundred fifteen degrees. Its neighbours on the line are — one hundred eighty degrees minus one hundred fifteen degrees equals sixty-five degrees — and the bottom crossing copies the top. All eight angles from one.
math/angles.35b315ba8d56: Split a straight angle with a ray. However the ray turns, the two angles always fill the half turn, so they add to one hundred eighty degrees. Two angles that add to one hundred eighty degrees are called supplementary.
math/angles.28ce977f3677: Common mix-up: Complementary angles add to ninety degrees, supplementary to one hundred eighty degrees, C comes before S, just as ninety comes before one hundred eighty. And corresponding or alternate interior angles are equal only when the two lines are parallel.
math/angles.0cce647d8a7e: Two lines cross and make four angles. Turn one line: the angles change, but opposite angles always match. Why? a plus b equals one hundred eighty degrees and b plus c equals one hundred eighty degrees, so a equals c. Opposite angles like these are vertical angles, and they are always equal.
math/angles.e453f235ccaa: Now a triangle. Its angles measure about sixty-three degrees, fifty-one degrees and sixty-six degrees. Tear off the three corners and put them side by side: together they make a straight line, one hundred eighty degrees.
math/angles.9afe5917b5c8: An angle measures how far something turns. Spin the yellow ray: a quarter turn is ninety degrees, a right angle, a half turn is one hundred eighty degrees, a straight angle, and a full turn is three hundred sixty degrees.
math/angles.b10b37c71f16: Use it: a triangle has angles of forty-seven degrees and sixty-eight degrees. The third angle is — x equals one hundred eighty degrees minus forty-seven degrees minus sixty-eight degrees equals sixty-five degrees.
math/angles.8605c4f108a4: Why always? Draw a line through the top corner, parallel to the bottom side. The Z shapes are alternate interior angles, so copies of the two bottom angles fit along that line beside the top angle. A straight line is one hundred eighty degrees, so a plus b plus c equals one hundred eighty degrees in every triangle.

math/area.c65037c561bb: A triangle seems harder. The trick: take a second copy, turn it halfway around and attach it. Two identical triangles make a parallelogram with area b h, so one triangle has half: A equals one half times b h equals one half times five times three equals seven point five.
math/area.b462c12828a2: Now push the top sideways to make a parallelogram. Unit squares no longer fit neatly. The base is still five, and the height, measured straight up from the base, is still three, even though the slanted side got longer.

math/area.e59db2295e79: Every formula came from the same idea: rearrange the shape into one you already know. Rectangles and parallelograms: b h. Triangles: half a parallelogram. Trapezoids: half a parallelogram with base b one plus b two.
math/area.e8ee03485ea3: Common mix-up: The height is measured straight up, perpendicular to the base, not along the slanted side! And the triangle and trapezoid formulas both have a one half because each is half of a parallelogram.
math/area.91586d957797: Now slide the top corner left and right, parallel to the base. The triangle changes shape, even leaning outside its base, but the base and height stay the same, so the area never changes: still seven point five.
math/area.05d1e20bbaad: Area counts how many unit squares it takes to cover a shape. This rectangle has three rows of five squares, so its area is — five times three equals fifteen square units.

math/exponents.55eb938a5c1e: Drag the slider: each whole step makes the field of view ten times wider or narrower. Zoom from a single atom to the Milky Way. The circles compare approximate sizes and distances using the same scale.
math/exponents.9eeb78dec2f3: Common mix-up: three to the fourth is not three times four equals twelve; it is three times three times three times three equals eighty-one. When you multiply powers of the same base you ADD the exponents, two cubed, two to the fourth equals two to the seventh, you don’t multiply them. A negative exponent on a nonzero base gives the reciprocal of the corresponding positive power, two to the power of minus three equals one eighth.
math/exponents.bd998ec895fb: Not equal to ten to the sixth
math/exponents.e9ac381c2d91: Question one of three. Simplify three squared divided by three to the fifth.
math/exponents.c8c07bdf7aa6: A transfer sends nine point six times ten to the eighth bytes at a steady rate of three point two times ten to the fifth bytes per second. How long does it take? Divide the size by the transfer rate.
math/exponents.009261f529b4: Each step left lowers the exponent by one and divides the value by the base. Follow the pattern through zero using the base you chose above.
math/exponents.fbd356b9e08f: Question one of two. In three to the fourth, how many factors are three?
math/exponents.af6cd981b544: two x to the power of eight
math/exponents.0102b21bccd9: A calculator may use E for “times ten raised to”. For example, one point five six E nine means one point five six times ten to the ninth.
math/exponents.4197c9bb0d45: Two files occupy four point eight times ten to the sixth bytes and seven point five times ten to the fifth bytes. How many bytes do they occupy together? Add the two file sizes. Rewrite the second size using the same power of ten.
math/exponents.c483ab186b06: One piece of thin wire is zero point zero zero zero three two meters long and another is eight times ten to the power of minus five meters long. Find the combined length.
math/exponents.138af8a8ee9f: x to the power of eight
math/exponents.40c310cc8634: Supports Georgia eight dot N R dot two, properties of integer exponents; using scientific notation to represent, estimate, compare and compute with very large and very small numbers. Before steps three to five, have students expand and count the factors themselves, then watch the animation to check. Step six’s “divide by ten each time” pattern is the most natural route to ten to the zero power equals one and negative exponents.
math/exponents.051412b1af7f: Use the exponent rules to decide whether each expression equals one million.
math/exponents.f4dcb0d08bcc: For higher powers, a bar chart can show how the numbers grow: two to the power of five equals two times two times two times two times two equals thirty-two. Each extra factor of two doubles the result.
math/exponents.5fc7d56432c5: Equal to ten to the sixth or not?
math/exponents.b79a2a65c919: A power of a power: two cubed, all squared means two groups of two cubed. That is three times two equals six twos: two cubed, all squared equals two to the power of the quantity three times two equals two to the power of six equals sixty-four. Multiply the exponents.
math/exponents.c41d571336a1: A transfer sends nine point six times ten to the eighth bytes at a steady rate of three point two times ten to the fifth bytes per second. How long does it take?
math/exponents.7981f0c7ea0d: A camera saves two thousand four hundred images, each using six point five times ten to the fifth bytes. How much storage do they need?
math/exponents.d0d4ee8f06d2: Question one of twelve. One sheet is eight times ten to the power of minus five meters thick. How thick is a stack of four times ten squared sheets?
math/exponents.b1bae0fd81fa: Given: two files take up three point six times ten to the sixth bytes and nine times ten to the fifth bytes. The transfer rate is one point five times ten to the fifth bytes per second.
math/exponents.c331899ecc37: Now follow a pattern. Going down the list, the exponent drops by one and the value is divided by ten. Keep going past ten to the power of one: next comes ten to the power of zero equals one, then ten to the power of negative one equals one over ten, then ten to the power of negative two equals one over one hundred.
math/exponents.3376397b35c2: Multiply two cubed times two to the power of four. Write out the factors: three twos and four twos. Together that is seven twos, so two cubed times two to the power of four equals two to the power of the quantity three plus four equals two to the power of seven. Same base: add the exponents.
math/exponents.70ffc4b611ef: A folder uses six point two times ten to the sixth bytes. You delete a file of eight times ten to the fifth bytes. How much space do the remaining files use?
math/exponents.0d04c2b3a7c4: Two files occupy four point eight times ten to the sixth bytes and seven point five times ten to the fifth bytes. How many bytes do they occupy together?
math/exponents.a0b7bf181c2e: Two files occupy four point eight times ten to the sixth bytes and seven point five times ten to the fifth bytes. How many bytes do they occupy together? Add the two file sizes. Rewrite the second size using the same power of ten. Factor out the shared power of ten. Add the coefficients. The result is in scientific notation.
math/exponents.7ebf94ba4ac2: Two files occupy four point eight times ten to the sixth bytes and seven point five times ten to the fifth bytes. How many bytes do they occupy together? Add the two file sizes. Rewrite the second size using the same power of ten. Factor out the shared power of ten.
math/exponents.367cc4ee988f: Answer: the combined length is four times ten to the power of minus four meters.
math/exponents.ebddb85c8eaa: Scientific notation tames huge numbers. The Sun is about one hundred fifty million kilometers away. Hop the decimal point left until just one nonzero digit is in front of it: eight hops, so the distance is one point five times ten to the power of eight kilometers.
math/exponents.a27e65bf4b2c: Worked example: the Sun is about one point five times ten to the power of eight kilometers from Earth and the Moon is about three point eight times ten to the power of five kilometers from Earth. About how many Earth-Moon distances fit into one Earth-Sun distance? Divide the coefficients and subtract the exponents: one point five over three point eight, times ten to the power of the quantity eight minus five is about zero point four times ten cubed equals four hundred. About four hundred times!
math/exponents.1b23bdaea007: Question one of three. A calculator returns two point five E minus four for a length in meters. Which length is that?
math/exponents.88b557a46d7d: Equal to ten to the sixth
math/exponents.7d2480b28324: In round one, you share a video with two friends. At every round, each person from the previous round shares it with two more people. If every share reaches a different new viewer, how many new viewers are there in round twenty? A positive whole-number exponent counts copies of the base used as factors.
math/exponents.99f513fa3386: In the Rule lab, set the quotient to m equals n and then m is less than n and discuss a to the zero power and a to the power of negative n.
math/exponents.1b5e7334138f: A folder uses six point two times ten to the sixth bytes. You delete a file of eight times ten to the fifth bytes. How much space do the remaining files use? Subtract the deleted file size.
math/exponents.d03f65d1925a: A camera saves two thousand four hundred images, each using six point five times ten to the fifth bytes. How much storage do they need? Multiply one image’s size by the number of images.
math/exponents.a8495c0f6eb9: A positive integer exponent counts how many copies of the base are multiplied. A three-by-three square has three times three equals three squared equals nine tiles; a three-by-three-by-three cube has three times three times three equals three cubed equals twenty-seven blocks. In three to the power of four, three is the base and four is the exponent.
math/exponents.646cad69d77c: So for any nonzero base: a to the power of zero equals one and a to the power of negative n equals one over a to the power of n. The quotient rule agrees: two cubed over two cubed equals two to the power of the quantity three minus three equals two to the power of zero, and any nonzero number divided by itself is one. Example: two to the power of negative three equals one over two cubed equals one over eight.
math/exponents.67f0aa9cf880: Divide two to the power of six over two squared. Each two on the bottom cancels one two on top. Four twos survive: two to the power of six over two squared equals two to the power of the quantity six minus two equals two to the power of four equals sixteen. Same base: subtract the exponents.
math/exponents.442e699ac704: x to the power of fifteen
math/exponents.de40f750467a: Question one of two. A ten to the power of minus six meter view gets ten times wider. What is its new width?
math/exponents.eb622b08ee55: Two files occupy four point eight times ten to the sixth bytes and seven point five times ten to the fifth bytes. How many bytes do they occupy together? Add the two file sizes.
math/exponents.6c52aee60d8a: Tiny numbers work the same way in reverse. A human hair is about zero point zero zero zero zero seven meters thick. Hop the point right five places to land after the seven: seven times ten to the power of negative five meters. Hops to the right give a negative exponent.

math/expressions.79640367fc1f: Let a blue bar stand for x and a small yellow square stand for one. Words turn into pictures, and pictures into expressions: “three more than a number” is x plus three; “triple a number” is three x, which means three times x.
math/expressions.e7d75190c4e6: Common mix-up: three times the quantity x plus two is NOT three x plus two! The three multiplies every term inside, so it is three x plus six. And x plus three can't be combined into three x: a bar and a square are not like terms.
math/expressions.64ca4874a89b: Memory hint: “The number outside shakes hands with everyone inside”: a shakes hands with b, then with c, giving a b plus a c.
math/expressions.0aa2ce90e093: Once we know what is in the box, we can evaluate. If x equals four, every bar is really four squares long. Count: four, eight, twelve, then thirteen, fourteen. So three x plus two equals three times four plus two equals fourteen.
math/expressions.fcbf003102e5: Now an area picture. A rectangle three tall and six wide holds three times six equals eighteen squares. Cut it into two pieces, three times four equals twelve and three times two equals six: together still eighteen. So three times the quantity four plus two equals three times four plus three times two.
math/expressions.8cea90daaab8: Now replace the four with an unknown length x. The blue piece becomes three x-bars, area three x; the yellow piece is still six. So three times the quantity x plus two equals three x plus six, whatever x is.
math/expressions.51aab55e4e51: Imagine a box holding some marbles. We don’t know how many, and the number could change: three, seven, twelve … So we give the box a name, a letter such as x. That letter is a variable.
math/expressions.be84948185e2: Factoring runs it backwards. Take the tiles of four x plus eight and arrange them into a rectangle with identical rows. It is four tall and x plus two wide, so four x plus eight equals four times the quantity x plus two.
math/expressions.b9114834844c: Worked example: simplify two times the quantity three x plus one, plus four x. Distribute the two: six x plus two plus four x. Combine like terms: ten x plus two. Check with x equals one: both forms give twelve.
math/expressions.55a177ef3454: Like terms are tiles with the same shape. In two x plus three plus x plus one, slide the bars together and the squares together: three x plus four. A bar and a square can never merge, because x and one are different sizes.

math/factoring.eaa2a68ccd1d: The four pieces fill a square of side a plus b. Both a b rectangles belong in the middle term.
math/factoring.88bad3cb215b: Set the number of unit spaces on each side. Pick a tile and tap a matching space. Tap a placed tile to take it back. The board draws x as two units long.
math/factoring.81fcbaa3f57a: Factor out the shared bracket. Expanding gives six x squared plus thirteen x plus six after combining like terms.
math/factoring.f7603fa24579: The two pieces now form a rectangle with sides a plus b and a minus b.
math/factoring.49afcfb9d516: The ends are squares of two x and five. Check that the middle is minus two times two x times five.
math/factoring.0617cd77b0a3: The coefficients share a factor of three. Both terms contain x, so the greatest common factor is three x.
math/factoring.c36efef5da1b: Factor three x from the first group and two from the second. Now two x plus three is a common factor.
math/factoring.a0d41652433b: Multiply every term in one factor by every term in the other, then combine like terms. The drawing uses x equals two and the absolute values of the coefficients for its lengths. Stripes mark products with negative coefficients.
math/factoring.b775d4747f77: Read the rows as x plus m and x plus n. To factor x squared plus p x plus q this way, the integers m and n must add to p and multiply to q.
math/factoring.2538e77694db: Identify the two squares and their bases: three x and four.

math/fractals.56add850d2a8: Each point is a complex number c, which has two coordinates. Start at zero and keep squaring the result and adding the same c. The values of c whose results stay within some fixed distance of zero forever make up the Mandelbrot set. Colors show how quickly points escape, and dark pixels show points that haven’t escaped within the drawing’s step limit.
math/fractals.a668976fc959: Build a tiny equilateral triangle outward on the middle third of each edge and erase its base. One edge becomes four edges a third as long, so the perimeter multiplies by four over three each round and grows without bound. After the first round, each round adds four ninths as much area as the previous round added, and the total area approaches one point six times the starting area.
math/fractals.b12889f2d39a: The trunk is level one. Each extra level grows two shorter branches from every tip in the previous level. The angle tells how far each new branch turns from the old branch’s direction, and the length ratio compares one new branch with the branch it grew from.

math/fraction-division.7bbd5faa88e9: Why does this work? Measure everything in the same unit, thirds. Three is nine over three and a piece is two over three. How many twos fit in nine? Nine over three, divided by two over three, equals nine divided by two equals four and a half. Same denominator, so just divide the numerators.
math/fraction-division.1f31de6aaf48: What if it does not fit evenly? In three divided by two thirds, four pieces fit and one third is left over. That leftover is half a piece, so the answer is four and a half, not four and a third.
math/fraction-division.b7e1ab0115e0: Common mix-up: Measure the leftover in PIECES, not in wholes. In three divided by two thirds, four pieces fit and one third is left; that one third is half a piece, so the answer is four and a half, not four and a third. And flip only the divisor, the second fraction, never the first one!
math/fraction-division.3bf6089bfbd2: Now four divided by two thirds. First cut every whole into thirds: twelve thirds in all. Each yellow piece is two thirds long, so twelve divided by two equals six pieces fit.
math/fraction-division.c955c7f93ad0: Another way to see it: dividing by two over three is two moves. How many thirds? Multiply by three, so three becomes nine thirds. How many groups of two thirds? Divide by two. Together: times three over two, the reciprocal of two over three.
math/fraction-division.2d3b22653eda: Worked example: you have two and a half cups of rice and one serving is three quarters of a cup. Five over two, divided by three over four, equals five over two, times four over three, equals twenty over six equals three and a third: three full servings and a third of another.
math/fraction-division.9b37935f6272: Same question with a fraction: four divided by one half, how many halves fit in four? Every whole holds two halves, so four wholes hold eight. Dividing by one half gives more, not less!
math/fraction-division.a46e59f053fc: Start with whole numbers. Six divided by two asks: how many twos fit in six? Lay pieces of length two under a bar of length six. Three fit, so six divided by two equals three.
math/fraction-division.6ea600202035: When the piece is bigger than what you have, not even one piece fits. One half divided by three quarters: the half fills only two of the three quarters in a piece, so the answer is one half times four thirds equals two thirds of a piece.

math/functions.730aa9ece4fd: Now plot each input-output pair from our machine as a point, x, y. They line up! Inputs in between work too: “two point five maps to six” lands on the same line. The graph is a picture of the whole function.
math/functions.783ee11879ec: Compare y equals x squared. Its outputs zero, one, four, nine jump by plus one, plus three, plus five: the rate of change keeps growing, so the graph bends. That is a nonlinear function. Equal steps in x with equal jumps in y means linear.
math/functions.9092bbecd864: Name it: a function gives each input exactly one output. For y equals two x plus one, every step of one to the right goes up two: the rate of change is two, and the starting value, at x equals zero, is one. A constant rate makes a straight line: a linear function.
math/functions.a14950c5e0c2: Not every rule is a function. "Give me a number whose square is x" sends four to both two and minus two: one input, two outputs, so it is NOT a function. But two inputs sharing one output, like negative two, all squared equals two squared equals four, is perfectly fine.
math/functions.6e1da518dc86: Common mix-up: Two different inputs sharing the same output is fine, two and minus two both square to four, and it is still a function. What is NOT allowed is one input with two or more different outputs.
math/functions.cf9db2f1e416: Meet a machine. Whatever number you drop in, it doubles it and then adds one. Drop in three… out comes seven.
math/functions.e7138db7d164: Worked example: a plant is three, five, seven, nine centimeters tall in weeks zero to three. It grows plus two centimeters each week, rate of change two, starting at three centimeters, so h equals two w plus three. In week ten: h equals two times ten plus three equals twenty-three centimeters.
math/functions.40e74d813bf2: Graphs tell stories. Here distance from home is a function of time: walking away, rising, stopped to chat, flat, rate zero, running, steeper equals faster, then walking home, falling, negative rate.

math/integers.5c3b631c888e: At three p.m. it is six degrees Celsius. Overnight the air cools to zero degrees Celsius, and keeps falling. By dawn it is four degrees below zero. We write that as minus four degrees Celsius: a negative number.
math/integers.64772ebba59d: The three rules in one place. Opposites: a and negative a are the same distance from zero. Absolute value: the absolute value of a is that distance, so the absolute value of a equals the absolute value of negative a. Order: a is less than b exactly when a is to the left of b.
math/integers.fb516a2facb9: Watch out: negative six has the larger absolute value, because it is farther from zero. But it is the smaller number. Being farther left always means smaller, no matter how far from zero.
math/integers.ba4003578fb0: On a number line, numbers get greater as you move right. Negative two is to the right of negative six, so negative two is greater than negative six. Think temperature: minus two degrees Celsius is warmer than minus six degrees Celsius.
math/integers.a01b1c2bbe85: Worked example: order negative five, three, negative one, zero, negative seven, six from least to greatest. Drop each number onto the line, then read from left to right: negative seven is less than negative five is less than negative one is less than zero is less than three is less than six.
math/integers.ffbe2766d48e: The absolute value of a is a number’s distance from zero. Negative five is five steps from zero, so the absolute value of negative five equals five; and the absolute value of five equals five too. A distance is never negative.
math/integers.36cbf21993de: Common mix-up: minus six looks like it has the “bigger number”, but it is LESS than minus two: on a number line, farther left means smaller. Minus six has the larger absolute value, which only means it is farther from zero, not that it is greater.
math/integers.12fd38150c7e: Turn the vertical scale on its side and you get a number line that keeps going left of zero. Positive numbers are to the right of zero, negative numbers to the left, and zero itself is neither.
math/integers.aee68b499e1a: Negative numbers describe the opposite direction from a zero point. Sea level is zero: a bird three meters above it is at plus three, a fish four meters below it is at negative four. Money works the same way: owing five dollars is negative five.
math/integers.afb0b220fc90: Three and negative three are the same distance from zero, on opposite sides. They are opposites: fold the line at zero and one lands on the other. The opposite of negative three is the negative of negative three, equals three.

math/inverse-proportion.eb2f32bc3299: In direct proportion, the ratio y over x is constant for nonzero x, and the full graph is a line through the origin. In inverse proportion, the product x y is constant and the graph is a hyperbola. Double a positive x and the direct output doubles while the inverse output halves.
math/inverse-proportion.8fdab4df9d91: Distance equals average speed multiplied by travel time. With distance fixed at one hundred twenty kilometers, twice the average speed takes half the time.
math/inverse-proportion.069a2a75c48a: Set the two expressions equal. Since x is not equal to zero, you can multiply both sides by x. Substitute each valid x into either original equation to find y.
math/inverse-proportion.5e9ba0d781d8: Average pressure is perpendicular force divided by contact area. With force fixed at six hundred newtons, doubling the contact area halves the average pressure.
math/inverse-proportion.f2f346f9ee2b: If y equals k over x, where k is a fixed nonzero number and x is not equal to zero, then y varies inversely with x. The graph is a hyperbola. Its two branches get closer to the axes without touching them. The perpendiculars from P to the axes form a rectangle with side lengths the absolute value of x and the absolute value of y, so its area is the absolute value of x y equals the absolute value of k. To see whether y rises or falls as x increases, look at one branch at a time.

math/linear-functions.5920d4dc6bb2: The graph ends at eight minutes, when the tank reaches zero liters.
math/linear-functions.6dc89fbb4579: Use the point minus two comma seven in y equals k x plus b. Seven equals three plus b. b equals four
math/linear-functions.9f0aaf3150a0: To graph y equals x plus two, substitute x equals zero. This gives y equals two, so plot, zero, two.
math/linear-functions.1cd08422476c: A line through quadrants two and four falls, so a minus two less than zero, a less than two.
math/linear-functions.46661f2ea939: Falls. Quadrants two and four. Marked points: zero, zero and one, negative one.
math/linear-functions.71baeb6e82f1: Write point-slope form. y minus one equals negative three halves times the quantity x minus two
math/linear-functions.4aef1386e4d1: Answer. y equals two x minus one. Check that x equals three gives y equals five.

math/negative-operations.fea6367f222b: Same trick for three minus negative two: add two zero pairs, then take away two red chips: five yellow remain. Taking away negative two gives the same result as adding plus two. Subtracting is adding the opposite: a minus b equals a plus negative b.
math/negative-operations.b1bf4e5096c7: Division undoes multiplication, so it follows the same rules. Since negative two times negative three equals six, we get six divided by negative two equals negative three. Since negative two times three equals negative six, we get negative six divided by negative two equals three. Same signs: positive; different signs: negative.
math/negative-operations.865df104e7c6: Another picture: chips. A yellow chip is plus one, a red chip is negative one, and one of each makes a zero pair: plus one plus negative one equals zero. In five plus negative three, three zero pairs vanish and two yellow chips remain, so the answer is two.
math/negative-operations.2f40fe71b7a1: Another way to see it: multiplying by negative one flips a number to the other side of zero. Flip three once: negative three. Flip again: back to three. So negative two times negative three means stretch negative three to negative six, then flip: plus six.
math/negative-operations.efd76ac945ce: But what is negative one times negative two? “Negative one group” makes no sense, so follow the pattern. Each time the first factor goes down by one, the answer goes UP by two. Keep going past zero: two, four, six. So a negative times a negative is positive!
math/negative-operations.d178979e7105: Adding means moving along the number line. Three plus four: start at three and step four to the right, landing on seven. Adding a negative steps LEFT: three plus negative five lands on negative two.
math/negative-operations.2e30e061c238: Put it together: negative two times three minus negative five. Multiply first: three jumps of negative two reach negative six. Then subtracting negative five means adding five: walk right five to land on negative one.
math/negative-operations.a7736f0ea5d6: Multiplication counts equal groups. Three times two is three groups of two yellow chips: six. Three times negative two is three groups of two red chips: negative six. A positive times a negative is negative.
math/negative-operations.b554b22f248c: Common mix-up: “Two negatives make a positive” is a rule for multiplying and dividing only! Adding is different: minus three plus minus four equals minus seven, two negatives added get MORE negative. And minus five minus three is minus eight, not minus two: subtracting three walks three more steps left.
math/negative-operations.18957584c2ea: Subtraction means take away. Five minus two: remove two yellow chips and three are left. But two minus five? There are only two to take! Add three zero pairs, that adds zero, so the value is still two, then take away five yellow chips: three red remain, so two minus five equals negative three.

math/percents.f3b3169b3684: So a percent of a number is just a multiplication: thirty percent of eighty is thirty over one hundred times eighty equals zero point three times eighty equals twenty-four. In words: part equals percent times whole.

math/percents.938f28d2e90f: A few benchmarks are worth knowing by heart. Fifty percent is half the grid, twenty-five percent is a quarter, ten percent is one column, and one percent is a single square.
math/percents.87b8060dfe8c: A percent bar lines the whole up with one hundred percent. To find thirty percent of eighty, cut the bar into ten equal parts. Each part is ten percent, worth eighty divided by ten equals eight. Three parts make three times eight equals twenty-four.
math/percents.a2a0e8932a7a: Common mix-up: A percent is always a percent OF some whole. Going up twenty percent and then down twenty percent does not bring you back: the second twenty percent is taken of the bigger new price, one hundred, one hundred twenty, ninety-six.
math/percents.1df31c8a7995: Now work backwards: twelve is forty percent of what number? Forty percent is four parts, so one part is twelve divided by four, which equals three. One part is ten percent. The whole is ten parts: ten times three equals thirty.

math/percents.9dd3bf90a97b: Percent means "per hundred". Here are one hundred equal squares. Shade thirty-seven of them and you have shaded thirty-seven over one hundred of the grid: that is thirty-seven percent.
math/percents.cf1a69467bcf: The whole is not always one hundred. In a class of twenty, twenty-five percent walk to school. Twenty-five percent is one over four: one out of every four students. Five groups of four give five walkers.

math/probability.14552560f3b6: Flip two coins. A tree diagram lists every outcome: H H, H T, T H and T T, four equally likely outcomes. One head and one tail happens in two of them, so its probability is two over four equals one over two, not one over three.
math/probability.a530554541c3: The key ideas: every probability is between zero and one. With equally likely outcomes, P equals favourable over total. And the chance that something does not happen is one minus P: for example, the probability of not rolling a six is one minus one over six equals five over six.
math/probability.369c004b5432: A fair die has six equally likely outcomes. Three of them are even: two, four and six. So the probability of rolling an even number is three over six equals one over two. Count the favourable outcomes, then divide by all the equally likely outcomes.
math/probability.8d8c7e251c98: Common mix-up: A coin has no memory: after five heads in a row, the next flip is still one half heads. And two coins have four equally likely outcomes, H H, H T, T H, T T, not three, so "one head and one tail" has probability one half, not one third.
math/probability.36ba71a80cf2: A bag holds three red, five blue and two green marbles. P of blue equals five over ten equals one over two and P of not red equals one minus three over ten equals seven over ten. Draw two hundred times, putting the marble back each time, and expect about two hundred times one over two equals one hundred blues.
math/probability.caf692bba967: Keep flipping: one hundred, one thousand, then ten thousand times. At first the fraction of heads jumps around, but as the flips pile up it settles closer and closer to zero point five. This is the law of large numbers: with many trials, experimental probability approaches theoretical probability.
math/probability.a9846db8bb04: Probability helps us predict. Roll a die six hundred times: we expect each number about six hundred times one over six equals one hundred times. The real counts land close to one hundred, but rarely exactly on it.
math/probability.68afe681cb68: Probability measures how likely something is, on a scale from zero, impossible, to one, certain. Rolling a seven on a normal die is impossible, a coin landing heads is an even chance, one over two, and rolling a number from one to six is certain.
math/probability.a5d2015880b9: Roll two dice. A six by six table shows all thirty-six equally likely outcomes. A total of seven can happen in six ways, more than any other total, so P of seven equals six over thirty-six equals one over six. A total of two happens in only one way.
math/probability.f5b03b13c81e: Theory says heads should come up half the time. Let's really flip a coin ten times. Seven heads! The experimental probability is seven over ten equals zero point seven, not zero point five. Is the theory wrong?

math/proportional.ec90e8079753: A hiker walks at a steady pace. After one hour she has gone three kilometers, after two hours six kilometers, after three hours nine kilometers, and after four hours twelve kilometers. Let's record it in a table.
math/proportional.28ceac4ed9ca: Walk along the line in steps: every one hour to the right, the line climbs three kilometers. The point one comma three shows the unit rate: three kilometers for ONE hour. That number is the constant of proportionality, k equals three.
math/proportional.70523900847c: Compare a taxi: four dollars just to get in, then two dollars per mile. The ratios six over one, eight over two, ten over three, twelve over four keep changing, and the line starts at zero, four, not at the origin. Being a straight line is not enough: y equals two x plus four is NOT proportional.
math/proportional.8f1cb4d20c20: Table, graph and equation are three views of the same relationship: y equals three x. In general, a proportional relationship is y equals k x, where k equals y over x is the unit rate, the constant of proportionality.
math/proportional.56f7000448f2: Divide each distance by its time: three over one, six over two, nine over three, twelve over four. Every row gives the same number, three. When the ratio y over x never changes, we say y is proportional to x.
math/proportional.ff3caa1a0246: Change k and the line turns around the origin. A slower hiker gives a flatter line. Here k equals one point five. A faster one gives a steeper line. Here k equals five. Every one of them still passes through the point zero comma zero.
math/proportional.4f9cc78bde27: Try it: five pounds of rice cost seven dollars and fifty cents. Unit rate: k equals seven point five zero divided by five equals one dollar and fifty cents per pound, so y equals one point five x. Then eight pounds cost one point five times eight equals twelve dollars.
math/proportional.77e629dd2b67: Extend the line backwards. At zero hours she has walked zero kilometers, so the line passes through the origin, zero, zero. A proportional relationship always graphs as a straight line through the origin.
math/proportional.d81697efeaf5: Common mix-up: A straight line does NOT automatically mean proportional! y equals two x plus four is a straight line too, but it misses the origin and y over x keeps changing. Proportional means BOTH: a straight line AND it passes through zero, zero.

math/pythagorean.8f351d313b88: Try a three-four-five triangle and count unit squares: three squared equals nine and four squared equals sixteen. The big square holds five squared equals twenty-five, and nine plus sixteen equals twenty-five. Coincidence? Let's find out why it always works.

math/radicals.ba7a5635fb30: Split the square into a six by six grid. There are thirty-six equal squares. Each has area seventy-two divided by thirty-six equals two.
math/radicals.91a0bee66b72: The area is seventy-two, so each side has length the square root of seventy-two.
math/radicals.d4209a11f6aa: In simplest radical form, there is no denominator inside the radical and no square factor left to take out. For a positive integer radicand, check for perfect-square factors greater than one. For example, three times the square root of eight simplifies to six times the square root of two. If the radicand is a perfect square, write the whole-number result, as in the square root of forty-nine equals seven.
math/radicals.3a92d144eb92: In the real numbers, an expression of the form the square root of a, with a is greater than or equal to zero, is a square-root expression. The symbol the square root of a means the principal square root of a, the nonnegative number whose square is a. The expression a under the radical sign is the radicand.
math/radicals.39921b61205a: Enter a whole number and test a perfect-square divisor. For example, seventy-two divided by thirty-six equals two. Divide the square of area seventy-two into six rows and six columns. Each small square has area two. Count along an edge to see the length of the big square.
math/radicals.08e55e6f63b1: Lift out a copy of the bottom row. Its six lengths of the square root of two add to six times the square root of two, so the square root of seventy-two equals six times the square root of two.

math/rational-expressions.2ac6c4d4138a: In English, a rational expression is one polynomial divided by another. Its denominator cannot be an expression that is always zero. The Chinese textbook term 分式 also requires a variable in the denominator. Exclude every value that makes the original denominator zero, even after reducing.
math/rational-expressions.4c425204a224: Each bar has one shaded piece. The two pieces have different sizes. Finding a common denominator, 通分, gives the fractions equal-sized pieces. Split a half and a third into x smaller pieces each and take one small piece from each. The denominators are now two x and three x, so use six x as their least common denominator. Here six is the least common multiple of two and three.
math/rational-expressions.935fa063558e: Divide out the common factor. Divide both products by x plus three. Keep minus three excluded because the original denominator is zero there.
math/rational-expressions.33475e0d5d4e: Each bar now has six equal pieces. The shaded lengths stay the same. Finding a common denominator, 通分, gives the fractions equal-sized pieces. Split a half and a third into x smaller pieces each and take one small piece from each. The denominators are now two x and three x, so use six x as their least common denominator. Here six is the least common multiple of two and three.
math/rational-expressions.029dde235b33: A rational equation has an unknown in a denominator. Exclude values that make an original denominator zero. Multiply every term on both sides by the least common denominator, then solve the resulting equation. Substitute each candidate into the original equation. If a candidate makes a denominator zero, it is an extraneous solution, 增根.
math/rational-expressions.0b96dd363ace: Given that A can finish the job alone in six hours, how long would B take alone? Each worker keeps the same rate alone or together. Move the slider to change the time they take together.
math/rational-expressions.673e30eb28d5: The top and middle shade the same length. Move left to divide out the common factor and return to one half. Split every piece into the same number of smaller pieces. The shaded length stays the same. Multiply or divide the numerator and denominator by the same polynomial. The fraction keeps its value wherever that factor is nonzero. To reduce, 约分, divide out a common factor. Let x count the smaller pieces made from each piece of the top bar. In the diagram x is a positive integer. The equation below holds for every nonzero real x.

math/ratios.7aaba1690d3a: Stretch the tapes into a double number line: blue on top, yellow below. Each jump adds one more batch, two cups of blue and three of yellow. Any two numbers lined up vertically make the same green.
math/ratios.397c46c561a4: How much yellow goes with one cup of blue? Halve both: two to three equals one to one point five. That is the unit rate: one point five cups of yellow per cup of blue. Now any amount is easy: seven cups of blue need seven times one point five equals ten point five cups of yellow.
math/ratios.6a06752cf2b0: Need more paint? Mix a second batch: now it is four to six. A third batch gives six to nine. The amounts grow together, and the colour stays exactly the same. These are equivalent ratios.
math/ratios.89de0473dc90: Worked example: a car goes one hundred fifty miles in three hours. How far in five hours? Find the rate for one hour, one hundred fifty divided by three equals fifty miles per hour, then scale up: five times fifty equals two hundred fifty miles.
math/ratios.25c70535b8ce: In a ratio table, go from two to three, to eight to twelve by multiplying both numbers by four: same shape, same green. But adding four to both gives six to seven. Yellow is no longer one point five times blue, so the colour changes!
math/ratios.60f5755ffdac: Squeeze each row into a tape diagram: blue is two equal parts, yellow is three, so five parts in all. For fifteen cups of paint, each part is fifteen divided by five equals three cups, so we need six cups of blue and nine cups of yellow.
math/ratios.a12f90c5b175: Plot each pair as a point, blue, yellow. Equivalent ratios all land on one straight line through zero: every two steps right, three steps up. Each pair gives the same quotient three over two equals one point five, the unit rate.
math/ratios.c10940fd226d: Common mix-up: To get an equivalent ratio you must MULTIPLY or divide both numbers by the same number. Adding the same amount to both changes the relationship, and the paint changes colour. In a case like this, the ratio two to three becomes three to four.
math/ratios.30867065e1d3: Unit rates settle shopping questions. Store A sells three notebooks for seven dollars and fifty cents; store B sells five for eleven dollars. Price of one: A is seven point five zero divided by three equals two point five zero, B is eleven divided by five equals two point two zero. Store B is the better buy.
math/ratios.ca72f05f39df: Here is a recipe for green paint: two cups of blue for every three cups of yellow. A ratio compares two amounts like this. We write two to three and read it "two to three".

math/roots-irrationals.37eb1b0b5a07: A square garden has an area of twenty-five square metres. How long is each side?
math/roots-irrationals.8b6f0054d74e: Squares of whole numbers, one, four, nine, sixteen, twenty-five, and so on are called perfect squares. Their square roots are whole numbers: the sides one, two, three, four, five.
math/roots-irrationals.a34af6a041d8: The same idea works in three D. A cube with volume twenty-seven has edge three, because three times three times three equals twenty-seven. So the cube root is the cube root of twenty-seven equals three.
math/roots-irrationals.921a59712d47: Count along the bottom: five tiles, because five times five equals twenty-five. The side length is the square root of the area: the square root of twenty-five equals five, since five squared equals twenty-five.
math/roots-irrationals.20da7310018c: How long is the square root of two? Swing the diagonal down onto the number line. Since one squared equals one is less than two is less than four equals two squared, it must land between one and two.
math/roots-irrationals.60f19386b20e: Worked example: solve x squared equals forty, so x equals plus or minus the square root of forty. Since thirty-six is less than forty is less than forty-nine, the square root of forty is between six and seven, and closer to six. Check: six point three squared equals thirty-nine point six nine, so the square root of forty is about six point three.
math/roots-irrationals.bf3624328e3f: Fractions behave differently: their decimals either end, one over four equals zero point two five, or repeat, one over seven equals zero point one four two eight five seven repeating. Those are rational numbers. Numbers like the square root of two and pi cannot be written as a fraction: they are irrational.
math/roots-irrationals.5457f6d9d683: Zoom in. One point four squared equals one point nine six is a bit less than two, and one point five squared equals two point two five is more, so the square root of two is between one point four and one point five. The first decimal digit is four.
math/roots-irrationals.10f30bc7990d: Common mix-up: the square root of two is not one point four one or even one point four one four: those are only approximations, and its decimal never ends. Also, a square root is not "divide by two": the square root of sixteen equals four, not eight. The equation x squared equals sixteen has two solutions, x equals plus or minus four, but the symbol the square root of sixteen means only the positive one.
math/roots-irrationals.0acc31ef5286: Now a puzzle: which square has area two? Cut two unit squares along their diagonals and slide two halves down. The four pieces form a tilted square of area two, so its side is the square root of two: the diagonal of a unit square.
math/roots-irrationals.2d089ebea93a: Keep zooming: one point four one, then one point four one four, … Every zoom reveals one more digit, and it never stops: the square root of two equals one point four one four two one three five six and so on. The digits never end and never settle into a repeating pattern.
