ushistory/us-civilrights.2785c0e336f7: Greensboro sit-ins. February first, nineteen sixty, Greensboro, North Carolina. Four Black college students sat at the “whites only” lunch counter at Woolworth’s and politely asked to be served. They were refused — and came back the next day with more students. Sit-ins, 静坐, spread to dozens of cities within weeks. In April, students founded Snick, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. In July nineteen sixty the Greensboro Woolworth’s served Black customers at the counter. Part of that counter is now in the Smithsonian.
ushistory/us-civilrights.bd45e23bd6d1: Brown versus Board of Education. May seventeenth, nineteen fifty-four, Topeka, Kansas. Linda Brown, a Black third-grader, had to travel far to a Black school although a white school was much closer. Her father joined an NAACP lawsuit. NAACP lawyer Thurgood Marshall argued the case, with four others combined, before the Supreme Court. All nine justices agreed: “separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.” School segregation was unconstitutional.
ushistory/us-civilrights.d260227dc728: Freedom Rides. May nineteen sixty-one, Washington, D.C., the Deep South. The Supreme Court had banned segregation on interstate buses and in their stations, but Southern states ignored it. Black and white “Freedom Riders” rode buses together from Washington into the South to test the law. Near Anniston, Alabama, a mob burned one bus; riders were beaten in Birmingham and Montgomery. More riders kept coming. In September nineteen sixty-one the Interstate Commerce Commission ordered segregation signs removed from bus stations.
ushistory/us-civilrights.d62d5114a25d: Don't mix up: The March on Washington happened in nineteen sixty-three; the Civil Rights Act it pushed for was signed in nineteen sixty-four.
ushistory/us-civilrights.18589fb54598: Memphis, nineteen sixty-eight. April fourth, nineteen sixty-eight, Memphis, Tennessee. King went to Memphis to support Black sanitation workers on strike for fair pay and safe working conditions, “I AM A MAN” signs. On April fourth, nineteen sixty-eight, he was assassinated at the Lorraine Motel. He was thirty-nine. The nation mourned. A week later Congress passed the Fair Housing Act, banning discrimination in selling and renting homes. Today the motel is the National Civil Rights Museum.
ushistory/us-civilrights.583eba775894: Atlanta: Dr. King’s hometown. SCLC founded nineteen fifty-seven, Atlanta, Georgia. Martin Luther King Jr. was born in Atlanta on January fifteenth, nineteen twenty-nine, and preached at Ebenezer Baptist Church. In nineteen fifty-seven King and other ministers founded the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, SCLC, based in Atlanta, to organize nonviolent protest. In nineteen sixty Atlanta’s college students held their own sit-ins. Today his birth home is part of a National Historical Park.
ushistory/us-civilrights.afae67aa1b42: Don't mix up: The Voting Rights Act protected voting. That act dates to nineteen sixty-five. The Civil Rights Act ended segregation in public places. That act dates to nineteen sixty-four.
ushistory/us-civilrights.a1813fe69b61: The Little Rock Nine. September nineteen fifty-seven, Little Rock, Arkansas. Nine Black students enrolled at all-white Central High School to carry out the Brown decision. Arkansas Governor Orval Faubus sent the state National Guard to keep them out, and an angry crowd gathered. President Eisenhower sent soldiers of the one hundred first Airborne Division to escort the students — the federal government enforcing the Supreme Court’s ruling.
ushistory/us-civilrights.eb693f99d7a0: The Albany Movement. Nineteen sixty-one to nineteen sixty-two, Albany, Georgia. Students, churches and the NAACP in Albany, Georgia, protested segregation across the whole city at once — buses, parks, libraries, stores. Hundreds were arrested; Dr. King was jailed there too. The police chief avoided violent scenes, so the nation paid less attention. Albany did not win quick victories, but leaders learned to focus on one target — a lesson they used in Birmingham.
ushistory/us-civilrights.5bcb2ece19b0: The Birmingham Campaign. April to May nineteen sixty-three, Birmingham, Alabama. Birmingham was one of the most segregated cities in America. Protesters held marches and sit-ins, and boycotted downtown stores. Jailed for marching, King wrote the “Letter from Birmingham Jail”, explaining why people could not keep waiting for justice. In May, children and teenagers marched. Police used fire hoses and dogs on them. TV pictures shocked the nation; in June President Kennedy proposed a civil rights bill. In September a bomb at the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church killed four girls.
ushistory/us-civilrights.d03569b3a07e: Don't mix up: The “Letter from Birmingham Jail”, April nineteen sixty-three, is different from the “I Have a Dream” speech, August nineteen sixty-three, Washington.
ushistory/us-civilrights.01ea8fd31634: Montgomery Bus Boycott. The fifth of December, nineteen fifty-five, to the twentieth of December, nineteen fifty-six, Montgomery, Alabama. The first of December, nineteen fifty-five: Rosa Parks refused to give her bus seat to a white man and was arrested. Black citizens stayed off the buses for three hundred eighty-one days. They walked, shared rides and organized a carpool system. A young pastor, Martin Luther King Jr., led the Montgomery Improvement Association. In nineteen fifty-six the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional; Montgomery’s buses were integrated in December nineteen fifty-six.
ushistory/us-civilrights.c5df7c42fe6d: Don't mix up: Brown overturned “separate but equal”, from Plessy versus Ferguson, eighteen ninety-six, for public schools — it was a court ruling, not a law passed by Congress.
ushistory/us-civilrights.26258d20797d: March on Washington. The twenty-eighth of August, nineteen sixty-three, Washington, D.C. About two hundred fifty thousand people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom — one of the largest protests in US history at the time. Martin Luther King Jr. gave his “I Have a Dream” speech. A young John Lewis, later a congressman from Georgia, also spoke. The march built support for the civil rights bill. On the second of July, nineteen sixty-four, President Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act, banning segregation in public places and job discrimination.
ushistory/us-civilrights.156c4263c76f: Don't mix up: The Freedom Rides were about interstate buses and stations. They took place in nineteen sixty-one. The Montgomery boycott was about city buses. It took place in nineteen fifty-five.
ushistory/us-civilrights.563b6a8e47e7: Selma to Montgomery. March nineteen sixty-five, Selma, Montgomery, Alabama. In Selma, only a tiny share of Black adults were allowed to register to vote. On the seventh of March, nineteen sixty-five, “Bloody Sunday”, state troopers attacked peaceful marchers, led by John Lewis and Hosea Williams, on the Edmund Pettus Bridge. Two weeks later, protected by federal troops, thousands marched fifty-four miles to Montgomery, a distance of eighty-seven kilometers. On the sixth of August, nineteen sixty-five, Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act, 选举权法.

ushistory/us-civilwar.0a6074004153: Appomattox Court House. The ninth of April, eighteen sixty-five, Virginia. Lee surrenders to Grant. Robert E. Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to Ulysses S. Grant in the parlour of Wilmer McLean’s house. Grant let Lee’s soldiers go home and keep their horses for spring planting. Other Confederate armies surrendered in the following weeks.
ushistory/us-civilwar.f058fa58928d: Shiloh. The sixth to the seventh of April, eighteen sixty-two, Tennessee. Union victory. A surprise attack on General Ulysses S. Grant’s army; Grant held on and won on the second day. About twenty-three thousand soldiers were killed, wounded or missing — a shock to both sides about the cost of the war.
ushistory/us-civilwar.2e736a14f538: Sherman’s March to the Sea, Savannah. The fifteenth of November to the twenty-first of December, eighteen sixty-four, Georgia. Union campaign. Sherman’s sixty thousand soldiers marched about two hundred eighty-five miles from Atlanta to Savannah, a distance of about four hundred sixty kilometers, wrecking railroads, farms and supplies in a path up to sixty miles wide. The goal was to break the South’s ability — and will — to keep fighting. Thousands of enslaved people followed the army to freedom. Sherman telegraphed Lincoln, offering Savannah as a “Christmas gift”.
ushistory/us-civilwar.54cef40a8903: First Bull Run, Manassas. The twenty-first of July, eighteen sixty-one, Virginia. Confederate victory. Picnickers from Washington came out to watch what they expected to be a quick Union win. The Union army retreated in confusion. General Thomas Jackson earned the nickname “Stonewall”. Both sides realised the war would be long.
ushistory/us-civilwar.25a938ef304a: Ford’s Theatre, Washington. The fourteenth of April, eighteen sixty-five. President Lincoln assassinated. Five days after Appomattox, actor John Wilkes Booth shot Lincoln at a play. Lincoln died the next morning. Vice President Andrew Johnson became president and led the first years of Reconstruction.
ushistory/us-civilwar.854e6cf77cb5: Fort Sumter. The twelfth to the thirteenth of April, eighteen sixty-one, South Carolina. Confederate victory — the war begins. Confederate cannons fired on a US Army fort in Charleston Harbor. Nobody was killed in the bombardment, but the fort surrendered. Lincoln called for seventy-five thousand volunteers. Four more states, Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina, Tennessee, then seceded.
ushistory/us-civilwar.a6001a3ff77a: Atlanta. Captured the second of September, eighteen sixty-four, Georgia. Union victory. General William T. Sherman captured Atlanta, a key railroad hub and factory city of the Confederacy. The good news helped Lincoln win re-election in November eighteen sixty-four. Before leaving, Union troops burned much of the city’s industry and railroads.
ushistory/us-civilwar.9b573c1a9b45: Gettysburg. The first to the third of July, eighteen sixty-three, Pennsylvania. Union victory — a turning point. The largest battle ever fought in North America: about one hundred sixty thousand soldiers and some fifty-one thousand casualties. Lee’s second and last invasion of the North failed; Pickett’s Charge on day three was thrown back. In November, Lincoln gave the Gettysburg Address at the new soldiers’ cemetery here.
ushistory/us-civilwar.70fce7cdab06: Vicksburg. Siege May to July; surrender the fourth of July, eighteen sixty-three, Mississippi. Union victory — a turning point. After a forty-seven-day siege, the city surrendered to Grant on the Fourth of July. The Union now controlled the whole Mississippi River and split the Confederacy in two — part of the “Anaconda Plan” to squeeze the South.
ushistory/us-civilwar.933a073557f7: Antietam. The seventeenth of September, eighteen sixty-two, Maryland. Union strategic victory. The bloodiest single day in American history: about twenty-three thousand casualties. Lee’s first invasion of the North was stopped. Five days later Lincoln announced the Emancipation Proclamation. Britain and France, which had thought about recognising the Confederacy, held back.

ushistory/us-colonies.f3a13711b38d: Monmouth. June twenty-eighth, seventeen seventy-eight. A long, hot battle in one hundred degrees Fahrenheit heat, or thirty-eight degrees Celsius; neither side wins clearly.
ushistory/us-colonies.43467d92d600: Trenton. December twenty-sixth, seventeen seventy-six. On Christmas night Washington crosses the icy Delaware River and surprises about one thousand five hundred Hessian soldiers; about nine hundred are captured.
ushistory/us-colonies.b9c7176fe327: Battle of Long Island. August twenty-seventh, seventeen seventy-six. The largest battle of the war: the British crush Washington’s army, which escapes across the East River by night in fog.
ushistory/us-colonies.379ccb5139c4: Bunker Hill, Breed’s Hill. June seventeenth, seventeen seventy-five. The British take the hill on the third charge, but with over one thousand killed or wounded.
ushistory/us-colonies.9965f5e3991c: Fall of Charleston. May twelfth, seventeen eighty. After a siege, about five thousand American soldiers surrender.
ushistory/us-colonies.20238933d897: Saratoga. October seventeenth, seventeen seventy-seven. American forces surround General Burgoyne’s army; about five thousand nine hundred British and German soldiers surrender.
ushistory/us-colonies.e16ac1474536: Battle of the Chesapeake, at sea. September fifth, seventeen eighty-one. Admiral de Grasse’s French fleet drives off a British fleet coming to rescue Cornwallis.
ushistory/us-colonies.98a604a4f06f: Guilford Courthouse. March fifteenth, seventeen eighty-one. Cornwallis holds the field against Nathanael Greene, but loses about a quarter of his army.
ushistory/us-colonies.d739924911c3: Siege of Savannah. October ninth, seventeen seventy-nine. French and American forces attack the British lines and are thrown back with heavy losses. Free Black soldiers from Saint-Domingue, today’s Haiti, fought with the French.
ushistory/us-colonies.3074af9c7c8f: Treaty of Paris. September third, seventeen eighty-three. Britain recognises the independence of the United States, with land west to the Mississippi River.
ushistory/us-colonies.19c724d143d4: Lexington and Concord. April nineteenth, seventeen seventy-five. The first shots of the war. Minutemen push the British back to Boston.
ushistory/us-colonies.1fcad5e40d49: Valley Forge, winter camp. December nineteenth, seventeen seventy-seven. Not a battle: about twelve thousand soldiers spend the winter in huts; about two thousand die of disease.
ushistory/us-colonies.01ffacf7d1c9: Siege of Boston ends. March seventeenth, seventeen seventy-six. Henry Knox drags fifty-nine cannons about three hundred miles from Fort Ticonderoga. Facing them, the British sail away.
ushistory/us-colonies.2e4d04b907cf: Yorktown. October nineteenth, seventeen eighty-one. About seventeen thousand American and French troops besiege Yorktown. Cornwallis surrenders about eight thousand men. James Armistead Lafayette, an enslaved spy, had sent key information.
ushistory/us-colonies.d2c9f6e5b4dd: Kettle Creek. February fourteenth, seventeen seventy-nine. Georgia and Carolina Patriot militia led by Andrew Pickens, John Dooly and Elijah Clarke defeat a larger Loyalist force.
ushistory/us-colonies.bc3d2e1c1322: Cowpens. January seventeenth, seventeen eighty-one. Daniel Morgan sets a clever trap: militia fire twice and fall back, then Continentals and cavalry strike.
ushistory/us-colonies.57b5692953d0: Kings Mountain. October seventh, seventeen eighty. “Overmountain Men” from the backcountry surround and defeat a Loyalist force on a ridge.

ushistory/us-expansion.1782adcdb3e3: The Louisiana Purchase. Bought from France, eighteen oh three. Fifteen million dollars — about three cents an acre. President Thomas Jefferson only wanted the port of New Orleans. Napoleon, short of money for his wars in Europe, offered the whole territory. It roughly doubled the size of the country — about eight hundred twenty-eight thousand square miles, parts of fifteen future states. Jefferson sent Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, the Corps of Discovery, to explore it, eighteen oh four to eighteen oh six.
ushistory/us-expansion.c88778c44a2b: Texas Annexation. Annexed, eighteen forty-five, independent Republic of Texas eighteen thirty-six to eighteen forty-five. Joined by vote of Congress; Mexico did not accept it. American settlers, invited by Mexico in the eighteen twenties, outnumbered Tejanos, Mexican Texans, by the eighteen thirties. Many brought enslaved people, although Mexico had abolished slavery in eighteen twenty-nine. Texas won independence in eighteen thirty-six, the Alamo, then victory at San Jacinto. Annexation in eighteen forty-five led straight to war with Mexico, because both countries claimed the land between the Nueces River and the Rio Grande.
ushistory/us-expansion.78ba4f396d6e: The Mexican Cession. From Mexico, Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, eighteen forty-eight, after the Mexican-American War. Fifteen million dollars, plus up to three point two five million dollars in claims. The Mexican-American War ended with US troops in Mexico City. It lasted from eighteen forty-six to eighteen forty-eight. Mexico lost about half of its territory — today’s California, Nevada, Utah and parts of four more states. About eighty thousand to one hundred thousand Mexican citizens living there could become US citizens; many later lost their land in courts.
ushistory/us-expansion.8cb8cfd9a9d6: The United States in seventeen eighty-three. From Britain, Treaty of Paris, seventeen eighty-three. Won in the Revolutionary War. The Treaty of Paris ended the American Revolution. Britain recognised US independence. The new border ran west to the Mississippi River, north to the Great Lakes, and south to Spanish Florida. Land between the Appalachians and the Mississippi was home to many Native nations — Shawnee, Miami, Cherokee, Creek and others — who had not signed the treaty.
ushistory/us-expansion.1ea3b4124144: Don't mix up: The thirteen states were only the eastern strip; the land out to the Mississippi was organised into territories later, for example the Northwest Territory, seventeen eighty-seven.
ushistory/us-expansion.3b277e5d7643: Don't mix up: Florida was Spanish, then British, seventeen sixty-three to seventeen eighty-three, then Spanish again before eighteen nineteen.
ushistory/us-expansion.2ba75f0deb23: Florida. From Spain, Adams-Onís Treaty, eighteen nineteen. US paid five million dollars of its citizens’ claims against Spain. After raids across the border and General Andrew Jackson’s invasion in eighteen eighteen, Spain agreed to give up Florida. The treaty also drew the border between the US and Spanish Mexico all the way to the Pacific. Seminole people in Florida later fought removal for decades.
ushistory/us-expansion.d401490ed982: The Gadsden Purchase. Bought from Mexico, eighteen fifty-three. Ten million dollars. The US wanted flat land south of the Gila River for a southern railroad to California. It completed the borders of the “lower forty-eight” states. Next came Alaska, bought from Russia, eighteen sixty-seven, and Hawaii, annexed eighteen ninety-eight.
ushistory/us-expansion.9d665882a61f: Red River Basin. From Britain, Convention of eighteen eighteen. Treaty — no payment. The US and Britain agreed that the border would run along the forty-ninth parallel from Lake of the Woods to the Rocky Mountains, at forty-nine degrees north. The two countries also agreed to share the Oregon Country for the time being.
ushistory/us-expansion.8b53534e7fcb: Oregon Country. From Britain, Oregon Treaty, eighteen forty-six. Treaty — split at forty-nine degrees north, no payment. From eighteen eighteen the US and Britain shared the Oregon Country. Thousands of American settlers arrived on the Oregon Trail from eighteen forty-three. Some Americans shouted “Fifty-four forty or fight!”, fifty-four degrees forty minutes north, but President Polk compromised at forty-nine degrees north. The Chinook, Nez Perce, Cayuse and many other nations had lived here for thousands of years.
ushistory/us-expansion.039869edf91a: Don't mix up: Texas was annexed, not bought. Its old claims stretched north to today’s Wyoming; it gave them up in eighteen fifty.

ushistory/us-industrial.cc9f4b39fd4b: The first transcontinental railroad. Golden spike: the tenth of May, eighteen sixty-nine. Union Pacific built west from Omaha; Central Pacific built east from Sacramento. They met at Promontory Summit, Utah. The Central Pacific hired thousands of Chinese workers, 华工 — at the peak most of its workforce. They blasted tunnels through the granite of the Sierra Nevada. A coast-to-coast trip shrank from months to about a week.
ushistory/us-industrial.22051689a4c9: Memory hook: “sixty-nine — the spike is fine”: East meets West in Utah.

ushistory/us-modern.104545937a4a: Houston: Mission Control. Nineteen sixty-five to today, Texas. NASA’s Manned Spacecraft Center, now the Johnson Space Center, took over Mission Control for crewed flights starting with Gemini four in nineteen sixty-five. July twentieth, nineteen sixty-nine: “Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.” Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon while Michael Collins orbited above. Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon between nineteen sixty-nine and nineteen seventy-two — all of them American.
ushistory/us-modern.da8348a10ede: Don’t mix up: Yuri Gagarin was the first human in space. He flew for the USSR in April nineteen sixty-one. Alan Shepard was the first American, in May nineteen sixty-one.
ushistory/us-modern.266bc51e30ef: Don’t mix up: NATO was the US and Western Europe’s alliance, formed in nineteen forty-nine; the Warsaw Pact was the Soviet side’s alliance, formed in nineteen fifty-five.
ushistory/us-modern.177d47120537: Don’t mix up: Microsoft was founded in nineteen seventy-five in Albuquerque, New Mexico, and moved to Washington State — not Silicon Valley.
ushistory/us-modern.76509e4e2e04: Washington: containment and NATO. Nineteen forty-seven, nineteen forty-nine, nineteen fifty-eight. Nineteen forty-seven: the Truman Doctrine promised help to countries resisting communism — a policy called containment, 遏制. April fourth, nineteen forty-nine: twelve countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington, creating NATO, 北约: “an attack on one is an attack on all.” Nineteen fifty-eight: after Sputnik, Congress created NASA. After the Cuban crisis, a Washington-Moscow “hotline”, nineteen sixty-three, let leaders talk directly.
ushistory/us-modern.78ce052cf7bb: Huntsville, Alabama: “Rocket City”. Marshall Space Flight Center, nineteen sixty. Wernher von Braun’s rocket team at the Redstone Arsenal built the rocket that launched Explorer one. NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center opened here in nineteen sixty and developed the Saturn five Moon rocket. The Saturn five stood three hundred sixty-three feet tall, or one hundred eleven meters — taller than the Statue of Liberty with its pedestal. Today Huntsville hosts Space Camp.
ushistory/us-modern.14d8bc8b9ecf: Cuban Missile Crisis. October sixteenth to twenty-eighth, nineteen sixty-two. After its nineteen fifty-nine revolution, Cuba under Fidel Castro allied with the Soviet Union. A US U two spy plane photographed Soviet nuclear missile sites about ninety miles from Florida, or one hundred forty-five kilometers. For thirteen days the world held its breath. Kennedy ordered a naval “quarantine”. Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles; the US promised not to invade Cuba and secretly agreed to remove its missiles from Turkey.
ushistory/us-modern.af0a2a419dea: Silicon Valley, California. Nineteen seventy-one to today. Named after the silicon used to make computer chips. In nineteen seventy-one Intel released the first commercial microprocessor — a computer’s “brain” on one chip. Nineteen seventy-six: Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak founded Apple; the Apple two was one of the first popular home computers. It came out in nineteen seventy-seven. IBM’s PC followed in nineteen eighty-one. Nineteen ninety-eight: Google was founded. Two thousand seven: Apple’s iPhone put the internet in people’s pockets.
ushistory/us-modern.27b6dcaa4100: ARPANET: the first four nodes. October twenty-ninth, nineteen sixty-nine, California and Utah. ARPA, a Defense Department agency set up in nineteen fifty-eight after Sputnik, paid for a network linking university computers. The first message went from UCLA to SRI: they tried to type “LOGIN”, but the system crashed after “L O”. By December four sites were linked. It used packet switching: messages are chopped into small packets that each find their own way. In nineteen eighty-three ARPANET switched to T C P I P — the common language of today’s internet.
ushistory/us-modern.8b1d9e660b9c: Don’t mix up: The failed Bay of Pigs invasion was in nineteen sixty-one; the Missile Crisis was in nineteen sixty-two, and the US did not invade.
ushistory/us-modern.5949e5655f42: Cape Canaveral and Kennedy Space Center. Nineteen fifty-eight to today, Florida. January thirty-first, nineteen fifty-eight: Explorer one, the first US satellite, launched here and discovered radiation belts around Earth. May fifth, nineteen sixty-one: Alan Shepard became the first American in space. February twentieth, nineteen sixty-two: John Glenn became the first American to orbit Earth, three orbits. July sixteenth, nineteen sixty-nine: Apollo eleven lifted off on a Saturn five rocket. Why Florida? It is far south, and rockets fly out over the ocean.
ushistory/us-modern.9cdf212f5a30: Don’t mix up: Apollo eleven launched from Florida; Houston was Mission Control.
ushistory/us-modern.7d702c2f7fa5: Trinity test, New Mexico. July sixteenth, nineteen forty-five. Scientists of the secret Manhattan Project, based at Los Alamos, tested the first atomic bomb in the New Mexico desert. In August nineteen forty-five the US dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki; Japan surrendered and World War two ended. In nineteen forty-nine the Soviet Union tested its own bomb. The nuclear arms race, 军备竞赛, had begun.
ushistory/us-modern.8600395b06e5: September eleventh, two thousand one. New York, Arlington, Virginia, Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Terrorists of the al-Qaeda group hijacked four passenger planes. Two struck the World Trade Center in New York and one struck the Pentagon. Passengers on United Flight ninety-three fought back; the plane crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Nearly three thousand people died that day. Afterwards the US created the Department of Homeland Security, tightened airport security and went to war in Afghanistan. Memorials stand at all three sites.

ushistory/us-worldwars.1eace61f10bf: Manzanar, California. Executive Order nine zero six six, nineteen forty-two. After Pearl Harbor, fear and prejudice led FDR to sign Executive Order nine zero six six, nineteen forty-two. About one hundred twenty thousand people of Japanese ancestry — two-thirds of them US citizens — were sent to camps such as Manzanar. No Japanese American was ever convicted of spying. Many young Japanese American men still served; the four hundred forty-second Regiment became one of the most decorated units. In nineteen eighty-eight the US government formally apologized and paid survivors.
ushistory/us-worldwars.428be0d913e7: Georgia. Native peoples lived here for thirteen thousand years before the colony was named for King George the Second in seventeen thirty-two. Today Georgia is the largest state east of the Mississippi River by land area, with one hundred fifty-nine counties.
ushistory/us-worldwars.a18458b4da93: The Great Migration. About nineteen fifteen to nineteen seventy. Push: Jim Crow segregation laws, 种族隔离法, violence, and poor pay as sharecroppers in the South. Pull: factory jobs in Chicago, Detroit, New York, Philadelphia — first in World War one, again in World War two. Black newspapers like the Chicago Defender urged people to come. In the second wave, nineteen forty to nineteen seventy, many went west too: Los Angeles, Oakland and the Bay Area shipyards. It reshaped American cities, music such as jazz and blues, and politics — and fed the Harlem Renaissance.
ushistory/us-worldwars.4e5a66dcd6c5: Dust Bowl. In the nineteen thirties, drought and over-plowed prairie turned the southern Great Plains into a “Dust Bowl”. On Black Sunday, April fourteenth, nineteen thirty-five, a wall of dust rolled over towns like Stratford, Texas, turning day into night, and thousands of farm families moved west to California.
ushistory/us-worldwars.bc67d9baed64: Hawaii. Native Hawaiians had their own kingdom until American businessmen overthrew Queen Liliuokalani in eighteen ninety-three, and the US annexed the islands in eighteen ninety-eight. Japan attacked Pearl Harbor here on December seventh, nineteen forty-one; Hawaii became the fiftieth state in nineteen fifty-nine.

worldhistory/africa-americas-before-1500.159d2ed84785: Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached the Caribbean in fourteen ninety-two and met Taíno people. This voyage began a period of sustained contact between Europe and the Americas.

worldhistory/industrialization-reform.ca3119ffbac7: Edison and his team made a practical incandescent lamp in eighteen seventy-nine. In eighteen eighty-two, the Pearl Street station in New York supplied electricity to customers. Lighting depended on an entire system of generators, wiring, and lamps.

worldhistory/industrialization-reform.589d544a5983: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels wrote the Manifesto for the Communist League. Its publication in eighteen forty-eight marked the birth of Marxism. They argued that owners and wage workers had conflicting interests. They urged workers to gain political power and bring factories and other means of production under collective control.

Heavy state grain collections worsened the nineteen thirty-two to nineteen thirty-three famine in Ukraine and other regions. At the height of the Great Purge in nineteen thirty-seven to nineteen thirty-eight, many people were arrested, imprisoned, or executed.

worldhistory/wh-cold-war.5cc0d48b213a: Berlin Wall. East Germany built the wall overnight to stop its people escaping to the West. In nineteen eighty-nine crowds climbed on it at the Brandenburg Gate and began to knock it down.
worldhistory/wh-cold-war.052adeaf62dc: The Soviet Union breaks up. December nineteen ninety-one. The Warsaw Pact dissolved in July nineteen ninety-one. In December the USSR split into fifteen independent countries, and Gorbachev resigned. The Cold War’s two-pole world was over. China’s textbook describes a world moving toward many centres of power, 多极化.
worldhistory/wh-cold-war.c22b90667997: Berlin. The Soviet Red Army took Hitler’s capital in nineteen forty-five. Then the city was split, the West kept alive by the nineteen forty-eight airlift, and divided by a wall from nineteen sixty-one to nineteen eighty-nine.
worldhistory/wh-cold-war.5ecd26fd6b71: Warsaw. German bombs destroyed most of the city in World War Two; Poles rebuilt the Old Town brick by brick. In nineteen fifty-five the Soviet bloc signed the Warsaw Pact here.
worldhistory/wh-cold-war.4824536098ee: Cuba. Cuba won independence from Spain after the Spanish-American War of eighteen ninety-eight. In October nineteen sixty-two American spy planes found Soviet missile sites here, only ninety miles from Florida, and for thirteen days the world feared a nuclear war.
worldhistory/wh-cold-war.d0030eee7836: Vietnam. A long, narrow country in Southeast Asia. US combat troops arrived in nineteen sixty-five to fight Communist North Vietnam — more than five hundred thousand by nineteen sixty-eight; the last US troops left in nineteen seventy-three, and the war ended with the North’s victory in nineteen seventy-five. Today visitors come from all over the world to see the limestone islands of Ha Long Bay.
worldhistory/wh-cold-war.92b0ccb80e5b: Don’t mix up: Russia is the largest of the fifteen countries that came out of the USSR — not the same thing as the USSR.
worldhistory/wh-cold-war.04af5cc1ca25: Independence for India and Pakistan. August fifteenth, nineteen forty-seven. Mohandas Gandhi led mass non-violent protests against British rule, such as the nineteen thirty Salt March. Britain left in nineteen forty-seven; British India was split, partitioned, into India and Pakistan. Millions were forced to move and many died in violence. India’s independence encouraged freedom movements across Asia and Africa.
worldhistory/wh-cold-war.52c9715bf48f: Don’t mix up: Bangladesh, once East Pakistan, became independent later, in nineteen seventy-one.

worldhistory/wh-exploration.d1f6a1856fb0: The Manila galleons, Spain. Fifteen sixty-five to eighteen fifteen. American silver across the Pacific to buy Chinese silk and porcelain. Each year Spanish galleons sailed between Acapulco, Mexico, and Manila, Philippines. They carried silver mined in Mexico and Peru; Chinese merchants in Manila traded silk and porcelain for it. A huge share of the world’s silver flowed to Ming China — and the Ming began collecting taxes in silver.
worldhistory/wh-exploration.94104098ef76: Bartolomeu Dias, Portugal. Fourteen eighty-seven to fourteen eighty-eight. First European to sail round the southern tip of Africa. Portugal had crept down Africa’s coast for seventy years, looking for gold and a sea road to Asian spices. A storm blew Dias’s two caravels far south; turning east, then north, he found the coast running east — Africa had an end! His tired crew made him turn back. The king renamed the “Cape of Storms” the Cape of Good Hope.
worldhistory/wh-exploration.7ce79204e124: Zheng He, China, Ming. Seven voyages, fourteen oh five to fourteen thirty-three. “Down to the Western Oceans” with the biggest wooden fleet of its time. The first voyage: sixty-two large “treasure ships” and over twenty-seven thousand eight hundred men, Ming History; two hundred or more ships in all are often quoted. Over twenty-eight years the fleet visited thirty or more countries and regions of Asia and Africa — as far as the east coast of Africa and the Red Sea. It carried silk and porcelain and brought back spices, gems — and a giraffe for the emperor, fourteen fourteen. Goal: show the Ming emperor’s power and build friendly “tribute” ties — not conquest or colonies. The voyages stopped after fourteen thirty-three.
worldhistory/wh-exploration.5881b12dda41: Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain. Fourteen ninety-two to fourteen ninety-three. Sailed west to reach Asia — and reached the Americas. An Italian from Genoa, paid by Spain’s Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand. Three ships: Niña, Pinta and Santa María. He believed Earth was round, true, but much smaller than it is, false — he thought Japan was about where America is. October twelfth, fourteen ninety-two: landing in the Bahamas, home of the Taíno people. He called them “Indians” because he thought he was in the Indies. His voyages began Spanish conquest and colonies; Taíno numbers collapsed from disease, forced labour and violence.
worldhistory/wh-exploration.fb7331d8aa4b: Vasco da Gama, Portugal. Fourteen ninety-seven to fourteen ninety-nine, India: May fourteen ninety-eight. Opened the sea road from Europe to India. Four ships, about one hundred seventy men. In the South Atlantic he swung far out to sea — about three months without seeing land. In East Africa, Malindi, he took on a local pilot who knew the monsoon winds across the Indian Ocean. He reached Calicut, India, in May fourteen ninety-eight. Only about fifty-five of his men made it home — many died of scurvy. The pepper and spices he brought back paid for the voyage many times over.

worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.4a9eb887739c: Carthage, near Tunis. A Phoenician trading city in North Africa and Rome’s great rival. Rome fought it in three Punic Wars, two hundred sixty-four to one hundred forty-six B C E, and destroyed it in one hundred forty-six B C E; Romans later rebuilt it as a Roman city.
worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.aaa160f91465: Syracuse. A rich Greek colony on Sicily, founded by Corinth about seven hundred thirty-three B C E. Home of the mathematician Archimedes, died two hundred twelve B C E.
worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.df35d2ccf59b: Rome. Legend says Rome was founded in seven hundred fifty-three B C E on seven hills by the Tiber River. Republic from five hundred nine B C E, Empire from twenty-seven B C E; about a million people lived here around one C E, estimate.
worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.4423f262aec0: Olympia. Site of the ancient Olympic Games, held every four years for Zeus from seven hundred seventy-six B C E. During the games a truce let athletes travel safely.
worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.92c89aa9e3b1: Coloured areas show who ruled where in the year on the slider. Borders are rough — ancient empires had no exact lines on the ground. Pericles: Leader of Athens in its golden age; paid citizens for public service and built the Parthenon. Socrates, Plato, Aristotle: Three Athenian philosophers: teacher, student, student. Aristotle then taught Alexander. Alexander the Great: King of Macedon, three hundred thirty-six to three hundred twenty-three B C E; conquered from Greece to the Indus River and spread Greek culture. Hannibal: Carthaginian general who crossed the Alps with elephants in two hundred eighteen B C E. Julius Caesar: Conquered Gaul, became dictator, was killed in forty-four B C E. Augustus, Octavian: First Roman emperor, twenty-seven B C E to fourteen C E; began two centuries of “Roman Peace”, Pax Romana.
worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.720efc743283: Babylon, near Baghdad. Conquered by Cyrus of Persia in five hundred thirty-nine B C E. Alexander died here in three hundred twenty-three B C E, aged thirty-two.
worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.c32068e28f6b: Hadrian’s Wall. A stone wall about one hundred eighteen kilometers long across northern Britain, guarding the edge of the Roman Empire. Soldiers lived in forts along it.
worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.3b22d5410803: Athens. The leading sea power of Greece and birthplace of democracy, reforms of Solon five hundred ninety-four B C E and Cleisthenes five hundred eight B C E. Under Pericles it built the Parthenon and led the Delian League. That period lasted from about four hundred sixty-one to four hundred twenty-nine B C E.
worldhistory/wh-greece-rome.094a7da8e20b: Sparta. A land power in the Peloponnese whose citizens trained as soldiers from age seven. Led the Peloponnesian League and defeated Athens in four hundred four B C E.

worldhistory/wh-middle-ages.1e22fb9b3fcc: Paris. Capital of the French kings; its university grew around twelve hundred; Notre-Dame was begun in eleven sixty-three.
worldhistory/wh-middle-ages.dcc9a8520b8e: Historians call four hundred seventy-six to fifteen hundred in Europe the Middle Ages, 中世纪 — the “middle” between ancient Rome and the modern world. Memory hook. “Four hundred seventy-six, the West falls. Eight hundred, Charlemagne crowned. Eight hundred forty-three, split in three. Fourteen fifty-three, the East falls.”
worldhistory/wh-middle-ages.2aee01efa336: Eastern Roman Empire. When the West fell in four hundred seventy-six, the East — rich, with strong walls around Constantinople — survived. Greek-speaking, Christian, and still calling itself “Roman”.
worldhistory/wh-middle-ages.8354c40c9c18: Samarkand. A Silk Road city; paper-making was known here by the seven hundreds.

worldhistory/wh-renaissance.dbdccd718aed: “Renaissance”, 文艺复兴, means “rebirth”: scholars revived Greek and Roman learning — but used it to celebrate human talent and life in this world. That idea is called humanism, 人文主义. Memory hook. “Fourteen fifty, the press. Fifteen seventeen, the protest. Fifteen fifty-five, the split.”
worldhistory/wh-renaissance.2ffd52ead05f: Don’t mix up: The Renaissance, art and ideas, from the thirteen hundreds, and the Reformation, religion, from fifteen seventeen, overlap, but they are different movements. Printing helped both.

worldhistory/wh-today.3c93768b8b6f: Don’t mix up: The SDGs replaced the earlier Millennium Development Goals. The SDGs span twenty fifteen to twenty thirty, and the Millennium Development Goals span two thousand to twenty fifteen.
worldhistory/wh-today.ffb55f85ff4f: The European Coal and Steel Community. Nineteen fifty-one to nineteen fifty-two. France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg pooled their coal and steel — the materials for weapons. French minister Robert Schuman wanted to make war between France and Germany “not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible.” It grew into the European Economic Community, nineteen fifty-eight, and the European Union, nineteen ninety-three.
worldhistory/wh-today.74e46e4b9934: The UK leaves the EU. January thirty-first, twenty twenty. In a twenty sixteen vote, fifty-two percent of British voters chose to leave the EU. The UK left in twenty twenty — the first country ever to leave. The EU now has twenty-seven members.
worldhistory/wh-today.e3ae4b38f38f: The World Trade Organization. Nineteen ninety-five, Geneva. The WTO replaced the GATT, nineteen forty-seven. Its members agree on trade rules and settle trade disputes. Over one hundred sixty members cover about ninety-eight percent of world trade.
worldhistory/wh-today.f9c4b3a94f51: The Treaty of Rome: a common market. Nineteen fifty-seven, in force nineteen fifty-eight. The six created the European Economic Community: no tariffs between members and one tariff for goods from outside. Trade among them grew fast; more countries joined in nineteen seventy-three, nineteen eighty-one, nineteen eighty-six and nineteen ninety-five.
worldhistory/wh-today.0a0dc5cf7b6d: Euro coins and notes. January first, two thousand two, currency since nineteen ninety-nine. Twelve countries swapped their old money for euros overnight; the European Central Bank is in Frankfurt. Today more than twenty EU countries use the euro, Bulgaria joined in twenty twenty-six. Some EU members, like Denmark and Sweden, keep their own currency.
worldhistory/wh-today.7c9886905809: One ship blocks world trade. March twenty twenty-one. The giant container ship Ever Given, about four hundred meters long, or one thousand three hundred feet, got stuck across Egypt’s Suez Canal for six days. Hundreds of ships waited; roughly twelve percent of world trade passes through the canal, approximately. It showed how tightly connected — and fragile — global supply chains are.
worldhistory/wh-today.ac77aded9e65: The Belt and Road Initiative. Twenty thirteen, Astana and Jakarta. China proposed the “Silk Road Economic Belt”, in Kazakhstan, and the “Twenty-first-Century Maritime Silk Road”, in Indonesia. It funds railways, ports, roads and power plants across Asia, Africa, Europe and beyond — like the China-Europe freight trains. Supporters point to new infrastructure; critics worry about debt in some countries. Both views are part of the debate.
worldhistory/wh-today.223f97171959: Seventeen Sustainable Development Goals. September twenty fifteen, UN, New York. All one hundred ninety-three UN members adopted seventeen goals for twenty thirty — from ending poverty and hunger to clean energy and climate action. In December twenty fifteen the Paris Agreement set the aim of keeping global warming well below two degrees Celsius, three point six degrees Fahrenheit.
worldhistory/wh-today.05211e7c240b: Reform and opening up, Shenzhen. Nineteen seventy-eight, Special Economic Zone nineteen eighty. In December nineteen seventy-eight China decided to reform its economy and open to the world, 改革开放, “reform and opening up”, led by Deng Xiaoping. In nineteen eighty Shenzhen, next to Hong Kong, became a Special Economic Zone welcoming foreign investment. A town of about three hundred thousand people grew into a city of over seventeen million, approximately. Today Shenzhen is a centre for electronics — many of the world’s phones and drones are designed or made there.
worldhistory/wh-today.cf716a32ce63: Don’t mix up: The League of Nations failed to stop World War two; the UN replaced it. The League of Nations dates to nineteen twenty, and the UN to nineteen forty-five.
worldhistory/wh-today.6da22189f188: The European Union is born. Maastricht Treaty, in force nineteen ninety-three. The European Community became the European Union, adding cooperation on foreign policy, justice and a future single currency. In most of the EU people can live, work and travel without passport checks, the Schengen area. After the Cold War, many former Warsaw Pact countries joined in two thousand four and two thousand seven.
worldhistory/wh-today.a668ed2ffc74: The United Nations is founded. San Francisco, June nineteen forty-five, in force October twenty-fourth, nineteen forty-five. Fifty countries signed the UN Charter in San Francisco; China’s delegation signed first, as the first country to fight the Axis. Goals: keep world peace, develop friendly relations among nations, and cooperate on economic, social and human-rights problems. October twenty-fourth is United Nations Day. Its headquarters is in New York.
worldhistory/wh-today.87db225f824f: Don’t mix up: Europe is not equal to the EU: Norway, Switzerland and the UK are in Europe but not in the EU. The UK has been out of the EU since twenty twenty.
worldhistory/wh-today.bc82b6a7a9e7: China joins the WTO. Approved at Doha, November two thousand one, member December eleventh, two thousand one. After fifteen years of talks, China became the WTO’s one hundred forty-third member. China’s share of world exports rose from about four percent in two thousand one to about fifteen percent in twenty twenty-four, the latter figure given approximately; it became the world’s biggest exporter of goods. Cheaper goods reached shoppers worldwide; factories and supply chains moved; China’s economy grew rapidly.

yuwen/yw-classics.a2f75c59c31c: Red Star Over China. In nineteen thirty-six the American reporter Edgar Snow — born in Kansas City, Missouri — slipped into the Red Army’s base in north Shaanxi and spent about four months there. He interviewed Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai and ordinary soldiers and recorded the story of the Long March. The book came out in nineteen thirty-seven.
yuwen/yw-classics.89ff0d8437dd: In nineteen twenties Beiping, today’s Beijing, a strong, honest country boy named Xiangzi pulls a rickshaw and dreams of owning one. He buys it three times and loses it three times. Crushed by a harsh society, he slowly becomes lazy and selfish.
yuwen/yw-classics.fc878bc3e36a: Characters: 蝉 cicada, 螳螂 praying mantis, 圣甲虫 sacred scarab, dung beetle, 萤火虫 firefly, 蟋蟀 cricket
yuwen/yw-classics.013192897baa: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas. Eighteen sixty-six: a “sea monster” is sinking ships. Professor Aronnax, his servant Conseil and the harpooner Ned Land are thrown aboard it — it is the submarine Nautilus, commanded by the mysterious Captain Nemo. For ten months they cross the world’s oceans: undersea forests, pearl beds, sharks, the South Pole ice, a giant squid, the ruins of Atlantis.
yuwen/yw-classics.6c0c7e3a1034: Memory hook: Nautilus equals 鹦鹉螺号. Verne is called “the father of science fiction”.
yuwen/yw-classics.dcff64a1131c: Summer Palace. Today: Haidian, Beijing. A huge royal garden with Longevity Hill and Kunming Lake. Its Long Corridor is painted with more than fourteen thousand pictures.
yuwen/yw-classics.1689d1c36fc6: The Scholars. A gallery of scholars ruined by the imperial exams and the hunger for fame. Fan Jin, after failing for decades, finally passes at fifty-four — and goes mad with joy until his butcher father-in-law slaps him. The miser Yan won’t die until one of two lamp wicks is put out to save oil.
yuwen/yw-classics.6ea7b3455e82: Characters: 范进 Fan Jin, 胡屠户 Butcher Hu, 严监生 Miser Yan, 周进 Zhou Jin, 王冕 Wang Mian, the good example

yuwen/yw-classics.0585cfd6f047: Flaming Mountains. Today: Near Turpan, Xinjiang. Red sandstone hills that seem to burn in the summer heat; the ground can get hotter than seventy degrees Celsius. They appear in “Journey to the West”.

yuwen/yw-classics.8ab4a4b9f554: Water Margin, Outlaws of the Marsh. In the last years of the Northern Song, corrupt officials push honest people into rebellion. One by one, one hundred eight heroes gather at the marsh fortress of Liangshan, 梁山泊, today’s Liangshan County, Shandong. In the end they accept the emperor’s pardon, 招安, fight his wars, and most die tragically.
yuwen/yw-classics.88582dab684a: Don’t mix up: Xiangzi is not lazy at the start — the tragedy is that society changes him. Don’t mix him up with Tigress’s father, 刘四爷.
yuwen/yw-classics.1f6436110efa: Selected Poems of Ai Qing. Modern free-verse poems written across sixty years. His big images are the LAND, suffering, beloved China, and the SUN, light and hope. 大堰河——我的保姆, nineteen thirty-three, honours the peasant woman who nursed him; 我爱这土地, nineteen thirty-eight, is in the Grade nine textbook.
yuwen/yw-classics.7f95742c1c04: Selected Poems of Ai Qing — Ai Qing, 艾青, nineteen ten to nineteen ninety-six, born 蒋海澄, China, modern free verse

yuwen/yw-classics.264a03dfbbd8: How the Steel Was Tempered. Pavel Korchagin, a poor boy, is guided by the sailor Zhukhrai, fights in the civil war, is badly wounded, and helps lay a railway through a freezing winter. Illness leaves him blind and paralysed — and he still fights on by writing a novel. Ostrovsky wrote it while blind and bedridden himself. He wrote it from nineteen thirty-two to nineteen thirty-four.
yuwen/yw-classics.7aaf6ebc37b6: The Harmas, Fabre’s garden. Today: Sérignan-du-Comtat, France. A stony, weedy garden in Provence that Jean-Henri Fabre bought so he could watch insects at home. He wrote most of The Insect World, 昆虫记, here.

yuwen/yw-expository.4404bdef655f: A definition, 下定义, captures the essence and can be reversed; an explanation, 作诠释, only explains one aspect. Exams love this pair.

Also the task group “Accumulating and organising language”.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.00d2d23408e7: Notes: oracle, bronze and seal forms are Wikimedia Commons tracings — real inscriptions vary. Clerical and regular are shown with system fonts, without a clerical font the browser falls back to Kai. Character counts are the commonly cited approximate figures. For an English speaker: think of 形旁 as like a Latin root that tells you the topic, and 声旁 as a rhyme hint.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.eaf0c7378b23: Wide, flat shapes; horizontal strokes start like a silkworm’s head and end like a swallow’s tail, 蚕头燕尾.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.14db4ccd084c: Calligraphy, 书法, is the art of writing with a brush. There are five main scripts, each with its own personality. The big characters below just name each script; real masterpieces are in the gallery.

yuwen/yw-hanzi.be6612934658: The Mao Gong Ding, 毛公鼎, a Western Zhou cauldron, carries nearly five hundred characters — the longest bronze inscription known.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.f7fb3bacf5bc: Over three thousand three hundred years ago, a scribe in the Shang dynasty carved 马, “horse”, as a little horse with a mane and four legs. Today 马 takes just three strokes. How did the picture turn into a character?
yuwen/yw-hanzi.f4ac41f95225: 贺, to congratulate: 加, to add, and 貝, a shell — money and gifts in ancient times: bringing gifts to add to someone’s joy. No older forms are shown here, so the first stages show today’s character faintly.

yuwen/yw-hanzi.77b6c50bef94: 鱼, fish: Head, scaly body, tail. In 魚 the tail turned into four dots; simplified 鱼 has one stroke instead.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.840a3cdb95b5: Mission two: crack the building code, the “six ways”, 六书
yuwen/yw-hanzi.825e4a831515: Example: the stone inscription on Mount Tai, 泰山刻石.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.ad4ab1f407ea: A person, 亻, leaning on a tree, 木, equals 休, rest. Sun plus moon equals 明, bright. One person following another equals 从, follow.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.e620e92121c7: 水, water: A stream in the middle with drops of water on both sides.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.2efbd7923157: Forbidden City. Twenty-four Ming and Qing emperors lived here. It covers about seven hundred twenty thousand square meters — the largest and most complete ancient palace complex still standing in the world, held together by wooden joints instead of nails.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.c6c28cc22251: Question one of twelve. 本, a mark at the root of 木, is a…
yuwen/yw-hanzi.7d0e29ee5a0e: The sound part 青, qīng, stays the same; swap the meaning part and you get a new word that sounds almost the same. Make four characters to complete Mission three.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.12b70dfaef28: Yin Ruins, Yinxu. Today: Anyang, Henan. Over one hundred fifty thousand oracle bones with the earliest Chinese writing were dug up here, and the eight hundred thirty-two kilogram Houmuwu Ding.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.953501bb929f: 月, moon: A crescent moon — the moon is usually not full, so the picture is a crescent.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.652087d9c40b: Mount Tai. Mount Tai in Shandong is one thousand five hundred forty-five meters high. Emperors climbed it to honour Heaven, and Du Fu dreamed of standing on its summit: “一览众山小”.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.0419536bae97: Bronze script. Shang and Zhou dynasties. Written in the clay mould, then cast into bronze ritual vessels — so the strokes look thick and soft. The Mao Gong Ding, 毛公鼎, a Western Zhou cauldron, carries nearly five hundred characters — the longest bronze inscription known. Still picture-like, but more regular than oracle bones.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.0c4e0ab5928f: Textbook links: the primary-school unit 遨游汉字王国, Grade five, volume two, lays the groundwork; writing and calligraphy appreciation run through grades seven to nine. Script history, the six ways and the calligraphers are background knowledge beyond the set texts.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.983e7cc7a611: 川, river: Two river banks with water flowing between them — the dots in the middle are the water. Later the dots joined into one line.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.8c52d4f8aec0: Regular script. Formed by the Wei-Jin era, perfected in the Tang. 楷 means “model”: every stroke clear and separate — the script children learn first. Tang masters: Ouyang Xun, 欧阳询, Yan Zhenqing, 颜真卿, Liu Gongquan, 柳公权. Since nineteen fifty-six mainland China uses simplified characters, 简化字, for example, 馬, 马.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.d0f7f83c2ab5: Busy government clerks needed speed: round curves became straight, square strokes. This change is called 隶变.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.6093741842d5: 车, cart: A cart seen from above: two wheels and the axle between them.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.9b3294b1b846: Trace a character through all five scripts
yuwen/yw-hanzi.b0ccee3f11cc: 宁, peaceful, calm: A roof, 宀, over a food vessel, 皿: a home with food on the table is a peaceful home. Seal script added a heart, 心. Simplified 宁 keeps only the roof and the part below.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.5012fc01ff5a: Sources: Shuowen Jiezi, nine thousand three hundred fifty-three entries; Kangxi Dictionary, forty-seven thousand thirty-five; State Council, General Standard Chinese Characters Table, twenty thirteen: eight thousand one hundred five, of which three thousand five hundred level one; Chinese Curriculum Standard twenty twenty-two, recognise about three thousand five hundred by grade nine. Oracle-bone count is approximate. Compare: an English dictionary has far more words — but most Chinese words are built from these few thousand characters.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.ae9d4ad92e9f: Write three characters with two mistakes or fewer.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.0ce28a1e84b5: 日, sun: A circle with a dot. The circle became a square — squares are easier to carve and to write with a brush.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.c6d1808c574c: Don't mix up: Small seal, 小篆, was the Qin standard; the big change to modern-looking strokes, 隶变, came with clerical script.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.6d8d208e6ec5: Memory hook: “Into the room first, then shut the door” — 先进人, 后关门 — that is why 国 closes last.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.4e39794dc4a1: 河, river, equals 氵, water: the meaning part, and 可, kě: the sound hint. Over eighty percent of modern characters are built this way!
yuwen/yw-hanzi.7e9813ca91a4: Memory hook: “甲金篆隶楷” — the five steps in order. Along the way, round lines become straight strokes.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.604293c7a68a: Small seal script. Qin dynasty, two hundred twenty-one B C E. After Qin Shi Huang united China he ordered “one script for all”, 书同文. Chancellor Li Si, 李斯, helped set the standard. Round, even lines of the same thickness; tall rectangular shapes. Example: the stone inscription on Mount Tai, 泰山刻石.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.5d56a4ca88e5: Shang and Zhou dynasties, Cast into bronze bells and cauldrons, 钟鼎文
yuwen/yw-hanzi.c296d2aa4c88: 先撇后捺 — left-falling before right-falling, 人
yuwen/yw-hanzi.e6e5a57c41ad: Found in eighteen ninety-nine; most come from Yinxu, 殷墟, near Anyang, Henan.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.9a44bc24a010: Ten characters per round. Choose how each was built — a streak earns bonus points. Get eight or more right to complete Mission two.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.7f3597cdc398: 马, horse: A horse standing on its tail: big eye, mane, legs. The four dots of 馬 are what is left of the legs!
yuwen/yw-hanzi.601f663201fb: Around one hundred C E the scholar Xu Shen, 许慎, listed six ways characters work. Four of them actually build characters — click each card to see how.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.a8b082fa3952: 吴, Wu, a state, a family name: A mouth, 口, next to a person tilting the head — someone talking or singing loudly. Later it became the name of the State of Wu on the lower Yangtze, and a family name.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.5b2c89bf3224: Orchid Pavilion. Today: Shaoxing, Zhejiang. In three hundred fifty-three Wang Xizhi and his friends wrote poems here beside a winding stream. His preface to the poems became the most famous piece of Chinese calligraphy.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.3734b4bebd37: 羊, sheep: A sheep’s face from the front — the two curly horns are at the top.

yuwen/yw-hanzi.fda01a122dce: Oracle-bone script. Late Shang dynasty, circa thirteen hundred to ten forty-six B C E. Kings asked their ancestors questions — “Will it rain?” “Will the hunt go well?” — and scribes carved the answers on bones.
yuwen/yw-hanzi.fa0c0d2172ef: Clerical script. Qin-Han dynasties, most used in the Han. Busy government clerks needed speed: round curves became straight, square strokes. This change is called 隶变. 隶变 is the great divide between ancient characters and modern characters — from here you can read most characters! Wide, flat shapes; horizontal strokes start like a silkworm’s head and end like a swallow’s tail, 蚕头燕尾.

yuwen/yw-idioms.66878baa8d4d: A couplet, 对联, is a pair of lines that mirror each other: the same number of characters, matching word types and structure, and opposite tones. Characters marked 入 were “entering tones” in old Chinese and count as 仄.

yuwen/yw-modern-classics.1ed4af211d4e: 好一个安塞腰鼓. The recurring exclamation acts like a refrain. It allows each new description to rise from the same rhythmic point.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.391432a35380: 整个世界. The phrase enlarges what looks like an ordinary act of carrying. The adults feel the weight of caring for the older and younger generations together.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.5272da740869: 望. This verb directs the eye across a wide landscape. The later historical discussion inherits that expansive scale.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.98c2910beac0: 繁多. The word puts visible variety into the argument. Unity matters here because differences are still visible.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.159f20813662: 勤劳一生. The phrase sums up years of daily work. The essay shows how the mother’s habits shaped the choices her son made as an adult.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.a372ee28322f: Mao Dun wrote this wartime essay in nineteen forty-one. Its description of northern landscapes makes room for a tribute to people who resist hardship.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.26da0eae2315: A short story first published in nineteen twenty-five and later collected in Stories of Family Life. Its first-person narrator looks back on an accusation he wishes he could take back.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.97caadd9c74c: A memoir first printed in Mangyuan in nineteen twenty-six and collected in Dawn Blossoms Plucked at Dusk. The adult writer revisits the places where he grew up in Shaoxing, Zhejiang. A private study of this kind was a traditional school run by a tutor.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.65eeb41dd0da: The American poet first published this poem in The Atlantic in nineteen fifteen. It was later collected in Mountain Interval. The path in the poem is a visible object a reader can also interpret as a life decision.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.f1e373fad6a7: Written in nineteen thirty-eight during the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression. Ai Qing imagines a bird singing in a wounded landscape.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.0480987e0e26: Bian, a poet and translator, uses a compact four-line lyric to shift the point from which ordinary scenes are seen. The poem dates to nineteen thirty-five.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.c332a09ac53a: 淡黑的起伏的连山, 仿佛是踊跃的铁的兽脊似的. The dark, rolling ridges looked like the backs of iron beasts bounding away. The dark ridges look like backs leaping backward because the boat is moving swiftly. The moving image carries the children’s impatience to arrive.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.cf6a6d3f0126: An excerpt from Yang’s memoir of Shenzhou five, China’s first crewed space mission, in two thousand three. He records what he could observe and how he responded to uncertainty.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.7a7dc30081db: 三哼经. A-Chang’s own way of saying the title Shan Hai Jing. Her misremembered title marks how unfamiliar the book is to her. The gap between those few sounds and her successful search makes the gift startling.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.db5af59e3f3d: 依依. The repeated sound makes remembering feel lingering and affectionate. The same mood ties together episodes that otherwise happen at different times and places.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.de42dbf25dc9: First published in New Youth in nineteen nineteen and collected in Call to Arms. A tavern worker remembers a poor man who clings to the status of a scholar in the world of the old examination system.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.3a68d96310e8: National textbook platform: Grade nine, Volume one
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.7a05ee398119: Written during the war in nineteen forty-one. Duanmu writes of northeastern China as a homeland remembered in absence.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.d3d380ad4f51: 愧怍. The last word makes the narrator reexamine her own conduct. It opens a question about dignity and recognition beyond the value of the gift.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.fcf6f495db2e: 年轻舵手. The image joins responsibility to uncertainty. Having the steering role raises the stakes of the storm.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.7535b6c740eb: Lu Xun began studying medicine here in nineteen oh four. The memoir recounts both the support of his anatomy professor and the experiences that preceded his departure.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.c6787351c16c: This canal-country story uses nicknames and lively narration to evoke local storytelling. The revised textbook moves the excerpt from Grade nine, Volume two to Volume one.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.a5b13b747679: 其实地上本没有路; 走的人多了, 也便成了路. The ground has no trail at first. When enough people walk there, a trail takes shape. A trail is made by repeated footsteps. The metaphor makes hope depend on what people do together. The moonlit setting returns as the narrator imagines that future.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.f8da94ee0dda: 一丈青大娘. The nickname recalls a Water Margin heroine and prepares the reader for a vigorous, outspoken character before any description is complete.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.a4a3f68d4087: Grade nine, Volume one, Unit four
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.514cbd529487: Grade nine, Volume one, Unit one
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.d16ad57a8643: Educator Yu Yi recalls how books, teachers and familiar views shaped her as a reader. This is a recent addition to the Grade seven reading unit.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.ae658fda1dfd: Wen spoke in Kunming on July fifteenth, nineteen forty-six, at a memorial meeting for Li Gongpu. Different records preserve slightly different wordings.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.f31dbce5c073: 定然. The repeated word of certainty makes an imagined scene sound vividly present. It gives a wish the force of conviction.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.e5bf4fc3207d: Dai’s short elegy remembers the writer Xiao Hong, who died in Hong Kong in nineteen forty-two. 口占 refers to composing aloud on the spot.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.593475258c28: A short story first published in New Youth in May nineteen twenty-one, later collected in Call to Arms. A return to an ancestral home frames a story about childhood closeness and adult social distance.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.6d2cf2a8b098: Published in Literary Weekly on November twenty-second, nineteen twenty-five. In this memoir a son looks back on a farewell at Pukou, across the Yangtze from central Nanjing. His grandmother has died and his father has lost his position.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.fce243c0dfe8: Frost moved to England with his family in nineteen twelve and returned to the United States in nineteen fifteen, the year The Road Not Taken first appeared.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.6c501a792c78: First published in New Youth in January nineteen eighteen. Shen was teaching at Peking University and taking part in the New Culture movement. The poem uses conversational wording and line breaks typical of early experiments in modern verse.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.0005b253e5b6: 我永无改正我的过失的机会了! After the death, the cry marks a change from certainty about the cat’s guilt to certainty about the narrator’s own wrongdoing.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.07ff05fcdd9d: Published in nineteen twenty-two as 天上的市街 and collected in Starry Sky. Older volumes put it among the readings, while the revised Grade seven volume places it with the Unit six writing materials.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.3b3df96044b2: 手牵着手, 肩并着肩. The repetition gives cooperation a bodily form. As the forest grows more oppressive, the image keeps the “we” together.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.564920143348: Grade seven, Volume one, Unit five
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.e84604e4296b: 瀑布. The metaphor gives a hanging mass of flowers direction and movement. That motion prepares the passage from standing still to walking again.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.d0d401a6ce14: Grade seven, Volume one, Unit four
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.14bf7dbe8a34: 燎原. A light held in one hand broadens into fire spreading across open country. The expanding scale matches the essay’s growing public concern.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.62aaed2833a1: Grade seven, Volume one, Unit six
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.448f13fdc600: Without the ending there are two silhouettes. With it the speaker’s posture becomes a choice. The continuing “着” also keeps the whole scene in the present.

yuwen/yw-modern-classics.3a989801bd9d: 明朗. A word often used for light describes a laugh. It gives the reader a sensory impression of warmth and openness.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.cfa8cb03446a: Mu Dan wrote this poem in nineteen thirty-eight. An opening scene of movement in nature grows into an imagined joining of human feeling and the world.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.cd8dc63ab8ad: 啊! 黄河! Direct address sets off successive sections and gives each a fresh surge of emphasis. The river becomes the figure the speaker can praise face to face.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.5ccd033bc1ae: 自由花. A living flower gives the abstract ideal of freedom a visible shape. The image sends the imagined result past the speaker’s own lifetime.

yuwen/yw-modern-classics.a89eea94e9cb: A nineteen twenty-six memoir from Dawn Blossoms Plucked at Dusk. In Sendai, Japan, Lu Xun studied medicine and met anatomy teacher Fujino Genkurō. The narrator recalls how the experience shaped his decision to leave medicine.
yuwen/yw-modern-classics.f05f8ba223c0: 静谧. This word gives the autumn scene a mood as well as a sound level. Notice how that mood prepares the inward turn.
