_shared.3102fb266537: Oregon City. The end of the Oregon Trail, beside the falls of the Willamette River. In eighteen forty-four it became the first incorporated US city west of the Rocky Mountains.
_shared.4530af91a3a6: Xiao and Xiang Rivers. Today: where the Xiao meets the Xiang, Yongzhou, Hunan. The Xiao River joins the Xiang at Yongzhou; the Xiang then flows north into Dongting Lake. In poems 潇湘 means the lands of southern Hunan — “南极潇湘”.
_shared.a89b454c642a: Rabun County. Cherokee mountain land given up in eighteen seventeen to eighteen nineteen became Rabun County, in Georgia’s far northeast corner. Its mountains, lakes and the deep Tallulah Gorge on its southern edge make it a favorite place for hikers.
_shared.ec761239c409: Carter Center. Jimmy and Rosalynn Carter started the Carter Center to watch over fair elections and fight diseases around the world. Its work has nearly wiped out Guinea worm disease — from about three point five million cases a year in nineteen eighty-six to only a handful today; the presidential library and museum share the same hilltop.
_shared.6e84015b2d73: Abilene. In eighteen sixty-seven a businessman built cattle pens next to the Kansas Pacific railroad in this Kansas town, and Texas cowboys drove huge herds up the Chisholm Trail to load them onto trains heading east. Later it was the hometown of President Dwight D. Eisenhower.
_shared.9d86aadd0aa9: Indus Valley. Today: mainly Pakistan. About four thousand five hundred years ago cities here, such as Mohenjo-daro, had brick houses on neat street grids and covered drains.
_shared.fceaf6af94fe: Ocmulgee Mounds. People have lived here for more than twelve thousand years — a Clovis spear point was found here — and around A D nine hundred Mississippian farmers built a town with big earth mounds. You can climb the fifty-five-foot Great Temple Mound and step inside the Earth Lodge, whose clay floor is about one thousand years old.
_shared.e582c732ab16: Anchorage. Alaska’s biggest city. In June the Sun shines for over nineteen hours a day; in December for less than six.
_shared.44c6cf92286c: Golconda. Late in eighteen thirty-eight, Trail of Tears groups crossed the Ohio River into Illinois by ferry at this little river town. The ferry owner charged the Cherokee a dollar a person — about eight times the usual fare.
_shared.0777987384c6: Lookout Mountain. A long, flat-topped mountain of the Appalachian Plateau that runs from Georgia into Alabama and Tennessee; Cloudland Canyon is cut into its side. In eighteen sixty-three Union soldiers won the “Battle Above the Clouds” on its northern end.
_shared.7e996fb00831: Titusville. In eighteen fifty-nine Edwin Drake drilled America’s first commercial oil well near this Pennsylvania town, striking oil at sixty-nine and a half feet. Within a few years the valley was crowded with wooden derricks in a real oil rush.
_shared.6ad7c2522c9a: Ravenna. The last Western Roman emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was removed here in four seventy-six. Its churches glitter with Byzantine mosaics of Emperor Justinian.
_shared.d59b53a7d1ad: Strait of Hormuz. The narrow sea passage out of the Persian Gulf. It is about forty kilometers wide at its narrowest. About a fifth of the world’s oil passes through it on tankers.
_shared.c3c66a198c71: Lake Pontchartrain Causeway. Today: Louisiana, USA. A pair of low bridges about thirty-eight kilometers long across a lake near New Orleans — one of the longest bridges over water in the world.
_shared.187c1b75f0b3: Tahlequah. After the Trail of Tears the Cherokee made Tahlequah their new capital in eighteen thirty-nine, and the last groups arrived in March. The brick Cherokee National Capitol was finished in eighteen sixty-nine, and the town’s street signs are written in both English and Cherokee.
_shared.d49ef3c7c047: Mount Hood. Oregon’s highest peak is a snow-capped volcano. It stands eleven thousand two hundred forty-nine feet high. The Barlow Road, opened in eighteen forty-six, went around its south side on the last stretch to Oregon City.
_shared.085b0ff58b56: Mombasa. Goods for much of East Africa arrive here. A new Chinese-built railway, opened in twenty seventeen, links the port to Nairobi.
_shared.a9f3ad841b6c: St. Augustine. Founded forty-two years before Jamestown, it is the oldest city in the US that Europeans started and people have lived in ever since. Its fort, the Castillo de San Marcos, is built of coquina, a stone made of tiny shells that swallowed cannonballs instead of cracking.
_shared.fc80ecdd56b1: Tyler Perry Studios. Filmmaker Tyler Perry turned about three hundred thirty acres of the old Fort McPherson army base into a studio campus, opened in twenty nineteen — one of the first major studios in the US owned by an African American. It has sound stages named after Black actors and even a full-size copy of the White House.
_shared.f9b918392688: Columbus. Founded in eighteen twenty-eight at the last falls of the Chattahoochee River, where water power ran big textile mills. Today it is Georgia’s second-largest city, next to Fort Benning, and its river has one of the longest city whitewater rafting runs in the world.
_shared.dadc9462df8c: Euphrates River. It flows about two thousand eight hundred kilometers from the mountains of Türkiye through Syria and Iraq to the Persian Gulf. Ur, Uruk and Babylon stood beside it.
_shared.d48a1997b951: Chickamauga. The biggest battle ever fought in Georgia: a Confederate victory with about thirty-four thousand six hundred men killed, wounded or missing. Union General George Thomas held firm and became the “Rock of Chickamauga”; in eighteen ninety the battlefield became the first national military park.
_shared.533c01b3baaf: Waco. The Chisholm Trail crossed the Brazos River at Waco, Texas. Its Suspension Bridge, finished in eighteen seventy, was the first bridge over the river, and cowboys paid a toll to drive their herds across it on the way to Kansas.
_shared.167ad9864883: Greensboro. On the first of February, nineteen sixty, four Black college students sat down at the “whites only” lunch counter in Greensboro’s Woolworth’s and politely asked to be served. Sit-ins spread to dozens of cities, and in July nineteen sixty the counter began serving Black customers; the old store is now the International Civil Rights Center and Museum.
_shared.b718ef36f174: Fort Bridger. Mountain man Jim Bridger opened this trading post in eighteen forty-three, where emigrants could rest, buy supplies and repair wagons. The route through it was longer than the Sublette Cutoff but had more water and grass.
_shared.73cd94e60d1e: Mogadishu. Today: Mogadishu, Somalia. A trading city on the east coast of Africa. Zheng He’s ships came here more than seventy years before Vasco da Gama.
_shared.5b781a3140ba: Rome. A city in the Valley and Ridge region where the Etowah and Oostanaula rivers meet to form the Coosa. Like ancient Rome it sits on seven hills — that is how it got its name in eighteen thirty-four.
_shared.1d5c10d912c4: Quito. Capital of Ecuador, almost exactly on the equator but two thousand eight hundred fifty meters up in the Andes, so it is about fourteen degrees Celsius all year — “eternal spring”.
_shared.8d20610925d8: Ngorongoro Crater. A huge collapsed volcano in Tanzania, about twenty kilometers across, full of wildlife. Maasai herders graze their cattle in the area.
_shared.d0c15f042670: Córdoba. Around the year one thousand it was one of the biggest cities in Europe, with paved streets, street lamps and huge libraries. Its Great Mosque has red-and-white arches.
_shared.d719a014d833: City of Manchester Stadium. A stadium in Manchester, England, with about fifty-three thousand seats — a fixed supply, whatever the demand for tickets.
_shared.8e0f8e1abede: Red Flag Canal. Today: Linzhou, Lin County, Henan. People of Lin County cut a one-thousand-five-hundred-kilometer canal network along the cliffs of the Taihang Mountains, mostly with hammers and chisels, to bring water from the Zhang River.
_shared.d826e6104f64: Guam. After about ninety-eight days on the open ocean, Magellan’s starving crew reached this island of the Chamorro people. Later Manila galleons stopped here.
_shared.50695f311e75: Mainz. Johannes Gutenberg printed his famous Bible here around fourteen fifty-five with metal movable type. The Gutenberg Museum still shows how it worked.
_shared.749f5353af1a: Fort Sumter. Confederate guns around Charleston Harbor fired on this US fort on an island for thirty-four hours until it surrendered — the Civil War had begun. Amazingly, no one was killed in the bombardment; today boats take visitors out to the fort.
_shared.3dd84b6126d4: Baghdad. Around seven ninety-three a paper mill opened in Baghdad, then the capital of the Arab empire. From the Arab world, paper later travelled on to Europe.
_shared.e966114676b3: Ozarks. The Ozarks are an old, worn-down highland of forested hills, caves and springs in Missouri and Arkansas. Trail of Tears groups struggled across them in the middle of winter eighteen thirty-nine, short of blankets, food and warm clothes.
_shared.9c7b45e7f1e2: Selma. On “Bloody Sunday”, March seventh, nineteen sixty-five, state troopers beat peaceful marchers, led by John Lewis, on the Edmund Pettus Bridge. Two weeks later thousands marched fifty-four miles from Selma to Montgomery, and Congress soon passed the Voting Rights Act.
_shared.53b8e1e9213d: King Street. Today: State Street, Boston. On the fifth of March, seventeen seventy, British soldiers fired into an angry crowd here, killing five people, including Crispus Attucks, a sailor of African and Native American descent. A ring of cobblestones in front of the Old State House marks the spot today.
_shared.43980dc0ecda: Puerto Rico. A Caribbean island that the United States took from Spain after the Spanish-American War of eighteen ninety-eight. Puerto Ricans have been US citizens since nineteen seventeen, and the old Spanish fortress El Morro still guards San Juan’s harbor.
_shared.331b2b5e48fa: Nevada. Part of the land Mexico gave up in eighteen forty-eight, it was rushed into the Union on the thirty-first of October, eighteen sixty-four, in the middle of the Civil War, after rich silver was found at the Comstock Lode. Hoover Dam stands on its border with Arizona.
_shared.803616a53494: William Frantz Elementary School. On the fourteenth of November, nineteen sixty, six-year-old Ruby Bridges walked into this New Orleans school past shouting crowds, guarded by federal marshals, as its first Black student. For most of that year she was the only child in her class, taught by her teacher Barbara Henry.
_shared.4b5e9f907a14: Tybee Island. Georgia’s northernmost barrier island, at the mouth of the Savannah River; a lighthouse has stood here since seventeen thirty-six. In eighteen sixty-two Union cannons on Tybee, about a mile away, broke a hole in Fort Pulaski’s brick walls in about thirty hours.
_shared.a080e0ef3087: Omaha. The Union Pacific began laying track west from Omaha, on the Missouri River, in eighteen sixty-five. Until a bridge opened in eighteen seventy-two, trains from the east crossed the river by ferry — and in one winter, on tracks laid across the ice!
_shared.56f4e4d9e1ed: Shenzhen. In nineteen eighty Shenzhen was a small border town next to Hong Kong. As a Special Economic Zone it grew into a high-tech city of over seventeen million people.
_shared.2ea9218bdadc: Cambrai. Nearly four hundred British tanks attacked together here, breaking through the German trenches for a short time.
_shared.4f7141207c8a: Chengdu Plain. Thanks to Dujiangyan, the Chengdu Plain has had no floods or droughts for two thousand years and became the “Land of Abundance”.
_shared.84234f1d66d3: Los Alamos. In nineteen forty-three the Army took over a boys’ ranch school on a remote mesa in New Mexico, and scientists led by J. Robert Oppenheimer secretly designed the first atomic bombs there. All their mail went to one address: P.O. Box one six six three, Santa Fe.
_shared.390dc885a0da: Camp Hancock. Today: site in Augusta, Georgia. Pennsylvania’s twenty-eighth “Keystone” Division trained at this camp on the edge of Augusta, which also had one of the Army’s first airfields. In nineteen eighteen the deadly flu struck and about three thousand soldiers fell sick, so the camp was quarantined.
_shared.e61b5b475f77: Padua. Galileo taught mathematics at the University of Padua for eighteen years. Here he built telescopes and found four moons circling Jupiter.
_shared.bcd0bc56ef68: Fort Frederica. Oglethorpe built this fort town on St. Simons Island to guard Georgia against the Spanish. After the soldiers left in seventeen forty-nine the town faded away; today you can walk its old streets past the brick foundations of the houses.
_shared.e1a664a09ce7: Wittenberg. Martin Luther taught at the university here. In fifteen seventeen he posted his ninety-five Theses — the story says on the door of the Castle Church.
_shared.7e4c995a1a6d: University of Georgia. Chartered on January twenty-seventh, seventeen eighty-five, it was the first state-chartered public university in the US; Abraham Baldwin wrote its charter. In January nineteen sixty-one Charlayne Hunter and Hamilton Holmes became its first Black students, after a federal judge ordered the university to admit them.
_shared.d2b7efab1d01: Chatham County. Home of Savannah and its busy port, on Georgia’s northern coast. It was one of Georgia’s first eight counties, created in seventeen seventy-seven.
_shared.8fdd4699fab6: Camp Stewart. Today: Fort Stewart, Hinesville, Georgia. In nineteen forty, as World War Two spread, the Army opened this huge camp near Hinesville to train soldiers to use anti-aircraft guns. Whole villages were moved out to make room; today Fort Stewart is the largest Army base east of the Mississippi.
_shared.c9d752a2bfcd: Hanyang. Today: Hanyang District, Wuhan. Hanyang lies across the Yangtze from the Yellow Crane Tower. Its Qingchuan Pavilion, 晴川阁, is named after Cui Hao’s line about the sunlit river.
_shared.e4139ec58109: Raleigh. In April nineteen sixty, after the lunch-counter sit-ins, Ella Baker brought student protesters to Shaw University in Raleigh, North Carolina, where they founded Snick, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. Snick soon moved its office to Atlanta.
_shared.e311b4b83248: Hazlehurst. A small town in south Georgia farm country. In the nineteen thirties the photographer Dorothea Lange took pictures of sharecropper families near here, showing that sharecropping and poverty lasted long after Reconstruction.
_shared.46b31cb13e86: Hawaii. A chain of volcanic islands in the middle of the Pacific, the fiftieth US state. On the Big Island, Kīlauea is one of the most active volcanoes on Earth.
_shared.32b21cf906f6: Frederick Douglass National Historic Site. Frederick Douglass, who escaped slavery as a young man, spent his last years in this hilltop house in Washington, D.C., which he called Cedar Hill. From the porch you can see the US Capitol, and his desk and more than one thousand of his books are still inside.
_shared.6be21673daf5: University of Utah. In Salt Lake City, at the foot of the Wasatch Mountains, it was one of the first four ARPANET sites in nineteen sixty-nine. Its computer-graphics pioneers made the famous “Utah teapot”, a three D model still used to test graphics today.
_shared.537f4ac2d0f0: Fairbanks. A town in central Alaska at about sixty-five degrees north, just south of the Arctic Circle. Around the summer solstice the Sun barely sets.
_shared.4924319a42b4: Ocute. Today: Oconee River valley, central Georgia. A powerful chiefdom on the Oconee River. In April fifteen forty de Soto marched here from Ichisi, and its chief gave the Spaniards food and hundreds of carriers for their journey.
_shared.9bd6525c7b8c: Glascock County. One of Georgia’s smallest counties, with about three thousand people; its county seat is Gibson. In the county unit system, its votes counted far more per person than votes in big cities like Atlanta.
_shared.a8299fce5cb7: St. Simons Island. One of Georgia’s “Golden Isles,” the barrier islands of the coast. Oglethorpe built Fort Frederica here, and in seventeen forty-two his soldiers stopped a Spanish invasion at Bloody Marsh; today a white lighthouse from eighteen seventy-two greets visitors.
_shared.d8ea32edff2f: Springfield. Today: Springfield Armory National Historic Site, Massachusetts. In January seventeen eighty-seven Daniel Shays led about one thousand five hundred angry farmers, crushed by debts and taxes, to seize the weapons stored here; state militia fired cannon and scattered them. The weak national government had no army to send — one reason leaders wanted a new Constitution.
_shared.831e2e34bf1e: Apalachee River. A Piedmont river that winds southeast through northeast Georgia and flows into the Oconee River at Lake Oconee. In eighteen eighteen the Creek gave up land near its headwaters.
_shared.b5778bc33243: Normandy. In ten sixty-six Duke William sailed from here to conquer England. On D-Day about one hundred fifty-six thousand Allied troops landed on its beaches to free France.
_shared.f2556d0634ec: Vicksburg. This city on high bluffs above the Mississippi was called the “Gibraltar of the Confederacy”. During the forty-seven-day siege, families dug caves into the hillsides to hide from the shells; when it surrendered to Grant on the fourth of July, eighteen sixty-three, the Union controlled the whole Mississippi River.
_shared.6b4fcda57d14: Pamirs, Congling. A knot of huge mountains where the Silk Road climbed over four thousand meters. China’s westernmost point is here.
_shared.e123cc41d779: Delaware River. On Christmas night seventeen seventy-six, George Washington’s army crossed this icy river in boats and surprised the enemy at Trenton the next morning. Every Christmas Day, people in costume re-enact the crossing at Washington Crossing.
_shared.dfffb7837f70: Mawangdui. Today: Changsha, Hunan. The tombs held silk maps, silk books and a robe that weighs only forty-nine grams. The finds are in the Hunan Museum.
_shared.0bf7a902f39b: Monmouth. Today: Freehold, New Jersey. On the twenty-eighth of June, seventeen seventy-eight, in heat near one hundred degrees Fahrenheit, thirty-eight degrees Celsius, the two armies fought all day with no clear winner — many soldiers collapsed from heatstroke. Legend says “Molly Pitcher” carried water to the troops here.
_shared.62436c9f141b: Xiaozhai Tiankeng. Today: Fengjie, Chongqing. The deepest known sinkhole in the world, about six hundred sixty meters deep — formed when the roof over an underground river fell in.
_shared.b48694013de4: Grand Bazaar, Istanbul. One of the largest and oldest covered markets in the world, with over four thousand shops under its domed roofs.
_shared.ac733f0eaa66: Bunker Hill, Breed’s Hill. Today: Charlestown, Boston. On the seventeenth of June, seventeen seventy-five, most of the fighting was actually on Breed’s Hill: the British took it on their third charge but lost more than one thousand men killed or wounded. Peter Salem, a Black soldier who had been enslaved, fought here; a two hundred twenty-one-foot granite obelisk stands on the hill today.
_shared.52da5f6d9629: Zebulon. The small county seat of Pike County; both the town and the county are named after the explorer Zebulon Pike, who gave his name to Pikes Peak. Its eighteen ninety-five courthouse stands in the middle of town.
_shared.b0172dd56ca2: Qinghai-Tibet Railway. Today: Xining to Lhasa, pin: Tanggula Pass, five thousand seventy-two meters. The highest railway in the world. Engineers kept the frozen ground cold with special pipes so the tracks would not sink.
_shared.4709082571a2: La Paz. Bolivia’s seat of government, about three thousand six hundred meters up in the Andes — the highest capital city in the world. Cable cars are part of its public transport.
_shared.2547e15af0ad: Nathan Deal Judicial Center. Opened in twenty nineteen next to the Capitol, this is the home of the Supreme Court of Georgia, whose nine justices hear the state’s most important appeals. It is named for Nathan Deal, governor from twenty eleven to twenty nineteen.
_shared.6f18f3284225: Marietta. A city northwest of Atlanta, just below Kennesaw Mountain. In nineteen fifteen a mob kidnapped Leo Frank, a Jewish factory manager, from prison and lynched him near here; in World War Two about twenty-eight thousand workers built B two nine bombers at the Bell plant.
_shared.655e03fc6707: Fort Wool. Today: New Echota, near Calhoun, Georgia. In May eighteen thirty-eight US soldiers built this stockade at the old Cherokee capital, and rounded-up Cherokee families were held inside before being marched to camps in Tennessee. Nothing is left of it; a sign at New Echota tells its story.
_shared.7c7a730b1ba7: Bai Causeway. Today: West Lake, Hangzhou. A one-kilometer dyke lined with willows, from the Broken Bridge to Gushan. It was already there in Bai Juyi’s time; later people named it after him because he loved it so much.
_shared.5fc28778f11e: Yongzhou. Today: Yongzhou, Hunan. A remote place in southern Hunan in the Tang. During ten years of exile Liu Zongyuan explored its hills and streams and wrote the “Eight Records of Yongzhou”, 永州八记.
_shared.a80a25d1165b: Bering Strait. About eighty-two kilometers wide, between Russia, Asia, and Alaska, North America. In the Ice Age it was dry land that people and animals walked across.
_shared.8f9cc1e8c49d: Linqing. Where the canal met the Wei River, 卫河, Linqing became one of the busiest trading cities of the Ming. Many bricks of Beijing’s Forbidden City were fired here and shipped north on the canal.
_shared.137d0c1ba823: Sanxingdui. Today: Guanghan, Sichuan. Huge bronze masks with bulging eyes and a four-meter bronze “sacred tree” show a rich civilisation in the southwest at the same time as the Shang.
_shared.09fa6394637b: Wuling. Today: Changde, Hunan. The fisherman of “桃花源记” came from Wuling, by the Yuan River. Tao Yuanming chose a real place to start an imaginary journey.
_shared.6dac4e48ca1e: Nagqu. Today: Tibet. A town at about four thousand five hundred meters on the northern Tibetan grasslands, a stop on the Qinghai-Tibet Railway.
_shared.66b297a70ba7: Arecibo Observatory. Today: Puerto Rico, USA. A three hundred five-meter radio dish hung in a sinkhole in Puerto Rico — the world’s largest for fifty-three years, until FAST. It collapsed in twenty twenty.
_shared.8573ec93251e: Big Shanty. Today: Kennesaw, Georgia. On April twelfth, eighteen sixty-two, Union spies led by James Andrews stole the locomotive “General” here while the crew ate breakfast, starting the Great Locomotive Chase. The real “General” is on display in the town’s Southern Museum today.
_shared.503171721e99: Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei. The capital region around Beijing, Tianjin and Hebei, home to over one hundred million people. Since twenty fourteen the three have planned transport, industry and the environment together.
_shared.fe6f3f8df303: Ringgold. The stolen “General” ran out of fuel just north of Ringgold after a chase of about eighty-seven miles, and the raiders fled into the woods and were caught. The town’s eighteen forty-nine stone depot still shows patches where Civil War cannonballs hit it.
_shared.1917335ad5fb: Kia Georgia plant. A car factory in West Point, Georgia, opened in two thousand nine. Robots and assembly lines — capital goods — help thousands of workers build hundreds of thousands of cars a year.
_shared.6351a9c005bb: Qaidam Basin. About three thousand meters high on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, rich in salt, oil and minerals. Its dry, red land looks like Mars.
_shared.3488d39e546a: Princeton. On the third of January, seventeen seventy-seven, a week after Trenton, Washington slipped around the British army at night and beat its rear guard here. The fighting reached Nassau Hall of the college that is now Princeton University.
_shared.589f1d15cd32: Red River Basin. Today: parts of North Dakota and Minnesota. The land drained by the Red River of the North, which flows north into Canada — unusual for an American river. The US gained its southern part from Britain in the Convention of eighteen eighteen, which set the border at forty-nine degrees north.
_shared.03203cf95626: Georgia Tech. Georgia’s big engineering university opened in eighteen eighty-five to help build a “New South” of factories and railroads. The brick Tech Tower, with “TECH” spelled down its sides in lights, is the campus landmark.
_shared.fc7a24e53aea: Tanggula Mountains. Today: Border of Qinghai and Tibet. The Yangtze begins at Geladaindong, the highest peak of these mountains. The Qinghai-Tibet Railway crosses them at over five thousand meters.
_shared.de943742f33b: Montgomery. In February eighteen sixty-one the seceded states met here, formed the Confederacy and chose Jefferson Davis as president. Almost a century later, Rosa Parks’s arrest started the three hundred eighty-one-day Montgomery bus boycott, and in nineteen sixty-five the Selma marchers ended their walk at the very same state capitol.
_shared.99ee71b71380: California. Gold was found at Sutter’s Mill in eighteen forty-eight, and within a few years about three hundred thousand people rushed in — Chinese miners called it “Gold Mountain”, 金山. It joined as a free state in eighteen fifty and today has more people than any other state.
_shared.f370cf81dcc6: Lintao. Today: Min County, Gansu. The Qin wall ran about five thousand kilometers from Lintao in the west to Liaodong in the east.
_shared.9259877779b4: St. Louis. In May eighteen oh four Lewis and Clark’s Corps of Discovery set out from near here up the Missouri River. Today the six hundred thirty-foot Gateway Arch, the tallest monument in the US, remembers the city as the “Gateway to the West.”
_shared.d5c7bf1bb5db: Centennial Olympic Park. Atlanta turned run-down blocks downtown into this park for the nineteen ninety-six Olympics. On July twenty-seventh, nineteen ninety-six, a bomb went off at a concert here, killing two people; today kids splash in its fountain shaped like the five Olympic rings.
_shared.05a7e01a561e: Yongning Temple. Today: Han-Wei Luoyang city site, east of Luoyang. Its nine-storey wooden pagoda was perhaps about one hundred forty meters high — one of the tallest buildings in the world then. It burned down in five thirty-four; only the base remains.
_shared.0bdeeba26977: Detroit. Henry Ford made Detroit the “Motor City”: his Model T came out in nineteen oh eight and his moving assembly line in nineteen thirteen. Black families came here in the Great Migration for factory jobs, and in World War Two the Willow Run plant nearby built bombers.
_shared.dc18b7b0eb4a: Manchester. Steam-powered cotton mills made Manchester the first great industrial city. In eighteen thirty the first inter-city railway linked it with Liverpool.
_shared.cb3c6a7aae36: Baoji. Many Zhou bronzes were dug up around Baoji in Shaanxi, including the He Zun, whose inscription has the oldest known “中国”.
_shared.d9234e32e149: Appian Way. The “queen of roads” ran from Rome to Brundisium, Brindisi. Its paving stones are still there after more than two thousand three hundred years.
_shared.c2bdd0ca7d57: Fort King George. Built in seventeen twenty-one near the mouth of the Altamaha, it was the first British fort on what became Georgia’s coast — twelve years before the colony began. Today a rebuilt wooden blockhouse stands near where the Highland Scots settled Darien in seventeen thirty-six.
_shared.7bc0a3dd1203: New Jersey. Between New York and Philadelphia, New Jersey saw so many battles that it is called the “Crossroads of the Revolution” — Washington crossed the icy Delaware to surprise Trenton in seventeen seventy-six. Later Thomas Edison invented the phonograph and a practical light bulb at Menlo Park here.
_shared.b2bd3cc95449: Los Angeles. Founded in seventeen eighty-one by forty-four Spanish-speaking settlers, more than half of them of African or Native descent, it is now the second-largest city in the US. The Southern Pacific’s Sunset Route linked it to New Orleans in eighteen eighty-three, and in the Great Migration many Black families moved here from the South.
_shared.b0fbfbcfd5b6: New Sweden. Today: Delaware and nearby. Sweden’s only colony in America lay along the Delaware River; the Dutch took it in sixteen fifty-five, and the English took it from them in sixteen sixty-four. Its Swedish and Finnish settlers probably brought the log cabin to America.
_shared.fd55893fd426: Santa Catalina de Guale. The main Spanish mission among the Guale people. Guale people burned it in a revolt in fifteen ninety-seven; it was rebuilt in sixteen oh five and abandoned in sixteen eighty after attacks, and archaeologists found its church in nineteen eighty-one.
_shared.dfcedd7e2630: Horseshoe Curve. To climb the steep Alleghenies near Altoona, the railroad bent its tracks into a giant U-shaped bend. It opened in eighteen fifty-four, and long freight trains still squeal around it today; in World War Two, German saboteurs were sent to blow it up but were caught first.
_shared.8cfc2ede59d3: Valley of the Kings. Pharaohs were buried in tombs cut deep into the rock of this desert valley. Tutankhamun’s tomb, found almost untouched in nineteen twenty-two, is here.
_shared.bd79d9fb870d: Stallings Island. A small island in the Savannah River just above Augusta. People camped here about four thousand five hundred years ago and left a huge heap of river mussel shells — along with some of the oldest pottery in North America.
_shared.a27cc7e3157a: English Channel. The strip of sea between Britain and France, only about thirty-three kilometers wide at the Strait of Dover. Trains cross under it in the Channel Tunnel.
_shared.2abc048a9a57: Fulton County. Georgia’s most populous county, home of Atlanta, the state capital. Under the old county-unit system its five hundred fifty-six thousand three hundred twenty-six people got just six unit votes — the same as three tiny rural counties — until the courts struck the system down in nineteen sixty-three.
_shared.49d818a281c6: Site where the nineteen fifty-four Constitution was drafted. China’s first Constitution was drafted in this house beside West Lake. Today it is a museum about the history of the Constitution.
_shared.7f5d0cbe4f8f: Pont du Gard. Three rows of stone arches carry an aqueduct forty-nine meters above the river. The water channel drops only about two point five centimeters in the whole bridge.
_shared.9f9bfedf0d6b: Fort Pulaski. Georgia troops seized this brick fort near Savannah in January eighteen sixty-one. In April eighteen sixty-two new Union rifled cannons on Tybee Island punched a hole through its thick walls in about thirty hours — brick forts were suddenly out of date. You can still see the cannonball scars.
_shared.7fcd2b12ca7e: Forsyth County. In nineteen twelve white mobs forced about one thousand Black residents out of this county north of Atlanta, and for decades it stayed almost all white. In January nineteen eighty-seven a small march for “brotherhood” was attacked; a week later about twenty thousand people marched here.
_shared.7795570328d0: Grand Canal. The longest canal of the ancient world. Grain boats sailed north on it to feed the capital. The Yuan “straightened” it to run from Hangzhou straight to Dadu, Beijing, about one thousand eight hundred kilometers. It became a World Heritage Site in twenty fourteen.
_shared.8e9f05ce3666: Taihang Mountains. The Taihang range runs about four hundred kilometers north-south, between the Loess Plateau and the North China Plain.
_shared.a1ca411c8db6: Hartford. In sixteen thirty-six the minister Thomas Hooker led about one hundred settlers, driving their cattle, through the woods from Massachusetts to found it. Today it is the capital of Connecticut, and Mark Twain wrote “Tom Sawyer” in his house here.
_shared.ceff467ab6b8: The Somme. On the first day alone, about fifty-seven thousand British soldiers were killed or wounded. Tanks were used in battle for the first time here.
_shared.512c2c69e2e5: Mount Fuji. Japan’s highest mountain, three thousand seven hundred seventy-six meters, a volcano with an almost perfect cone. It last erupted in seventeen oh seven.
_shared.938492b675f4: Dahlonega. In eighteen twenty-eight to eighteen twenty-nine gold was found on Cherokee land here, and thousands of “Twenty-Niners” rushed in — America’s first big gold rush. The old courthouse on the town square is now a gold museum, and Dahlonega gold covers the dome of the State Capitol.
_shared.ac10771425c1: Damascus. One of the oldest cities in the world that people still live in. The Umayyad caliphs built its Great Mosque in the early seven hundreds.
_shared.969e0f5671b4: Longmen Grottoes. Today: south of Luoyang, Henan. The seventeen-meter Vairocana Buddha at Fengxian Temple was finished in six seventy-five under Empress Wu Zetian.
_shared.2018f6bb38e4: Kansas River. The first big river crossing on the Oregon Trail: families paid about five dollars for a ferry or risked fording it with their wagons. It flows east to join the Missouri River at Kansas City.
_shared.fbf6f10dccbf: Norris Dam. The first dam built by the Tennessee Valley Authority, TVA, on the Clinch River in Tennessee, begun in nineteen thirty-three and finished in nineteen thirty-six. TVA dams across seven states stopped floods and brought electricity to farms that had never had it.
_shared.c80ac9a398cf: Promontory Summit. Today: Golden Spike National Historical Park, Utah. On the tenth of May, eighteen sixty-nine, the Central Pacific and Union Pacific tracks met here, and a golden spike was tapped in — a telegraph sent one word, “DONE”, across the country. Today working copies of the two locomotives, Jupiter and Number one one nine, steam up and face each other nose to nose.
_shared.d326f57eb611: Kolomoki Mounds. One of the oldest and largest Woodland-period towns in the Southeast, in southwest Georgia. Its Mound A rises fifty-seven feet — the biggest Woodland platform mound in eastern North America — and you can climb the steps to the top.
_shared.a6823c69f6a5: Lorraine Motel. Today: National Civil Rights Museum, Memphis. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. had come to Memphis to support striking sanitation workers when he was shot on the balcony outside Room three oh six on the fourth of April, nineteen sixty-eight. The motel is now the National Civil Rights Museum, and a wreath hangs on the balcony where he stood.
_shared.c5ab7ed0de98: Fort Morris. An earthen fort at Sunbury guarding the Medway River. When the British demanded its surrender in November seventeen seventy-eight, Colonel John McIntosh replied “Come and take it!” — they backed off, though the fort fell in January seventeen seventy-nine; its earth walls can still be seen.
_shared.9727b20e0691: Lake Titicaca. A lake about three thousand eight hundred meters up in the Andes on the Peru-Bolivia border, often called the highest navigable lake in the world.
_shared.78c6a0807e0d: Ural Mountains. Old, low mountains running about two thousand five hundred kilometers north to south across Russia. They are the usual boundary between Europe and Asia.
_shared.56a034cfbb12: Denali. North America’s highest mountain, six thousand one hundred ninety meters, in Alaska. Its name means “the high one” in the local Koyukon language.
_shared.6a13d40dabc6: Cahokia. Near today’s St. Louis, Native Americans built a town of earth mounds; Monks Mound is about thirty meters high. Around eleven hundred it was the largest town north of Mexico.
_shared.ac73f8bccfca: Guilford Courthouse. Today: Greensboro, North Carolina. On the fifteenth of March, seventeen eighty-one, Cornwallis won the field against Nathanael Greene but lost about a quarter of his army. Worn out, he marched north to Virginia — and toward defeat at Yorktown.
_shared.68e2279c6d2c: Liberty Bell. This bell carries the words “Proclaim LIBERTY throughout all the Land.” Abolitionists fighting slavery gave it its name; its famous crack grew so big that it has not rung since eighteen forty-six.
_shared.de6c025ff8bb: The Arch, UGA. This iron arch, shaped like the one on Georgia’s state seal, is the front gate of the University of Georgia in Athens. In January nineteen sixty-one Charlayne Hunter and Hamilton Holmes walked through it as UGA’s first Black students, facing an angry crowd.
_shared.57da83538ab8: Wilkes County. A backcountry county made in seventeen seventy-seven from the seventeen seventy-three “New Purchase,” land the Creek and Cherokee were pressed to give up to pay off traders’ debts. The Battle of Kettle Creek was fought here, and its county seat, Washington, was the first town in the US named for George Washington.
_shared.3ba7046ef4b6: Washington Territory. Today: Washington State. Formed in eighteen fifty-three in the far Northwest. The Northern Pacific Railroad, finished in eighteen eighty-three, crossed the northern plains and Rocky Mountains to reach it, and settlers poured in; it became the state of Washington in eighteen eighty-nine.
_shared.34e602e45bdb: Kentucky. Kentucky was part of Virginia until it became a state in seventeen ninety-two. In the Civil War it was a slave state that stayed in the Union — Lincoln, who was born there, is said to have joked that he hoped to have God on his side, but he must have Kentucky.
_shared.e4a8c5fa3076: Cherokee Nation. Today: Northwest Georgia, the Nation is now based in Tahlequah, Oklahoma. The Cherokee Nation had its own written laws, a newspaper and a capital at New Echota. Georgia raffled off its land in the eighteen thirty-two lotteries, and in eighteen thirty-eight soldiers forced the Cherokee out on the Trail of Tears — the Nation rebuilt itself in Oklahoma, where it is based today.
_shared.ae50d328abf1: Sacramento. The Central Pacific began building east from California’s capital in eighteen sixty-three. Almost every rail, engine and spike had to come by ship all the way around South America first!
_shared.b8219a0cf213: Canary Islands. Columbus took on water and food at La Gomera, then let the trade winds blow him west. About thirty-six days later he sighted land.
_shared.a07ff1051ac3: Atlanta. It began in eighteen thirty-seven as “Terminus,” the end of a railroad line, then became Marthasville and, in eighteen forty-five, Atlanta. Burned in eighteen sixty-four, it rose again as the state capital, Dr. King’s hometown and host of the nineteen ninety-six Olympics — and its airport is one of the busiest in the world.
_shared.9be9185b3aa1: Saigon. Today: Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. North Vietnam took Saigon in nineteen seventy-five, ending the Vietnam War and reuniting the country. The city was renamed Ho Chi Minh City.
_shared.bfd3bf60fce4: Augusta. Founded in seventeen thirty-six as a fur-trading post at the Savannah River’s Fall Line, it is where treaties of seventeen sixty-three and seventeen seventy-three took huge areas of Creek and Cherokee land. Later its canal powered cotton mills, and today golfers know it for the Masters tournament.
_shared.8bf9a2804d24: Mount Kilimanjaro. Africa’s highest mountain, five thousand eight hundred ninety-five meters, a volcano in Tanzania. It has glaciers on top even though it is close to the equator.
_shared.7d38fadb75dc: Crozet, Virginia. A small town in Virginia where, in June two thousand eight, gas passed four dollars a gallon for the first time — world oil demand had grown faster than supply.
_shared.cf20bc8c619d: Jinggangshan. Today: on the Jiangxi-Hunan border. Mao Zedong led his troops into these mountains. In nineteen twenty-eight Zhu De’s army joined them here, and the Red Army began the road of “surrounding the cities from the countryside”.
_shared.cc8e7ffffb9b: Gettysburg. The largest battle ever fought in North America, with about fifty-one thousand casualties in three days — a turning point of the Civil War. On the second day Union soldiers held the rocky hill Little Round Top, and in November eighteen sixty-three Lincoln gave his short Gettysburg Address here.
_shared.1b114ac03b9f: Hudson River. Henry Hudson sailed up it in sixteen oh nine looking for a sea route to Asia, and the Dutch then built fur-trading posts along it. When the Erie Canal opened in eighteen twenty-five, boats could travel from the Hudson all the way to Lake Erie.
_shared.98d8b136eff8: Union Stock Yards. Opened in Chicago in eighteen sixty-five, it became the biggest meatpacking center in the world: trains brought in cattle and hogs, and millions of animals passed through every year. The yards closed in nineteen seventy-one, but the old stone entrance gate still stands.
_shared.13f36d7a9afe: Arkansas. Arkansas left the Union in May eighteen sixty-one, after Fort Sumter, and was readmitted in eighteen sixty-eight. In nineteen fifty-seven its governor, Orval Faubus, sent the state National Guard to keep nine Black students out of Little Rock’s Central High School.
_shared.02a23d1800f6: Brooklyn Bridge. When it opened in eighteen eighty-three it was the longest suspension bridge in the world, hanging from four huge cables of steel wire. To prove it was safe, the showman P. T. Barnum led twenty-one elephants across it in eighteen eighty-four!
_shared.7363bc3c1940: Chatsworth. A small mountain-edge town in Murray County, close to the Chief Vann House. Just east of town, Fort Mountain State Park has a mysterious ancient stone wall about eight hundred fifty-five feet long.
_shared.367024719d3a: Chanzhou, Chanyuan. Today: Puyang, Henan. After fighting here, the Song and Liao made peace; the Song paid silver and silk each year, and there was peace for over one hundred years.
_shared.c0adaf825240: Johnson Square. Savannah’s first square, laid out by Oglethorpe in seventeen thirty-three. Under the tall stone monument in the middle lies Nathanael Greene, a general of the American Revolution.
_shared.85eb8ea3caef: West Point. A small mill town on the Chattahoochee River at the Alabama line. In two thousand nine Kia opened its first US car factory here, bringing thousands of jobs; the plant can build hundreds of thousands of cars a year.
_shared.a2d2a310de71: Shijiazhuang. About one hundred years ago Shijiazhuang was a village. Railways crossing here turned it into a big city.
_shared.f48533756148: Cangzhou. Today: Cangzhou, Hebei. In the Song, criminals were sent to this remote coastal land. It is famous for martial arts and for a forty-tonne Iron Lion cast in nine fifty-three.
_shared.82bcbbf7d732: Galveston. On the nineteenth of June, eighteen sixty-five, two months after the war ended, Union General Gordon Granger arrived in this Texas port and announced that all enslaved people in Texas were free. Their celebration became Juneteenth, now a national holiday.
_shared.57c4b80ae9c6: Pentagon. The five-sided headquarters of the US military stands in Arlington, Virginia, just across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C. On the eleventh of September, two thousand one, a hijacked plane struck it and one hundred eighty-four people were killed; a memorial with one hundred eighty-four benches now stands beside it.
_shared.c69b4e10e5f5: Cusseta. Today: Near Columbus, Georgia. A leading Lower Creek town on the Chattahoochee near today’s Columbus — a “white” town, where peace talks were held. Its people were forced west in the eighteen thirties, but the Georgia town of Cusseta keeps its name.
_shared.95fa04e34b91: Gezhouba Dam. Today: Yichang, Hubei. Built thirty-eight kilometers below the Three Gorges Dam; it evens out the water released by the big dam.
_shared.6ad71c216c73: barrier islands. A chain of sandy islands along Georgia’s coast, from Tybee in the north to Cumberland in the south; Spain built missions on them in the fifteen hundreds and sixteen hundreds. They take the pounding of waves and storms and shelter the salt marshes behind them, and their shapes keep changing as the sand moves.
_shared.49d9d98b3c0e: North Carolina. North Carolina at first refused to ratify the Constitution, saying yes only in seventeen eighty-nine once a bill of rights was on the way. Cherokee who escaped removal in its mountains became the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians, and in nineteen sixty college students founded Snick in Raleigh.
_shared.a4c746f2021a: Brasstown Bald. Georgia’s highest point, four thousand seven hundred eighty-four feet up in the Blue Ridge Mountains. That’s one thousand four hundred fifty-eight meters. On a clear day you can see four states — Georgia, Tennessee, North Carolina and South Carolina — from the tower on top.
_shared.881d4ebe3fab: Plains. A tiny farm town of about six hundred people near Americus. Jimmy Carter was born here in nineteen twenty-four, grew peanuts, went off to be governor and president, came home again, and died here on December twenty-ninth, twenty twenty-four, at age one hundred.
_shared.24ddba0380e8: Illinois. In the winter of eighteen thirty-eight to eighteen thirty-nine thousands of Cherokee waited for weeks in freezing southern Illinois while ice blocked the Mississippi, and many died. Later the state became an industrial giant, with Chicago as its booming railroad and factory city.
_shared.4cac619f6ed6: Colorado River. It flows about two thousand three hundred kilometers from the Rocky Mountains to Mexico. Over about six million years it cut the Grand Canyon, grinding the rock with sand and stones.
_shared.bd4bcd9997ce: Alaska. The US bought Alaska from Russia in eighteen sixty-seven for seven point two million dollars — about two cents an acre — and critics called it “Seward’s Folly.” It is by far the largest state, more than twice the size of Texas.
_shared.ec19cb9b2e0d: Trilith Studios. One of the biggest film studios in North America, with dozens of sound stages in Fayetteville. Marvel movies such as Black Panther and Avengers: Endgame were filmed here, helping film spending in Georgia reach about four point four billion dollars in twenty twenty-two.
_shared.6c62e110be47: Caucasus Mountains. A high range between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea, often used as part of the Europe-Asia boundary. Mount Elbrus is its highest peak, at five thousand six hundred forty-two meters.
_shared.ce5c5c75ca8b: Bibb County. Home of Macon, near the middle of the state where the Ocmulgee River crosses the Fall Line. In eighteen sixty-eight Henry McNeal Turner represented this area in the legislature, one of Georgia’s first Black lawmakers.
_shared.ce8b9bb5a308: Trenton. At dawn on the twenty-sixth of December, seventeen seventy-six, after crossing the icy Delaware, Washington’s army surprised the Hessian soldiers here and captured about nine hundred. Today Trenton is New Jersey’s capital, and the Old Barracks where the Hessians stayed still stands.
_shared.1d6f18708506: Pike County Courthouse. Built in eighteen ninety-five in Zebulon, this courthouse is a good example of a Georgia county seat. Every one of Georgia’s one hundred fifty-nine counties has a courthouse, where trials are held and land and marriage records are kept.
_shared.058bc1a200c8: Jonesboro. Sherman’s troops won here and cut the Macon and Western Railroad, the last rail line feeding Atlanta. With no more supplies coming in, Hood left the city, and Union soldiers marched into Atlanta on September second, eighteen sixty-four.
_shared.bd56b61a190d: Atlanta. The capital of Georgia, at about thirty-three point seven degrees north, eighty-four point four degrees west. It has hot, humid summers and mild winters — a humid subtropical climate.
_shared.3e5f3dafa487: Memphis. King came to this Mississippi River city in Tennessee to support Black sanitation workers on strike, who carried signs saying “I AM A MAN”. He was shot on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel on April fourth, nineteen sixty-eight; the motel is now the National Civil Rights Museum.
_shared.140cb55619e4: Flint River. It begins underground beneath Atlanta’s airport and flows about three hundred forty miles south past Albany to join the Chattahoochee at Lake Seminole. The Creek lived along it; after an eighteen twenty-one treaty it marked the edge of Creek land until the rest was taken in eighteen twenty-five to eighteen twenty-seven.
_shared.f1c0e6887ce0: Lake Chad. A shallow lake on the edge of the Sahel that has shrunk by about ninety percent since the nineteen sixties, because of drought and water taken for farming.
_shared.79b32b820d1d: Salzburg. Today: Salzburg, Austria. A city in the Alps, then ruled by an archbishop. In seventeen thirty-one he drove out about twenty thousand Protestants for their faith; some of them sailed to Georgia in seventeen thirty-four and founded Ebenezer.
_shared.06e3a693a278: Ebenezer Baptist Church. Martin Luther King Jr. was baptized here as a boy and later preached beside his father, “Daddy King”. His funeral was held here in April nineteen sixty-eight; today the old church is part of the King National Historical Park, and you can hear recordings of his sermons inside.
_shared.db127291c9b4: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum. On the National Mall in Washington, D.C., this museum shows the real nineteen oh three Wright Flyer, a Sputnik one replica and the Apollo eleven command module, Columbia. It is one of the most visited museums in the world — and it is free.
_shared.8b652e91c015: Rocky Mountains. The “backbone” of western North America, running about four thousand eight hundred kilometers from Canada to New Mexico. Many peaks rise above four thousand meters.
_shared.e867750c088a: Liuzhou. Today: Liuzhou, Guangxi. After Yongzhou, Liu Zongyuan was sent even further south to Liuzhou, where he dug wells, freed bond-servants and died. People still call him 柳柳州.
_shared.99887336bc22: Penghu Islands. About ninety small islands in the Taiwan Strait, dry and windy, with cliffs of dark basalt.
_shared.f3d409e3870b: Gulf of Guinea. The great bend of Africa’s west coast, where the equator meets the prime meridian in the open sea, at zero degrees latitude and zero degrees longitude.
_shared.25ccb4d75eb4: Lincoln Memorial. On August twenty-eighth, nineteen sixty-three, about two hundred fifty thousand people filled the space in front of this marble memorial to Abraham Lincoln for the March on Washington, and King gave his “I Have a Dream” speech from its steps. The spot where he stood is carved into the step.
_shared.693991fba900: Nara, Heijō-kyō. Today: Nara, Japan. Japan copied Chang’an’s chessboard streets for its capital. Jianzhen arrived in seven fifty-four and built the Tōshōdai-ji temple here.
_shared.8c33750117a9: Massachusetts. Named after the Massachusett people, it was where the Pilgrims landed at Plymouth in sixteen twenty and the Puritans founded Boston in sixteen thirty. The Revolution’s first battles were fought at Lexington and Concord in seventeen seventy-five, and Shays’ Rebellion pushed leaders to write a stronger Constitution. The rebellion lasted from seventeen eighty-six to seventeen eighty-seven.
_shared.b474ef29d95e: Tropic of Capricorn sign, Namibia. A road sign in the Namib Desert, Namibia, marking the Tropic of Capricorn, about twenty-three point four degrees south. Around December twenty-first the noon Sun is straight overhead here.
_shared.5a7b72aaecb1: Lake Erie. The shallowest and warmest of the five Great Lakes, named after the Erie people who once lived on its shores. In eighteen twenty-five the Erie Canal linked it to the Hudson River, so boats could travel from the Great Lakes to New York City.
_shared.34d592ef9c9d: Riyadh. Capital of Saudi Arabia, an oasis city in the middle of the Arabian desert. Summer days often pass forty-five degrees Celsius.
_shared.6d68c5ff2db0: Long Island. Today: Brooklyn, New York City. On the twenty-seventh of August seventeen seventy-six the British attacked Washington’s army in Brooklyn in the largest battle of the whole war and beat it badly. The battlefield now lies inside New York City, under Prospect Park and Green-Wood Cemetery.
_shared.e9763346e1c2: Kettle Creek. About four hundred Patriot militia under Andrew Pickens, John Dooly and Elijah Clarke beat about seven hundred Loyalists under Colonel Boyd here in Wilkes County. Austin Dabney, a Black soldier who fought for the Patriots, was badly wounded here; Georgia later honored him with land for his service.
_shared.d254c9cf456a: Little White House. Today: Roosevelt’s Little White House State Historic Site. President Franklin D. Roosevelt built this small white cottage in nineteen thirty-two and came here to rest. On April twelfth, nineteen forty-five, he collapsed here while an artist was painting his portrait — the “Unfinished Portrait” still hangs in the museum.
_shared.5d1e7f15cd43: Lake of the Woods. A huge lake with more than fourteen thousand islands on the US-Canada border. The eighteen eighteen border ran from here west along the forty-ninth parallel to the Rocky Mountains, and an old mapping mistake left Minnesota’s “Northwest Angle” cut off from the rest of the US.
_shared.e8bf411161c5: Master of the Nets Garden. Today: Suzhou, Jiangsu. One of the smallest famous gardens, about zero point five hectares, arranged around one pond. A copy of one of its courtyards stands in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.
_shared.ad2dedcf0d19: Toa. Today: Flint River near Montezuma, Georgia. A large town on the Flint River that de Soto’s army reached on March twenty-third, fifteen forty, on its way north toward Ichisi.
_shared.9e941495972a: Sea Island. One of the Golden Isles, Sea Island is a small barrier island famous for its beach resort, opened in nineteen twenty-eight. In two thousand four the leaders of the world’s biggest economies met here for the G eight summit.
_shared.b2f30eee21a6: Dublin. The Book of Kells, painted by Irish monks around eight hundred, is kept in the library of Trinity College here. In thirteen forty-eight the Black Death crossed the sea to Dublin.
_shared.8e2bf1613728: UC Santa Barbara. A university on the Pacific coast near Santa Barbara, California; in nineteen sixty-nine it became one of the first four ARPANET computer sites. The campus sits right beside the ocean, with its own beach and lagoon.
_shared.ce4a88abb155: Great Green Wall, Sahel. A project started in two thousand seven by African countries to plant a belt of trees and grassland about eight thousand kilometers long across the Sahel, from Senegal to Djibouti, to hold back the desert.
_shared.19c8ce1569a1: Washington. The northern part of the old Oregon Country became Washington, the forty-second state, in eighteen eighty-nine — the only state named after a president. Microsoft, founded in Albuquerque, moved to the Seattle area in nineteen seventy-nine.
_shared.75a4470c1dc9: Keelung. Winter monsoon winds bring rain on more than two hundred days a year.
_shared.840af6ca7231: Virginia. Jamestown made Virginia the first lasting English colony, and its House of Burgesses was the first elected assembly in English America. Jamestown dates to sixteen oh seven, and the House of Burgesses to sixteen nineteen. Four of the first five presidents came from Virginia, and the Revolution’s last big battle was fought at Yorktown.
_shared.6fbe116b96a4: New York City. The biggest city in the USA, with about nineteen million people in its metro area. When the New Year’s ball drops in Times Square, it is already the next morning in Beijing.
_shared.e2a0b82aa1ce: Greene County. A county of farms and pine forests east of Atlanta; its county seat is Greensboro. In nineteen forty-one Jack Delano photographed life here, from young CCC workers building fences to farm women washing clothes by hand.
_shared.a56f6b286c1b: Huangguoshu Waterfall. Today: Anshun, Guizhou. One of Asia’s biggest waterfalls, about seventy-eight meters high and one hundred meters wide, in the karst hills of Guizhou. You can walk through a cave behind the curtain of water.
_shared.9d6764d813b2: Atlanta University. Today: Clark Atlanta University, merged nineteen eighty-eight. After the Civil War, Atlanta University, Clark, Morehouse and Spelman colleges grew up side by side to educate freed people and their children. W. E. B. Du Bois taught here and wrote The Souls of Black Folk; today the campuses form the largest group of Black colleges in the US.
_shared.85bbb47ce6bc: Mohe. In Mohe’s “Arctic Village” winters fall below minus forty degrees Celsius, and in summer you can sometimes see the northern lights.
_shared.23d218e28129: Camilla. In September eighteen sixty-eight a few hundred mostly Black Republicans marched into town for a political rally. Armed white men opened fire and then hunted the marchers in the countryside; about a dozen Black people were killed — violence meant to stop Black people from voting.
_shared.e5c0d326632f: Souther Field. Today: Jimmy Carter Regional Airport, Americus. Almost two thousand military pilots learned to fly at this field northeast of Americus in World War One. In nineteen twenty-three a young Charles Lindbergh bought his first airplane here and made his first solo flight — four years before he flew alone across the Atlantic.
_shared.1d6a2a6fa496: Yellow Sea. Silt from rivers once made its water yellowish — hence the name. It is about forty-four meters deep on average.
_shared.c757540a96ef: Highland Park plant. Ford added the moving assembly line here in nineteen thirteen: instead of workers walking around the car, the car was pulled past them, and each worker did one job. Building a chassis dropped from about twelve and a half hours to about one and a half hours.
_shared.6425bed9d687: Oregon Country. Today: Oregon, Washington and Idaho. Home to the Chinook, Nez Perce and many other Native nations, this rainy, forested land was shared by the US and Britain from eighteen eighteen, and thousands of settlers came on the Oregon Trail in the eighteen forties. In eighteen forty-six a treaty split it along the forty-ninth parallel — still the US-Canada border.
_shared.660a33661cab: Bell Bomber plant. Today: Lockheed Martin plant, Marietta. In World War Two about twenty-eight thousand Georgians — many of them women — built B two nine Superfortress bombers in one of the biggest factory buildings in the South. After the war Lockheed took over the plant, and it still builds military airplanes today.
_shared.0e203cdda66c: Dabie Mountains. On the borders of Hubei, Henan and Anhui. Marching one thousand li into these mountains turned the PLA from defence to attack.
_shared.9e7a3386c8c3: Fort Benning. Founded near Columbus in nineteen eighteen, it became the world’s largest infantry school in World War Two, and paratroopers learned to jump from its tall towers. It was renamed Fort Moore in twenty twenty-three, then Fort Benning again in twenty twenty-five.
_shared.8d7f8a925716: St. John’s Parish. Today: Liberty County, Georgia. This coastal parish was Georgia’s hotbed of revolution: in seventeen seventy-five, before the rest of the colony joined, it sent its own delegate, Lyman Hall, to the Continental Congress. In seventeen seventy-seven it was renamed Liberty County to honor that spirit.
_shared.3fabcd59830c: Camp Gordon. Today: DeKalb-Peachtree Airport, Chamblee. In nineteen seventeen the Army built this camp in Chamblee, northeast of Atlanta, and trained the eighty-second Division — nicknamed “All-American” because its men came from every state. Sergeant Alvin York, a famous war hero, trained here; the land is now an airport.
_shared.7cf94ff576b3: Santa Fe. Founded by the Spanish around sixteen ten, it is the oldest state capital in the US. After eighteen twenty-one traders drove wagons about nine hundred miles along the Santa Fe Trail from Missouri to sell their goods here.
_shared.8430d8233c41: Danube River. It flows east about two thousand eight hundred fifty kilometers through ten countries — more than any other river — and four capitals, including Vienna and Budapest, to the Black Sea.
_shared.9c6f00ee9fa7: Nile River. At about six thousand six hundred fifty kilometers it is one of the two longest rivers on Earth. Every summer it flooded and left rich black mud on the fields — “Egypt is the gift of the Nile”.
_shared.ede6d9346642: Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport. For most years since nineteen ninety-eight the world’s busiest airport by passengers. Planes and cargo from here link Georgia with the whole world.
_shared.068d4f090863: Machu Picchu. An Inca city built in the fourteen hundreds on a ridge about two thousand four hundred thirty meters high in the Andes of Peru, with farming terraces cut into the steep slopes.
_shared.a60b629ac6cc: Mohenjo-daro. Today: Sindh, Pakistan. A planned city with straight streets, covered drains and a “Great Bath”. Perhaps forty thousand people lived here four thousand five hundred years ago.
_shared.9e3e6cde4d05: Chief Vann House. James Vann, a wealthy Cherokee leader, built this brick mansion in eighteen oh four — one of the finest houses on the frontier. The Vann family also held about one hundred enslaved African Americans, a hard truth the historic site tells today; in eighteen thirty-five Georgia forced Joseph Vann out of the house.
_shared.b623f9b499b2: Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center. Today: Ejin Banner, Inner Mongolia, in the desert. China’s first satellite went up from here in nineteen seventy, playing the song “The East Is Red”, and Yang Liwei flew to space from here in two thousand three.
_shared.9bd2b7d16916: Greene County, Georgia. A rural county in Georgia’s Piedmont. In the nineteen thirties and nineteen forties many farmers here still ploughed cotton fields with mules.
_shared.107d9fc2010c: Thirteen Hongs. Today: Guangzhou, Guangdong. From seventeen fifty-seven Western merchants could trade only in Guangzhou, through the licensed Chinese merchants of the Thirteen Hongs, and they had to live in the row of factories by the river.
_shared.5be2d04a72b7: Strait of Gibraltar. Only about fourteen kilometers wide, it separates Europe, Spain, from Africa, Morocco, and joins the Atlantic to the Mediterranean.
_shared.edb8ace20442: Dunkirk. Today: Dunkerque, France. Trapped by the German army, about three hundred thirty-eight thousand British and French soldiers were carried across the Channel by warships and hundreds of small boats.
_shared.609decadfdb9: Cumberland Island. Georgia’s largest barrier island, about seventeen miles long, is a National Seashore you can reach only by ferry. Wild horses roam its dunes, beaches and live-oak forests.
_shared.6e43b0b7b5a8: Tianjing. Today: Nanjing, Jiangsu. The Taiping army took Nanjing in eighteen fifty-three and renamed it Tianjing, “Heavenly Capital”. It fell in eighteen sixty-four and the movement failed.
_shared.d5535187eb2a: Erie Canal. It linked the Great Lakes to the Hudson River and New York City, about five hundred eighty kilometers long with eighty-three locks — they work just like the locks on China’s Grand Canal.
_shared.80a753cb4f6e: Lhasa. Lhasa is about three thousand six hundred fifty meters above sea level and has so many sunny days that it is called the “City of Sunlight”. The Potala Palace towers over the city.
_shared.f0fbc7281e04: Ohio River. The Ohio flows about nine hundred eighty miles from Pittsburgh to the Mississippi. The Northwest Ordinance of seventeen eighty-seven banned slavery north of it, so it became a border between slave and free states — and Trail of Tears groups crossed it by ferry at Golconda in eighteen thirty-eight.
_shared.9c42283882e6: Taipa, Coloane and Cotai. Macao filled in the sea between Taipa and Coloane to create Cotai, roughly doubling its land since nineteen twelve.
_shared.61dfcc98e653: Wuqi. Today: Wuqi County, Shaanxi. After about twelve thousand five hundred kilometers, or twenty-five thousand li, the Central Red Army arrived in northern Shaanxi here.
_shared.d0d84b29c7e6: Tangshan. A coal and steel city in Hebei. It was destroyed by a huge earthquake in nineteen seventy-six and rebuilt as a new city.
_shared.b7e34d79e790: Minute Man National Historical Park. On the nineteenth of April seventeen seventy-five British troops marched to Concord to seize Patriot weapons; at the North Bridge the militia fired back — Emerson’s “shot heard round the world.” All along the Battle Road back to Boston, militiamen shot at the British from behind stone walls and trees.
_shared.42b6287d23f5: Nueces River. Texas said its southern border was the Rio Grande; Mexico said it was this river, farther north. When US troops marched into the land between the two rivers in eighteen forty-six, the Mexican-American War began.
_shared.47bdc05da623: Panama Canal. Locks lift ships twenty-six meters up over the hills of Panama and down again, linking the Pacific and the Atlantic. Many ships from Asia to Savannah pass through it.
_shared.0ebd4fd1ac63: Lingering Garden. Today: Suzhou, Jiangsu. Famous for its long corridors, framed windows and the six point five meter Cloud-Capped Peak, a giant Taihu rock.
_shared.0eeb777a8cf4: Little Rock. In September nineteen fifty-seven nine Black students — the Little Rock Nine — tried to enter all-white Central High School in Arkansas’s capital; President Eisenhower sent soldiers of the one hundred first Airborne to escort them past angry crowds. The school is still open today, and it is also a National Park Service historic site.
_shared.02f74b040860: Mount Lu. Today: Jiujiang, Jiangxi. A misty mountain by the Yangtze and Poyang Lake. Li Bai’s waterfall “飞流直下三千尺” and Su Shi’s “不识庐山真面目” were both written about it.
_shared.e713ff6112dd: Versailles. Louis the Fourteenth built this giant palace. The French Revolution began with a meeting of the Estates-General here, seventeen eighty-nine, and the treaty ending World War One was signed in its Hall of Mirrors.
_shared.29f913e2bf8f: Jekyll Island. In eighteen eighty-six some of America’s richest families, like the Rockefellers and Morgans, made this barrier island their private winter club. Today it is a state park, with Driftwood Beach, where storm-killed trees lie bleached on the sand.
_shared.c7b9febabb0d: Genoa. Its merchants traded from the Black Sea to England. Christopher Columbus was born here around fourteen fifty-one.
_shared.264bfc9e0487: Alice Springs. A desert town in the very middle of Australia, almost on the Tropic of Capricorn. It gets less than three hundred millimeters of rain a year.
_shared.ca8c4524a7ee: Qinghai Lake. China’s largest lake, a salty lake about three thousand two hundred meters up on the plateau. Every summer migrating birds nest on its islands.
_shared.d70ced85710e: Willow Run. Ford built this enormous factory west of Detroit during World War Two; at its peak it rolled out a B two four Liberator bomber about every hour, part of America’s “arsenal of democracy”. Its airfield, Willow Run Airport, is still in use.
_shared.c2c8104bd91a: Fangmatan. Today: Tianshui, Gansu. In nineteen eighty-six archaeologists found a scrap of paper with a map drawn in ink in a Western Han tomb here — proof that China had paper before Cai Lun.
_shared.0b91213399e5: Chongqing. A “mountain city” where the Jialing River meets the Yangtze. In nineteen forty-five Mao Zedong came here for peace talks with the Nationalists.
_shared.3ff96ca89c0e: Bryan County. A fast-growing coastal county next to Savannah; its county seat is Pembroke. Georgia gave Hyundai about two point one billion dollars in incentives to build its Metaplant here.
_shared.04bc78834a7c: Messina. Twelve Genoese galleys docked here in thirteen forty-seven with sick sailors on board — the Black Death’s doorway into western Europe.
_shared.5b4fd924f8ce: Lei Feng Memorial. A museum in Lei Feng’s home town in Wangcheng District, Changsha, Hunan, about the young soldier remembered for helping others. He lived from nineteen forty to nineteen sixty-two.
_shared.4b3ae1805951: SRI, Menlo Park. Today: SRI International, Menlo Park, California. A research institute in Menlo Park, California — not Edison’s Menlo Park in New Jersey. Its computer received ARPANET’s first message from UCLA in nineteen sixty-nine, and SRI scientist Douglas Engelbart invented the computer mouse here.
_shared.a84b745df87f: New Orleans. Whoever held this port near the mouth of the Mississippi controlled the river trade, so Jefferson tried to buy it — and in eighteen oh three Napoleon offered all of Louisiana instead. It was the South’s biggest city, and largest slave market, when the US Navy captured it in eighteen sixty-two; in nineteen sixty, six-year-old Ruby Bridges integrated a school here.
_shared.f419c5274c79: West Virginia. When Virginia seceded, the mountain counties in the west refused to go along — few families there enslaved people. They broke away and joined the Union as the new state of West Virginia in eighteen sixty-three, right in the middle of the war.
_shared.5a87f6f9b8e0: Mexican Cession. Today: California, Nevada, Utah and parts of four more states. After the Mexican-American War, Mexico gave up about half its land in the eighteen forty-eight Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, and the US paid fifteen million dollars. Tens of thousands of Mexicans and many Native nations living there suddenly found themselves inside the United States.
_shared.86e5f32327a8: Reflecting Pool. This long pool stretches from the Lincoln Memorial toward the Washington Monument and mirrors it in the water. On the twenty-eighth of August nineteen sixty-three about two hundred fifty thousand people crowded around it for the March on Washington, where Dr. King gave his “I Have a Dream” speech.
_shared.4ba8df114f2b: Yorktown. About seventeen thousand American and French soldiers trapped the British army here, and on October nineteenth, seventeen eighty-one, Cornwallis surrendered about eight thousand men — the last major battle of the Revolution. Today the battlefield is part of Colonial National Historical Park, together with Jamestown.
_shared.43ce82f1efb6: Jakarta-Bandung High-Speed Railway. Southeast Asia’s first high-speed line: one hundred forty-two kilometers in Indonesia at up to three hundred fifty kilometers per hour, built jointly by Indonesian and Chinese companies.
_shared.a7e7d72da40f: São Paulo. Brazil’s biggest city and the largest city in the Southern Hemisphere, with about twenty-two million people in its metro area.
_shared.2548a817ec90: Congo River. Africa’s river with the most water — and the deepest river in the world, over two hundred twenty meters. It crosses the equator twice as it arcs through the rainforest.
_shared.4d9a8ea275cd: French Louisiana. Today: Louisiana and the Mississippi valley. In sixteen eighty-two France claimed the whole Mississippi valley and named it for King Louis the Fourteenth. The United States bought the huge land west of the river, with New Orleans, in the Louisiana Purchase of eighteen oh three.
_shared.6a58b556a4d5: Chongming Island. Built up from Yangtze silt over about one thousand three hundred years — the world’s largest alluvial island in a river mouth.
_shared.01f124d97e84: Maine. Maine was part of Massachusetts until eighteen twenty, when it joined as a free state to balance slave state Missouri, the Missouri Compromise. It is the most northeastern state, famous for forests, lobsters and rocky coasts.
_shared.7f47220532a8: Kings Mountain. On the seventh of October seventeen eighty the backcountry “Overmountain Men” climbed this wooded ridge in South Carolina and wiped out a Loyalist force in about an hour. Almost everyone who fought was American — Patriots against Loyalists.
_shared.c66dbaab02ca: Xingtai. The Yuan astronomer and water engineer Guo Shoujing was born here. He built new instruments and helped make the Shoushi calendar, with a year of three hundred sixty-five point two four two five days.
_shared.30d30467d2a6: Merv. Today: near Mary, Turkmenistan. A great oasis city on the Silk Road where caravans rested between Persia and Central Asia. In the eleven hundreds it may have been the biggest city in the world.
_shared.6e63738c7646: Georgia Governor’s Mansion. The governor’s official home, a Greek Revival mansion with thirty columns finished in nineteen sixty-seven in Atlanta’s Buckhead neighborhood. Visitors can tour its rooms full of early eighteen hundreds furniture.
_shared.de1167cf205c: Qiongzhou Strait. Only twenty to forty kilometers wide. Trains ride across on ferries to Haikou.
_shared.cf42fd508d81: Mammoth Cave. Today: Kentucky, USA. The longest known cave system in the world, more than six hundred eighty kilometers of passages in limestone.
_shared.c9bb41e9a9e7: Ocmulgee River. It rises east of Atlanta, crosses the Fall Line at Macon and joins the Oconee to form the Altamaha. Creek towns lined its banks, and in the eighteen hundreds steamboats carried cotton down it toward the coast.
_shared.52a5f736ef62: San Cristóbal, Cuba. A US spy plane photographed Soviet nuclear missile sites near this town. For thirteen days the world feared a nuclear war.
_shared.fb231e1809d1: Manaus. A city of about two million people in the middle of the Amazon rainforest, near where the dark Rio Negro meets the Amazon.
_shared.bd8d0d30f48b: UN Headquarters, New York. Today: New York, USA. On the twenty-fifth of October nineteen seventy-one the UN General Assembly voted to restore the PRC’s seat.
_shared.2edc57e2ed63: Diaoyu Islands. Diaoyu Dao and its islands, such as Chiwei Yu, lie in the East China Sea about one hundred seventy kilometers northeast of Taiwan.
_shared.4fbaf876ac7f: Andes. The longest mountain range on land — about seven thousand kilometers down the whole west side of South America. Its highest peak, Aconcagua, is six thousand nine hundred sixty-one meters.
_shared.d1a7b4de320a: Hagia Sophia. For almost one thousand years its dome was the biggest in the world. It was a church, then a mosque after fourteen fifty-three; the minarets were added by the Ottomans.
_shared.3415c13f4ae5: Combahee River. On a June night in eighteen sixty-three, Union gunboats guided by Harriet Tubman steamed up this South Carolina river and freed more than seven hundred enslaved people from the rice plantations. Tubman became the first woman to help lead an armed raid in the Civil War.
_shared.88415d9416ff: Fort Christina. Today: Wilmington, Delaware. Swedish and Finnish settlers built this fort in sixteen thirty-eight, named for Sweden’s twelve-year-old Queen Christina — the first permanent European settlement in the Delaware Valley. They may have built America’s first log cabins here.
_shared.d67d4bd436f1: Ellis Island. From eighteen ninety-two to nineteen fifty-four about twelve million immigrants entered the USA through the station on this island in New York Harbor.
_shared.8fa9dcf16635: Des Moines. In December nineteen sixty-five students here, including thirteen-year-old Mary Beth Tinker, wore black armbands to school to protest the Vietnam War and were suspended. In nineteen sixty-nine the Supreme Court ruled that students do not lose free speech “at the schoolhouse gate.”
_shared.3b17b6822ce7: Great Barrier Reef. The largest coral reef system on Earth, stretching about two thousand three hundred kilometers off Queensland, Australia. It can be seen from space.
_shared.8031ae91645f: Humble Administrator’s Garden. Today: Suzhou, Jiangsu. The largest classical garden in Suzhou, about five point two hectares — half of it water. Paths, bridges and windows keep changing the view at every step, 移步换景.
_shared.dc3f8a3a117e: Boston Harbor. On the night of the sixteenth of December seventeen seventy-three, Patriots disguised as Mohawk Indians dumped three hundred forty-two chests of East India Company tea into this harbor — the Boston Tea Party. Britain punished the town by closing the port in seventeen seventy-four.
_shared.7be3a9bb4998: Tropic of Cancer marker, Ruisui. A marker on the Tropic of Cancer in Ruisui, Hualien County, Taiwan Province, China. The Tropic of Cancer is at about twenty-three point four degrees north. Around June twenty-first the noon Sun is straight overhead here.
_shared.6d8ea318a2f2: Albany Civil Rights Institute. This museum in Albany, Georgia, tells the story of the Albany Movement of nineteen sixty-one to nineteen sixty-two. On some Saturdays the Freedom Singers still perform the songs that once filled the church next door during mass meetings.
_shared.22bc8e00c54c: Shiloh. Confederates surprised Grant’s army at dawn near a little log church called Shiloh; Grant held on and won on the second day. About twenty-three thousand soldiers were killed, wounded or missing — more than in all of America’s earlier wars put together.
_shared.a4304d748ebe: Walton County. Created in eighteen eighteen on land taken from the Creek, and named for George Walton, one of Georgia’s three signers of the Declaration of Independence. Its county seat is Monroe, east of Atlanta.
_shared.e0b1759aabff: Inner Mongolia Plateau. Wide, flat and about one thousand meters high, with huge grasslands such as Hulunbuir and Xilin Gol — “the sky is blue, the land is vast”.
_shared.6cd32a5286f7: Atlanta City Hall. The mayor and city council run Atlanta from this nineteen thirty tower. On his first day in office in nineteen sixty-two, Mayor Ivan Allen Jr. ordered the “White” and “Colored” signs taken down inside it.
_shared.f66278e70fa6: Honolulu. The capital of Hawaii, on the island of Oahu in the middle of the Pacific. It uses U T C minus ten, five hours behind Atlanta in winter.
_shared.428e937319e6: Cartersville. A small city in northwest Georgia near the Etowah River; just outside town are the Etowah Indian Mounds. Downtown you can still see the world’s first painted wall sign for Coca-Cola, from eighteen ninety-four.
_shared.9e7f6d552e47: Oklahoma. Much of it was set aside as “Indian Territory,” where the US government forced the Cherokee, Creek and other Southeastern nations to move in the eighteen thirties. The Cherokee Nation rebuilt there and has its capital at Tahlequah today.
_shared.20bd924b62be: Ulibahali. Today: Rome, Georgia. A town of the Coosa chiefdom where two rivers meet to form the Coosa River. De Soto’s army passed through in August fifteen forty; today the city of Rome stands on the spot.
_shared.eced8a0ab3bf: George Washington Carver National Monument. George Washington Carver was born into slavery on a farm here, near Diamond, Missouri, around eighteen sixty-four. In nineteen forty-three it became the first national monument honoring an African American, and you can walk a trail through the woods where young Carver studied plants.
_shared.82ba03576871: Cobb County. A county northwest of Atlanta, home to Marietta and Kennesaw Mountain, where a big Civil War battle was fought in eighteen sixty-four. This site’s lessons were checked against Cobb County’s school frameworks for Georgia standards.
_shared.e94f3449c696: San Jacinto. Today: near Houston, Texas. On the twenty-first of April eighteen thirty-six Sam Houston’s army surprised Santa Anna’s camp here during the afternoon rest and won in about eighteen minutes, shouting “Remember the Alamo!” The victory won Texas its independence; a five hundred sixty-seven-foot monument now stands on the battlefield.
_shared.affff4521d6c: Chengpu. Today: southwest of Juancheng, Shandong. Jin pulled back ninety li, “retreat three days’ march”, to keep a promise, then defeated Chu here.
_shared.486a821dc518: Cloudland Canyon. Creeks have cut canyons hundreds of feet deep into the edge of Lookout Mountain here. Hikers climb down about six hundred steps to reach two waterfalls at the bottom.
_shared.69d94131bc90: Seville. Magellan’s fleet left from here in fifteen nineteen, and the only ship to return, the Victoria, came back here in fifteen twenty-two. American silver poured in through its port.
