_shared.628e72a0df5e: Heilongjiang, Amur, River. A great river of northeast Asia, about four thousand four hundred kilometers long. Today part of it is the border between China and Russia, and Heilongjiang Province is named after it.
_shared.a8dc076a0319: Equator monument, Kikorongo. A monument in Kasese District, Uganda, where the road crosses the equator, zero degrees latitude.
_shared.aa97cfe6dc53: Luling. Today: Ji’an, Jiangxi. Ouyang Xiu’s family came from Luling, so he signed “醉翁亭记” “庐陵欧阳修也”. The Southern Song hero Wen Tianxiang was from here too.
_shared.2fe1d66a6b92: Chickamauga Creek. In September eighteen sixty-three Confederate General Bragg crossed the bridges over West Chickamauga Creek to attack Rosecrans’ Union army. The quiet creek still winds through the battlefield park.
_shared.1190c0da0220: Topeka. In Kansas’s capital, third-grader Linda Brown had to travel far to a school for Black children, though a white school was close to home. Her family’s case, Brown versus Board of Education, led the Supreme Court on May seventeenth, nineteen fifty-four, to rule school segregation unconstitutional; Topeka’s Monroe School is now a national historical park.
_shared.cf746441581c: Ellabell. A quiet rural community west of Savannah that suddenly became home to one of Georgia’s biggest factories: Hyundai’s electric-vehicle Metaplant, which began full production in October twenty twenty-four.
_shared.c79c0a25c510: Tondee’s Tavern. Peter Tondee’s tavern in Savannah, where the Liberty Boys met in seventeen seventy-four to seventeen seventy-five to protest British laws; Georgia’s first Provincial Congress gathered here in July seventeen seventy-five. The building is gone, but a historical marker shows the spot.
_shared.88054189b87c: Hopkinsville. Cherokee leaders White Path and Fly Smith died near this Kentucky town in November eighteen thirty-eight. Their graves lie in the Trail of Tears Commemorative Park, one of the few places where people who died on the march are known to be buried.
_shared.251e11f18303: Qinling Mountains. Along the Qinling-Huaihe line the January average is about zero degrees Celsius and yearly rain about eight hundred millimeters. North of it people grow wheat; south of it, rice. Giant pandas live in these mountains.
_shared.a8c7bc6cb156: Thomasville. The boll weevil was first found in Georgia here in nineteen fifteen, and within a few years it was wrecking cotton across the state. Today Thomasville is known for its Big Oak, a live oak more than three hundred years old, and its yearly Rose Show.
_shared.9e826c412433: Indian Springs. Creek people prized the mineral spring here for healing. In eighteen twenty-five William McIntosh signed away the last Creek lands in Georgia at Indian Springs, even though Creek law forbade it — and he was killed for it a few months later.
_shared.41cab5e4b88f: Jintian. Today: Guiping, Guangxi. In January eighteen fifty-one Hong Xiuquan led a peasant uprising at Jintian village and named his movement the “Taiping Heavenly Kingdom”.
_shared.f45a32f4406c: Dahlonega Mint. Today: Site of Price Memorial Hall, University of North Georgia, Dahlonega. From eighteen thirty-eight to eighteen sixty-one this branch of the US Mint turned gold from the old Cherokee Nation into coins stamped with a small “D.” After the building burned in eighteen seventy-eight, Price Memorial Hall was built on its foundations — its steeple shines with Dahlonega gold.
_shared.a853605395ec: Checkpoint Charlie. The best-known crossing point between East and West Berlin. In nineteen sixty-one American and Soviet tanks stood just metres apart here for sixteen hours.
_shared.22609f99b295: Olympic stadium or Turner Field. Today: Center Parc Stadium, Georgia State University. Built as the main stadium of the nineteen ninety-six Olympics, it became the Braves’ Turner Field and is now Georgia State’s football stadium. Next door stood Atlanta Stadium, nineteen sixty-five, which brought the Braves and Falcons to town; Hank Aaron hit his record seven hundred fifteenth home run there in nineteen seventy-four.
_shared.116b6b0029c4: Quanzhou. Marco Polo called it one of the greatest ports in the world. Arab, Persian and Indian merchants lived here, and a Song ship was dug up in its bay in nineteen seventy-four.
_shared.1d7db932cb0a: Jingshan. A forty-five meter hill just north of the Forbidden City. The pavilion on top sits exactly on the Central Axis — the best place to see the palace’s golden roofs.
_shared.a310d7d4fdec: Haitian Monument. It honors more than five hundred free Black soldiers from Saint-Domingue, today’s Haiti, who fought beside the French and Americans in the seventeen seventy-nine Siege of Savannah. Legend says one twelve-year-old drummer boy was Henri Christophe, who later became king of Haiti.
_shared.5e12ae4ad29d: Great Wall of Qi. Today: central Shandong. Over six hundred kilometers of wall across the hills of Shandong — one of the oldest long walls in China.
_shared.e0edcb1b5618: Huai’an. Here the canal met the Huai River, so every grain boat passed through. In nine eighty-four Qiao Weiyue built a lock with two gates nearby — one of the earliest locks of this kind in the world.
_shared.ba1a2214b18e: Weihaiwei. Today: Weihai, Shandong. The Beiyang Fleet’s headquarters was on Liugong Island. In early eighteen ninety-five the fleet was wiped out here in the Sino-Japanese War. The island is now a war museum.
_shared.769edc9792d7: Melbourne. Australia’s second-largest city, on Port Phillip Bay in the south-east. It was the country’s capital from nineteen oh one to nineteen twenty-seven.
_shared.f0299232433d: Tsukiji fish market. Tokyo’s famous fish market, where early-morning tuna auctions set prices. The wholesale market moved to nearby Toyosu in twenty eighteen.
_shared.ea59412179f6: Wulingyuan, Zhangjiajie. Today: Zhangjiajie, Hunan. Over three thousand sandstone pillars, some more than two hundred meters tall, shaped by water and weather over millions of years.
_shared.5d837978df1b: Tiger Leaping Gorge. Today: Lijiang, Yunnan. Legend says a tiger jumped across the river here on a rock. The cliffs rise about three thousand nine hundred meters above the water.
_shared.204aecbcd3c6: Louisiana. Today’s state is only a small corner of the huge Louisiana Purchase; it became the eighteenth state in eighteen twelve. It seceded in January eighteen sixty-one, lost New Orleans to the Union in April eighteen sixty-two, and was readmitted in eighteen sixty-eight.
_shared.722b4a09ec20: Zhoushan Islands. Over one thousand three hundred islands off Zhejiang. Warm and cold currents meet here, so there are lots of fish.
_shared.8f0d72ac31f9: Andersonville. The largest Confederate prison camp: about forty-five thousand Union soldiers were packed inside a log stockade with little food, no shelter and a dirty creek for water, and nearly thirteen thousand died. Rows of their white headstones fill the national cemetery next to it.
_shared.d24512ab03b3: Richmond County. Home of Augusta on the Savannah River, Georgia’s second-oldest city. Since nineteen ninety-six Augusta and Richmond County have shared one combined government.
_shared.ce3dd3a081df: Nancy Hart’s cabin. Today: Cabin site in Elbert County, Georgia. Legend says that in seventeen seventy-nine Nancy Hart, a tall frontier woman, captured a group of Loyalist soldiers who barged into her cabin, holding them at gunpoint until help came. A replica cabin, built with stones from her real chimney, stands at the site today.
_shared.6839b203445a: Kennesaw Mountain. Confederates dug in on this mountain, and on June twenty-seventh, eighteen sixty-four, Sherman tried his one big head-on attack of the campaign — it failed, with about three thousand Union losses. Today you can hike to the top and see the earthworks and the Atlanta skyline.
_shared.94e1242ec3aa: Nanyang. Today: Nanyang, Henan. An old city in Henan: the hermit Liu Ziji of “桃花源记” came from here, and Zhuge Liang farmed here before Liu Bei visited him three times, 三顾茅庐.
_shared.8fa48645b7c1: Habersham County. Cherokee mountain land given up in eighteen seventeen to eighteen nineteen became Habersham County in northeast Georgia. Today its hills are known for apple orchards — the town of Cornelia has a giant red apple monument.
_shared.ae2d97cd2a2b: Yiwu. A city in Zhejiang with one of the world’s largest wholesale markets for small goods — about seventy-five thousand booths selling toys, socks, decorations and more to buyers from around the world.
_shared.6093f1e8fc68: Ebenezer. Today: Town site in Effingham County, Georgia. Protestant refugees from Salzburg built this town up the Savannah River. They raised silkworms and spoke out against slavery; the town is gone, but their brick Jerusalem Lutheran Church still holds services. The church dates to seventeen sixty-seven.
_shared.28331c232fba: Pittsburgh. Coal, iron and three rivers made Pittsburgh America’s “Steel City”. Andrew Carnegie’s Edgar Thomson Steel Works opened nearby in eighteen seventy-five using the Bessemer process, and immigrants from Europe worked its fiery furnaces — it still makes steel today. In nineteen twenty the city’s KDKA began the first regular radio broadcasts.
_shared.e137e20d1fd6: Carters Lake. A deep reservoir in the north Georgia mountains, made when Carters Dam was finished on the Coosawattee River in nineteen seventy-seven. The site of Coosa, the great Mississippian town de Soto visited, now lies under its water.
_shared.2a4140673c58: Aoraki or Mount Cook. New Zealand’s highest mountain, three thousand seven hundred twenty-four meters, in the Southern Alps of the South Island.
_shared.30ef579a41ba: Nubia, Kush. Today: Sudan and southern Egypt. The land up the Nile, south of Egypt, rich in gold. Its kings later built more than two hundred steep pyramids at Meroë — more than Egypt has.
_shared.4151c853f288: Saint-Domingue, Haiti. Today: Haiti. France’s richest sugar colony, worked by enslaved Africans. Led by Toussaint Louverture, they won their freedom and founded Haiti in eighteen oh four.
_shared.38b130005eed: Minnesota. A northern state of forests, farms and “ten thousand lakes”, where the Mississippi River begins. In the late eighteen hundreds many immigrant families from Scandinavia, Germany and the Netherlands came to farm here — like the Dykhof family in the lesson.
_shared.758f4911e90e: Taiwan Strait. About one hundred thirty kilometers wide at its narrowest, between Pingtan Island in Fujian and Taiwan. Big ships sail through it every day.
_shared.7330b13e0841: Granada. The Alhambra palace, with its fountains and carved ceilings, looks down on the city. In fourteen ninety-two Spain’s Catholic monarchs took Granada.
_shared.b40987cb1c5b: Nairobi. Capital of Kenya, just south of the equator but about one thousand seven hundred meters high, so it is mild all year. Wild animals roam a national park at the city’s edge.
_shared.a453e9346168: Tennessee. Georgia’s neighbor to the north. It was the last state to leave the Union in eighteen sixty-one and the first to rejoin in eighteen sixty-six; in the nineteen thirties the Tennessee Valley Authority’s dams brought electric power to its farms.
_shared.0504ca3005ef: Yangshan Port. Today: Shanghai, on islands of Zhejiang. Shanghai built its deepest port on small islands thirty kilometers out to sea, linked by the thirty-two-kilometer Donghai Bridge.
_shared.ce61943ea92f: Lake Lanier. Buford Dam on the Chattahoochee created this huge reservoir in the nineteen fifties, and it stores much of metro Atlanta’s drinking water. Its winding shoreline is about six hundred ninety miles long, and millions of people boat and swim here every year.
_shared.ad289096a63f: Macon. Macon grew where the Ocmulgee River leaves the hills at the Fall Line, and steamboats carried its cotton downriver. At the edge of town stand the Ocmulgee Mounds, about nine hundred years older than the city.
_shared.0b07a3a4b1a4: Harbin. Winters reach minus thirty degrees Celsius, and every year Harbin builds a city of ice sculptures for its Ice and Snow Festival.
_shared.b96d7ff6d1a3: Sapelo Island. About four thousand years ago Native people here piled oyster and clam shells into great rings, some three hundred feet across. Today the island can be reached only by ferry, and a small community descended from people once enslaved on its plantations still lives there.
_shared.cb8c9ec7c534: Piedmont Park. In eighteen ninety-five Atlanta held a giant fair here to show off the “New South”, and Booker T. Washington gave his famous “Atlanta Compromise” speech. Today it is Atlanta’s biggest park, with a lake and a view of the Midtown skyline.
_shared.26f8c8f61c30: Li River. The Lingqu Canal joined the Li River, Pearl River system, to the Xiang River, Yangtze system. Its karst hills near Guilin are printed on the back of the twenty-yuan note.
_shared.e57e047726ae: Clarke County. Named for Elijah Clarke, the Wilkes County militia leader of the Revolution. It is Georgia’s smallest county by area, and since nineteen ninety-one it and the city of Athens have shared one government, Athens-Clarke County.
_shared.04f37116b979: Kuye Island. Today: Sakhalin, Russia. A long, cold island north of Japan. The Treaty of Nerchinsk counted it as Chinese land, but Russia seized it in the nineteenth century.
_shared.d63f91de6a6e: Antietam. About twenty-three thousand soldiers were killed or wounded here near Sharpsburg, Maryland, in a single day — still the bloodiest day in American history. Lee’s army had to turn back, which gave Lincoln the moment to announce the Emancipation Proclamation. The stone Burnside Bridge over Antietam Creek still stands.
_shared.c78022d07a8c: Camp Wheeler. Just east of Macon, this camp trained the thirty-first “Dixie” Division of soldiers from Georgia, Alabama and Florida for World War One. It reopened in nineteen forty, and tens of thousands more trained here for World War Two.
_shared.22b8097c99f3: Etowah Mounds. Today: Etowah Indian Mounds Historic Site, near Cartersville. A fifty-four-acre Mississippian town with six mounds, a plaza and a defensive ditch; it was probably the town of Itaba that de Soto saw in fifteen forty. Mound A, sixty-three feet tall and built basket by basket, is the tallest in Georgia, and a pair of painted marble statues was found here.
_shared.07782d4d8d1b: Nashville. In October eighteen thirty-eight about a dozen Cherokee groups of roughly one thousand people each passed Nashville on the northern route of the Trail of Tears. Today Tennessee’s capital is “Music City,” the home of country music.
_shared.628689810cb2: Utah. Part of the Mexican Cession, where Mormon pioneers founded Salt Lake City in eighteen forty-seven. The two halves of the first transcontinental railroad met at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May tenth, eighteen sixty-nine.
_shared.d7837eef0567: Valley Forge. In the hard winter of seventeen seventy-seven to seventeen seventy-eight, about two thousand of Washington’s twelve thousand soldiers died here of disease. The Prussian officer Baron von Steuben drilled the rest into a real army; rebuilt log huts stand in the park today.
_shared.d7b00d7f1c26: Lamar mound site. Two mounds in the river swamp near Macon, part of Ocmulgee Mounds National Historical Park. One has a rare spiral ramp winding to its top; this was probably the center of Ichisi when de Soto came in fifteen forty.
_shared.0cd6eb7e688c: Bayeux. A seventy-metre embroidered cloth kept here tells the story of the Norman Conquest like a comic strip.
_shared.ff1f24de6d86: Plymouth. In December sixteen twenty the Mayflower’s Pilgrims began their colony here, after signing the Mayflower Compact on board to govern themselves. About half of them died that first winter; in sixteen twenty-one the Wampanoag leader Massasoit made a treaty with the survivors.
_shared.9627896354f7: Putnam County. A farming county in middle Georgia; its county seat is Eatonton, where the writer Alice Walker was born. In the nineteen thirties Black CCC workers here served in separate, segregated camps.
_shared.e10aadfdfad7: Fort Hawkins. Today: Macon, Georgia. Built in eighteen oh six on a hill above the Ocmulgee River, where the river leaves the hills at the Fall Line, this fort was a trading post with the Creek — and the city of Macon grew up beside it. A blockhouse rebuilt in nineteen thirty-eight stands on the site today.
_shared.fd4e7f932795: Baling, Yueyang. Today: Yueyang, Hunan. A city where Dongting Lake meets the Yangtze. Demoted official Teng Zijing governed it so well that “政通人和” — and rebuilt its tower.
_shared.73133d8ae30d: Connecticut. Thomas Hooker’s settlers wrote the Fundamental Orders of sixteen thirty-nine, often called the first written constitution in America. At the Convention, its delegates Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth proposed the Great Compromise that created today’s Senate and House.
_shared.80e6b4ac98b2: Black Forest. Wooded mountains in south-west Germany. In the nineteen eighties acid rain killed many of its trees, which led to cleaner power plants and cars.
_shared.effb9a293a09: Creek Agency. Today: On the Flint River near Roberta, Georgia. US agent Benjamin Hawkins ran a big farm here on the Flint River, trying to get Creek families to farm the American way. In the eighteen eighteen Treaty of the Creek Agency, the Creek gave up more land near the heads of the Ocmulgee and Apalachee rivers.
_shared.6134f7628de9: San Francisco. Delegates of fifty countries met here and signed the Charter of the United Nations. China was the first to sign.
_shared.795ef1335b7e: Mississippi River. The great river of the United States, about three thousand seven hundred kilometers long. Like the Yellow River it carries lots of mud and has levees to stop floods.
_shared.5919c81de1fa: Yelang. Today: the western Hunan and eastern Guizhou area. Yelang was an ancient kingdom in the southwest, the idiom 夜郎自大 comes from it; the Tang county of Yelang lay near Longbiao. Li Bai’s moon will follow his friend even “west of Yelang”.
_shared.496e9c7d5ac3: Mississippi River. North America’s great river flows about two thousand three hundred forty miles from Minnesota to the Gulf of Mexico. It was the US western border in seventeen eighty-three; Cherokee families on the Trail of Tears crossed it in icy winter, and capturing Vicksburg on its bank gave the Union the whole river in eighteen sixty-three.
_shared.c0d23b9b00d5: Wuchao. Today: between Fengqiu and Yanjin, Henan. Cao Cao led five thousand men on a night raid and set the grain on fire; Yuan Shao’s huge army collapsed.
_shared.3022903500a7: Menlo Park. Today: Edison, New Jersey. Thomas Edison built his “invention factory” in this New Jersey village in eighteen seventy-six; the phonograph and a long-lasting light bulb came from here, and he was called the “Wizard of Menlo Park”. The phonograph dates to eighteen seventy-seven, and the light bulb to eighteen seventy-nine. Henry Ford later moved the lab building to his museum in Michigan, and the town was renamed Edison.
_shared.cc980b990980: Bay of Pigs. In April nineteen sixty-one about one thousand four hundred Cuban exiles trained and armed by the CIA landed on this bay to overthrow Fidel Castro, but they were defeated within three days. The failure pushed Castro closer to the Soviet Union — one step toward the nineteen sixty-two missile crisis.
_shared.0f7808ed4508: Humen. In eighteen thirty-nine Lin Zexu destroyed over a million kilograms of opium on the beach here. Its forts guarding the Pearl River were attacked in the Opium War.
_shared.c7f1e2e79d83: Giant Wild Goose Pagoda. Today: Xi’an, Shaanxi. Xuanzang translated Buddhist books here for years. The pagoda still stands in Xi’an, about sixty-four meters tall.
_shared.c4fced218a4a: Kiritimati, Christmas Island. A coral atoll in Kiribati that uses U T C plus fourteen — one of the first places on Earth to start each new day.
_shared.7ee049b55224: East River. After losing the Battle of Long Island, Washington secretly ferried about nine thousand soldiers across this tidal strait in a single night, hidden by a lucky morning fog. Today the Brooklyn Bridge crosses it.
_shared.24f166e3fa60: Wuchang. Today: Wuhan, Hubei. On October tenth, nineteen eleven, revolutionary soldiers rose up in Wuchang and took the city in one night. Province after province followed — this was the nineteen eleven Revolution.
_shared.d6579360d79a: Aachen. Charlemagne built a palace and a domed chapel here and is buried in it. German kings were crowned in Aachen for six hundred years.
_shared.07fae833f4a0: Longxi. Today: Gansu. In one hundred thirty-eight a dragon on Zhang Heng’s seismoscope in Luoyang dropped its ball, though nobody felt anything. Days later a messenger arrived: an earthquake had hit Longxi, hundreds of kilometres away.
_shared.38b1dbeec15c: Danjiangkou Reservoir. Today: Hubei and Henan. A huge reservoir on the Han River. Since twenty fourteen its water flows north for about one thousand four hundred kilometers to Beijing and Tianjin without any pumps — downhill all the way.
_shared.4c17ff8109aa: Dasan Pass. Today: south of Baoji, Shaanxi. A mountain pass in the Qinling. After eleven forty-one the Song-Jin border ran from the Huai River in the east to Dasan Pass in the west.
_shared.949a300c5dc3: Augsburg. Here in fifteen fifty-five the German princes agreed that each ruler could choose whether his land would be Catholic or Lutheran.
_shared.f93b733fca56: Kuwait. A small, oil-rich country at the top of the Persian Gulf. Iraq invaded it in nineteen ninety; when a US-led coalition drove Iraq’s army out in nineteen ninety-one, the retreating troops set more than six hundred oil wells on fire.
_shared.155f7b99efc4: Yazoo lands. Today: Most of today’s Alabama and Mississippi. Georgia once claimed land all the way west to the Mississippi River. In seventeen ninety-five bribed lawmakers sold thirty-five million acres of it cheaply to land companies; furious voters threw them out, and the next legislature burned the law in public.
_shared.eddf8f54b0b2: Niagara Falls. Three waterfalls on the border of the USA and Canada, between Lake Erie and Lake Ontario. Every second about two thousand eight hundred tonnes of water pour over them.
_shared.8d3ae58c6ddf: Shanhai Pass. Today: Qinhuangdao, Hebei. Squeezed between the Yan Mountains and the Bohai Sea — its name means “mountain-sea pass”. At Old Dragon’s Head the wall runs right into the sea. In sixteen forty-four the Qing army entered China proper here.
_shared.44073e21b349: Hemudu. Today: Yuyao, Zhejiang. About seven thousand years ago people here grew rice, lived in stilt houses and already joined timbers with mortise-and-tenon joints.
_shared.f05a8e0ed95f: Robins Field. Today: Robins Air Force Base. From nineteen forty-two workers here repaired thousands of warplanes, and a whole new city, Warner Robins, grew up around the gate. Today the base is one of Georgia’s biggest employers, and its Museum of Aviation shows more than eighty-five aircraft.
_shared.1e599ef41213: Chernobyl. In nineteen eighty-six a reactor at the nuclear power plant here exploded, spreading radioactive dust over much of Europe. A thirty-kilometer zone around it is still closed.
_shared.4cbf16d2b96f: Sardis. Today: near Salihli, Türkiye. Rich King Croesus ruled here, and some of the first coins in the world were made here. Cyrus took it in about five hundred forty-six B C E.
_shared.95d578d2b7ed: Bastille. Today: Place de la Bastille, Paris. Parisians stormed this old royal fortress-prison to seize gunpowder. July fourteenth is now France’s national day. The fortress was pulled down; a column stands in the square.
_shared.86ff237cce35: Port of Savannah. One of America’s busiest container ports: in fiscal year twenty twenty-two it handled a record five point seven six million T E U, twenty-foot containers. Its river channel was deepened to forty-seven feet so giant ships can reach the docks. The work ran from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-two.
_shared.886d6c25e963: Jimmy Carter National Historical Park. In Plains you can visit Carter’s boyhood farm, his old high school, now the visitor center, and the little train depot that was his campaign headquarters in nineteen seventy-six. On the farm you can still see the peanut fields where young Jimmy worked.
_shared.01801864d979: Afghanistan. A mountainous country in Central and South Asia. The nine eleven attacks were planned by al-Qaeda, which had bases there, so in two thousand one the United States went to war in Afghanistan; the last US troops left in twenty twenty-one.
_shared.d7f03b083f74: Savannah River. This three hundred-mile river forms most of the border between Georgia and South Carolina. Augusta grew at its Fall Line rapids and Savannah near its mouth — today giant container ships sail up it to the port.
_shared.6c75aeefe387: Du Fu Thatched Cottage. Today: Chengdu, Sichuan. After years of war Du Fu built a thatched hut here and wrote about two hundred forty poems, including the one about the autumn wind tearing off his roof, 茅屋为秋风所破歌.
_shared.3b8143453b86: Capachequi. Today: Near Albany, Georgia. A chiefdom in southwest Georgia, near today’s Albany and the Flint River. De Soto’s army passed through in March fifteen forty, the first Europeans to reach the area.
_shared.a71254c44037: Lagos, Nigeria. Nigeria’s biggest city and port, on the Gulf of Guinea — one of the fastest-growing cities in Africa, with over fifteen million people.
_shared.3c6f66751658: Doha. At a WTO meeting here, members approved China joining the World Trade Organization. China became a member on December eleventh, two thousand one.
_shared.238f3b990dfb: New France. Today: Quebec, Canada. France’s colony stretched from Quebec along the Saint Lawrence River and the Great Lakes; most French colonists were fur traders who worked closely with Native nations. After the French and Indian War, France lost Canada to Britain in seventeen sixty-three.
_shared.44becc32417c: University of Mississippi, Ole Miss. In September nineteen sixty-two James Meredith became the first Black student at this university in Oxford, Mississippi. A violent riot broke out on campus, and President Kennedy sent federal marshals and thousands of soldiers to protect him; a statue of Meredith now stands on the campus.
_shared.7ea38bc367ac: Brunswick. This coastal port city, the seat of Glynn County, ships huge numbers of cars overseas. In World War Two its J. A. Jones shipyard built ninety-nine Liberty ships in about two years, as farm workers poured in for jobs.
_shared.b567273f05b5: Los Angeles. The second-largest US city, on the Pacific coast of California. It is three hours behind Atlanta.
_shared.4a80d3f8a07f: Boston. It became the center of protest against British rule: the Boston Massacre and the Boston Tea Party happened here, and Britain closed its harbor as punishment in seventeen seventy-four. The Boston Massacre happened in seventeen seventy and the Boston Tea Party in seventeen seventy-three. Today the two point five-mile Freedom Trail leads past sixteen historic sites.
_shared.ffee7206858e: Yuanmou. Two front teeth found here in nineteen sixty-five belong to Yuanmou Man, who lived about one point seven million years ago — the earliest ancient human yet confirmed in China.
_shared.589f048ef6f6: Fort Ticonderoga. In May seventeen seventy-five Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys captured this fort by surprise. That winter Henry Knox dragged fifty-nine of its cannons about three hundred miles on ox sledges to Boston, forcing the British to leave the city.
_shared.91731045e374: Xiang River. Today: upper reaches in northern Guangxi. The Xiang flows north to Dongting Lake. Near its source the Lingqu Canal links it to the Li River. In nineteen thirty-four the Red Army broke through the enemy’s fourth blockade line here at a terrible cost.
_shared.80f6d433c2d4: Port of Brunswick. Georgia’s second deep-water port, one of the busiest US ports for shipping cars and trucks on “roll-on roll-off” ships.
_shared.dd9c02be385e: Luding Bridge. Today: Luding, Sichuan. An iron-chain bridge built in seventeen oh six. The enemy had removed the planks; twenty-two soldiers climbed across the bare chains under fire and captured it.
_shared.b0f78dc16c67: Indian Territory. Today: Oklahoma. The Indian Removal Act of eighteen thirty sent the Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw and Seminole nations west to this land beyond Arkansas. At the end of the Trail of Tears the Cherokee rebuilt their nation here, with Tahlequah as capital; in nineteen oh seven it became part of the state of Oklahoma.
_shared.de110ef4d0fd: Oregon Trail ruts near Guernsey. Today: Oregon Trail Ruts State Historic Site, Wyoming. So many wagons rolled over this soft sandstone ridge that their wheels wore ruts up to about five feet deep. They are some of the best-preserved Oregon Trail ruts anywhere.
_shared.01ea0bb7c173: Pennsylvania. William Penn, a Quaker, founded it in sixteen eighty-one as a “holy experiment” where people of every faith could worship freely. Both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution were written in its city of Philadelphia, and in eighteen sixty-three Lee’s second invasion of the North failed at Gettysburg.
_shared.b5102d40d856: Oak Ridge. A whole city built in secret in the Tennessee hills for the Manhattan Project — by nineteen forty-five about seventy-five thousand people lived there, yet it was on no map. Its giant plants, running on TVA electricity, made uranium fuel for the atomic bomb.
_shared.8ddc1df80ab2: Silicon Valley. The south end of San Francisco Bay, named for the silicon in computer chips. Intel’s first microprocessor, Apple, Google, and the iPhone all came from here — and both Apple and Google started in a garage! Intel’s first microprocessor dates to nineteen seventy-one, Apple to nineteen seventy-six, Google to nineteen ninety-eight, and the iPhone to two thousand seven.
_shared.da5047b862a9: Washington, D.C. The nation’s capital, home of Congress, the President and the Supreme Court — the original Declaration of Independence and Constitution are kept at the National Archives here. On August twenty-eighth, nineteen sixty-three, about two hundred fifty thousand people filled the National Mall for the March on Washington.
_shared.abed4d07870b: Oslo. The capital of Norway, where the Nobel Peace Prize is given every December. In nineteen sixty-four Martin Luther King Junior received it here; at thirty-five he was then the youngest person ever to win it, and he gave all the prize money to the civil rights movement.
_shared.e119ef9a982c: Stone Forest. Today: Shilin County, Yunnan. Rain slowly dissolved the limestone and left a “forest” of stone pillars, some over thirty meters tall.
_shared.04a5ab17f8a6: Iraq. A country along the Tigris and Euphrates rivers — the land of ancient Mesopotamia. In August nineteen ninety Iraq’s army invaded Kuwait, and in nineteen ninety-one a US-led coalition drove it out in the Persian Gulf War.
_shared.dfc355f0c2f5: Golden Gate Bridge. Today: San Francisco, USA. San Francisco’s famous red suspension bridge, two point seven kilometers long — a good yardstick for how long China’s new bridges are.
_shared.accff1033fa4: Uluru, Ayers Rock. A giant sandstone rock, three hundred forty-eight meters high, in the dry Red Centre of Australia. It is sacred to the Anangu people and glows red at sunset.
_shared.970c7e614dbf: Ceylon. Today: Sri Lanka. A stone tablet Zheng He set up at Galle in fourteen oh nine is written in Chinese, Tamil and Persian. It is now in the Colombo National Museum.
_shared.5ce9bb89036f: Auschwitz-Birkenau. Today: Oświęcim, Poland. The largest Nazi camp, where about one point one million people, most of them Jews, were murdered. It is now a memorial so that the world remembers.
_shared.ebed60551d66: New Delhi. Capital of India. Greater Delhi has over thirty million people and is one of the world’s largest city areas.
_shared.c699def8cb32: Auburn Avenue. When segregation kept Black Atlantans out of white businesses, they built their own here — banks, insurance companies, newspapers and churches — and “Sweet Auburn” was called “the richest Black street in the world”. Martin Luther King Junior was born on this street in nineteen twenty-nine.
_shared.83f7805fb68c: Statue of Liberty. France gave this copper statue to the United States, and it was dedicated in eighteen eighty-six; Emma Lazarus’s poem on the pedestal welcomes the “huddled masses yearning to breathe free”. It was once copper-brown and slowly turned green — and even with its pedestal it is shorter than a Saturn five rocket.
_shared.8e70b737c834: San Antonio. Founded by the Spanish in seventeen eighteen around a chain of missions, one of which was the Alamo, besieged in eighteen thirty-six. Today the River Walk winds through downtown below street level, lined with cafés.
_shared.f9479d864b03: Miami. A big city near the southern tip of Florida, only about two hundred thirty miles from Havana. During the nineteen sixty-two Cuban Missile Crisis it was well within range of the Soviet missiles in Cuba.
_shared.7a88a4cd61ab: Old Governor’s Mansion. Finished in eighteen thirty-nine in grand Greek Revival style, it was home to Georgia’s governors while Milledgeville was the capital, and General Sherman made it his headquarters in November eighteen sixty-four. Today it is a museum that also tells the stories of the enslaved people who worked there.
_shared.38610bbcfbee: Colosseum. About fifty thousand people could watch gladiator fights here. Its arches and vaults are still copied in stadiums today.
_shared.0f279dd91f63: Manzanar. Today: Manzanar National Historic Site, California. After Executive Order nine zero six six in nineteen forty-two, more than ten thousand Japanese Americans — most of them US citizens — were forced to live behind barbed wire in this dusty camp below the Sierra Nevada. Ansel Adams photographed daily life here with Mount Williamson rising behind, and a guard tower has been rebuilt at the site.
_shared.cf98c0852901: International Date Line. A line in the Pacific, mostly along one hundred eighty degrees longitude, where the calendar date changes. Cross it going west and you skip ahead one day.
_shared.405baa89af4c: Americus. In nineteen sixty-three police arrested young civil rights protesters here, and four leaders were charged with “insurrection”, a crime that could bring the death penalty, before a federal court freed them. Americus is also where Habitat for Humanity, which builds homes around the world, began in nineteen seventy-six.
_shared.e3bd3d4dd74d: Midway. The heart of Saint John’s Parish. Its rice planters, who enslaved many people, were also Georgia’s most eager Patriots and sent Lyman Hall to Congress in seventeen seventy-five; Midway Church and its old cemetery still stand. The church dates to seventeen ninety-two.
_shared.d209f1f8effc: Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America. This giant electric-vehicle factory near the Port of Savannah began full production in October twenty twenty-four and held its grand opening in March twenty twenty-five. Robots do much of the work, and about eight thousand five hundred jobs are planned by twenty thirty-one.
_shared.e815563edf31: Hart County. Created in eighteen fifty-three and named for Nancy Hart — the only Georgia county named for a woman. Much of it borders Lake Hartwell, a big reservoir on the Savannah River.
_shared.ce4084ac4548: Little Stone Pool. Today: Lingling, Yongzhou, Hunan. A small pool on the Yu Stream, 愚溪, west of old Yongzhou, with a rock bottom and fish that seem to “float in the air”. A small pool there is shown to visitors as the one in the essay.
_shared.5899c1378b7e: Pickrick restaurant. Today: site now part of Georgia Tech. On July third, nineteen sixty-four, the day after the Civil Rights Act became law, owner Lester Maddox chased away three Black students with a pistol. He closed the restaurant rather than serve Black customers — and two years later was elected governor.
_shared.d0d04dc80dd4: Dazexiang. Today: southeast of Suzhou, Anhui. Stuck in heavy rain and facing death for being late, nine hundred conscripts rose up here — the first big peasant uprising in Chinese history.
_shared.50f07bf1bd64: Orléans. In the Hundred Years’ War, seventeen-year-old Joan of Arc led a French army that broke the English siege of Orléans.
_shared.0ab7da876260: Pingtan Island. From Pingtan in Fujian it is only about one hundred thirty kilometers across the strait to Taiwan.
_shared.5b220c865969: Stone Mountain. A huge dome of granite near Atlanta, rising about two hundred fifty meters above Georgia’s Piedmont hills.
_shared.ea47e1b00022: Accra. Capital of Ghana, on the Gulf of Guinea. It lies very close to the prime meridian, so it uses U T C plus or minus zero.
_shared.e674c68835d9: Harpers Ferry. Today: Harpers Ferry, West Virginia. In October eighteen fifty-nine John Brown and twenty-one men seized the US arsenal here, hoping to arm enslaved people for an uprising. Marines captured him in the small brick fire-engine house now called “John Brown’s Fort”, which still stands where the Potomac and Shenandoah rivers meet.
_shared.89eae3e395d0: Manhattan. In sixteen twenty-six the Dutch “bought” this island from the Lenape for trade goods worth sixty guilders — but the Lenape probably thought they were agreeing to share the land, not selling it forever. The Dutch town of New Amsterdam at its southern tip later became New York City.
_shared.3811d6b0d0b0: Rome. Rome grew from a small republic into an empire around the Mediterranean. In fifteen eighty-two the calendar we use today was issued here, with a year of three hundred sixty-five point two four two five days — the same as Guo Shoujing’s calendar three hundred years earlier.
_shared.c7ea79830654: Lagos, Portugal. Prince Henry the Navigator’s ships sailed down the African coast from this harbour. Sadly it also had Europe’s first market for enslaved Africans, fourteen forty-four.
_shared.27d66ba0d37e: Mississippi. Most of Mississippi was once part of Georgia’s Yazoo lands, and after Indian Removal cotton planters took over its rich soil. It seceded in January eighteen sixty-one; a century later, in the nineteen sixty-four Freedom Summer, volunteers went door to door here helping Black citizens register to vote.
_shared.45cc39cbf0fe: Amazon River. The river with the most water on Earth, flowing about six thousand four hundred kilometers east to the Atlantic. Its basin holds the world’s largest rainforest.
_shared.a314172890f3: Luoyang Bridge, Quanzhou. Today: Quanzhou, Fujian. Builders grew oysters on the stones to glue the foundations together — a clever trick from nine hundred years ago.
_shared.f924c575c823: Lion Grove Garden. Today: Suzhou, Jiangsu. Its rockery is a maze of Taihu rocks shaped like lions, with tunnels to get lost in. In the twentieth century it belonged to the family of the architect I. M. Pei.
_shared.8b331015e736: Little River. A river in east Georgia that flows into the Savannah River above Augusta. The seventeen seventy-three “New Purchase” took about two million acres of Creek and Cherokee land north of it, which became Wilkes County.
_shared.4455c2c5ca0a: Nerchinsk. Today: Nerchinsk, Russia. In sixteen eighty-nine China and Russia signed a treaty here that fixed the eastern part of their border along the Argun River and the Outer Khingan Mountains.
_shared.a5404fcc4ffe: Mombasa-Nairobi Railway. About four hundred eighty kilometers from the port of Mombasa to Kenya’s capital Nairobi, built by a Chinese company. It cut the trip from over ten hours to about five.
_shared.9515bdb8df8b: Mount Huang. Today: Huangshan, Anhui. Granite peaks famous for strange pines, odd rocks, seas of cloud and hot springs. The highest, Lotus Peak, is one thousand eight hundred sixty-four meters.
_shared.546491ff1dcb: New York. The Dutch town of New Amsterdam became English New York in sixteen sixty-four, and in seventeen eighty-nine the first Congress under the Constitution met here. The Erie Canal made it the nation’s busiest port, millions of immigrants arrived here, and in eighteen eighty-two Edison’s Pearl Street station began lighting its streets with electricity.
_shared.525649847bad: Red River, Texas-Oklahoma. Named for its reddish mud, this river forms much of the border between Texas and Oklahoma. In eighteen nineteen the US and Spain agreed to make it part of the boundary between their lands.
_shared.1f5e0a752c35: Sunbury. Today: Historic site in Liberty County. Once a busy port that rivaled Savannah. In November seventeen seventy-eight the British demanded the surrender of its Fort Morris, and Colonel John McIntosh answered “Come and take it!”; after the war the town faded away, and only its old cemetery is left.
_shared.a457df0ab303: Darien. Highland Scots founded Darien in seventeen thirty-six to guard the frontier, and in seventeen thirty-nine they signed a petition against bringing slavery into Georgia. After the Civil War, Tunis Campbell organized freedpeople here and was elected a state senator.
_shared.869c71b1d16e: Java. Today: Java, Indonesia. A big island of Indonesia that Zheng He’s fleet visited. Today more than one hundred fifty million people live there.
_shared.0f0b9bc039a2: Independence, Missouri. In the eighteen forties wagon trains bought oxen, flour and supplies here before starting the two thousand-mile Oregon Trail. Today the National Frontier Trails Museum tells their story.
_shared.a3a5611ca631: Camp David. The president’s private mountain retreat in the woods of Maryland. In September nineteen seventy-eight Jimmy Carter kept the leaders of Israel and Egypt here for thirteen days until they agreed to the Camp David Accords, which led to peace between the two countries.
_shared.db24948b3604: Aiwan Pavilion. Today: Mount Yuelu, Changsha, Hunan. A pavilion among maple trees on Mount Yuelu. Its name comes from Du Mu’s line “停车坐爱枫林晚” — every autumn the leaves turn red.
_shared.022e65a169d3: Jakarta. A month after Astana, China proposed a “Twenty-first-Century Maritime Silk Road” in Jakarta — the “Road” of the Belt and Road.
_shared.ed40f21fa118: Great Dividing Range. Mountains running about three thousand five hundred kilometers down Australia’s east coast. They catch moist Pacific air, so the coast is rainy and the inland is dry.
_shared.f5b305474fee: Carcassonne. A whole hilltop town wrapped in two rings of walls with fifty-two towers — what a medieval fortress city looked like.
_shared.1164d4784d4d: Charles Town. Today: Charleston, South Carolina. Rice grown by enslaved Africans made it the richest city in the colonial South. In April eighteen sixty-one the first shots of the Civil War were fired at Fort Sumter, in its harbor.
_shared.948e90d171a2: Piraeus. The port of Athens, Greece’s biggest. A Chinese shipping company has run its container terminals since two thousand nine, and it became one of the Mediterranean’s busiest.
_shared.bdd1a0e3ca7f: Malindi. Today: Malindi, Kenya. The giraffe from Malindi reached Beijing in fourteen fifteen; people thought it was the magical qilin.
_shared.536be9b4d8d5: Albany, New York. The capital of New York State, on the Hudson River. Don’t mix it up with Albany, Georgia, where the Albany Movement for civil rights took place in nineteen sixty-one to nineteen sixty-two.
_shared.a6a14428f2d6: Texas. Texas broke away from Mexico in eighteen thirty-six and was its own republic until the US annexed it in eighteen forty-five — which led straight to war with Mexico. Cowboys later drove Texas cattle north to the railroads, and with two hundred fifty-four counties it is the only state with more counties than Georgia’s one hundred fifty-nine.
_shared.8e697c968a54: Badaling. The most-visited stretch of the Great Wall. The wall is about seven point eight meters high and so wide on top that five horses could ride side by side.
_shared.526a947c1efd: Wormsloe Historic Site. Noble Jones, one of the first settlers, built a small fortified house here of tabby, a concrete made with oyster shells; its ruins are the oldest standing building in Savannah. Visitors arrive along a one point five-mile avenue of about four hundred live oaks hung with Spanish moss.
_shared.b80f7dfc0ec1: Almaty. Kazakhstan’s largest city, below the snowy Tian Shan mountains. In twenty thirteen the “Silk Road Economic Belt” was first proposed in Kazakhstan.
_shared.d872a4503eee: Chattanooga. Railroads from four directions met here, so it was called the “gateway to Georgia”. After the Union won the “Battle Above the Clouds” on Lookout Mountain in November eighteen sixty-three, Sherman’s march on Atlanta began here in May eighteen sixty-four.
_shared.ba55a56469d2: Xinzheng. Today: Xinzheng, Henan. Han, 韩, the smallest of the seven Warring States, was the first that Qin conquered, two hundred thirty B C E.
_shared.36af97354ecc: New York. The Dutch colony of New Netherland became New York when England took it in sixteen sixty-four. The state stretches from New York City to Niagara Falls, and its capital is Albany — not the same Albany as the one in Georgia.
_shared.fa0915ca0eba: Jokhang Temple. Today: Lhasa, Tibet. In front of the temple stands the Tang-Tubo Alliance Tablet of eight twenty-three, which speaks of the two as “uncle and nephew”, one family.
_shared.4b63d3866900: Zengmu Ansha. An underwater coral bank in the Nansha Islands, about seventeen meters below the sea surface.
_shared.02574fdcbec8: White House. Every president since John Adams in eighteen hundred has lived and worked in this white house at sixteen hundred Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C. In nineteen seventy-seven Jimmy Carter became the first president from Georgia to move in.
_shared.679e8498042d: Massalia, Marseille. Today: Marseille, France. Greek sailors founded Massalia about two thousand six hundred years ago. In thirteen forty-seven the Black Death arrived here by ship and spread into France.
_shared.8167fe84c51c: Birmingham. In nineteen sixty-three police in Birmingham, Alabama, turned fire hoses and dogs on marching children, and King wrote his “Letter from Birmingham Jail”; the pictures shocked the nation. That September a bomb at the sixteenth Street Baptist Church killed four Black girls.
_shared.98a429579e64: World Trade Center. On September eleventh, two thousand one, terrorists flew two hijacked planes into the Twin Towers, and nearly two thousand eight hundred people died here. Today two huge waterfall pools fill the towers’ footprints, with the victims’ names cut into bronze around them, and One World Trade Center rises one thousand seven hundred seventy-six feet nearby.
_shared.677f48a73bea: Lazikou Pass. Today: Têwo, Diebu, County, Gansu. A narrow gap between cliffs, only about thirty meters wide — the “gateway to Gansu”. The Red Army took it in one night.
_shared.1225b0997e63: Cold Harbor. Here, near Richmond, Grant ordered a head-on attack against dug-in Confederate trenches on June third, eighteen sixty-four, and thousands of Union soldiers fell in about an hour — Grant later said he regretted it. The old trench lines can still be seen in the woods.
_shared.511e8bbe1661: Dayton. Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio, and built their gliders and the nineteen oh three Flyer here before shipping them to Kitty Hawk. Their old cycle shop is now part of a national historical park.
_shared.a62a930e9902: Anniston. On May fourteenth, nineteen sixty-one, a mob chased a Greyhound bus carrying Freedom Riders out of this Alabama town and set it on fire with a firebomb. All the riders escaped, and more Freedom Riders soon took their place; the old bus station is now part of the Freedom Riders National Monument.
_shared.a021f1f0c5b1: Boston Common. Facing the Massachusetts State House stands a bronze memorial to Colonel Robert Gould Shaw and the fifty-fourth Massachusetts, one of the first Black regiments in the Union army. Cows grazed on the Common until eighteen thirty!
_shared.b46254fda03a: Wyoming. A high, windy land of mountains and plains crossed by the Oregon Trail — you can still see wagon ruts near Guernsey. In eighteen sixty-nine Wyoming Territory became the first place in the US to give women the right to vote.
_shared.296b1561cb1e: Custer County. The photographer Solomon Butcher took thousands of pictures of homesteaders here, like the Mitchell family’s sod house in eighteen eighty-eight. With almost no trees on the plains, settlers cut blocks of grassy earth to build their homes.
_shared.fc7c931b1585: Creek, Muscogee, Nation. Today: Central and western Georgia, eastern Alabama. In the seventeen eighties the powerful Creek Nation was frontier Georgia’s strong neighbor — one reason Georgia wanted a strong national government. Treaty by treaty its land was taken: by eighteen twenty-seven no Creek land was left in Georgia, and in eighteen thirty-six most Creek people were forced west to Indian Territory.
_shared.7e18e2e0cae9: Dalton. Dalton calls itself the “Carpet Capital of the World” — its mills make most of the carpet sold in the United States. In May eighteen sixty-four Sherman’s army of about one hundred thousand faced Johnston’s sixty thousand near here, and the Atlanta Campaign began.
_shared.dbdc726635b5: Volga River. Today: Russia. Europe’s longest river. In seventeen seventy-one the Torghut people under Ubashi set out from here and trekked thousands of kilometres east to return to China.
_shared.d3d5b80b7f62: Pataliputra. Today: Patna, India. Ashoka ruled his huge empire from here. A Greek visitor described its wooden walls with five hundred seventy towers.
_shared.11bac09f573e: Harappa. Today: Punjab, Pakistan. The first Indus city that archaeologists dug up, nineteen twenties, so the whole civilization is also called “Harappan”. It had large granaries and brick houses.
_shared.cf0e30d320c0: Astana. In a speech here in twenty thirteen, China proposed building a new “Silk Road Economic Belt” across Asia to Europe — the “Belt” of the Belt and Road.
_shared.0fbd8974ff12: Congregation Mickve Israel. Jewish settlers reached Savannah just five months after the colony began, and Oglethorpe let them stay. Their congregation is one of the oldest in America, and its Gothic-style synagogue on Monterey Square still keeps a Torah scroll they brought in seventeen thirty-three.
_shared.30a8fe131716: Nile Delta. A green fan of farmland where the Nile reaches the Mediterranean. About thirty-nine million people live here, with desert all around.
_shared.d557b67766ee: Miaodao Islands. Today: Changdao, Yantai, Shandong. About thirty islands strung between Shandong and Liaodong.
_shared.9f9c340882a3: Albuquerque. Bill Gates and Paul Allen founded Microsoft in this New Mexico city in nineteen seventy-five, to be near the company that made the Altair computer; in nineteen seventy-nine they moved to Washington State. Every October hundreds of hot-air balloons fill its sky at the Balloon Fiesta.
_shared.8dfb810c6715: Tallulah River. This mountain river carved Tallulah Gorge, about two miles long and nearly one thousand feet deep. In nineteen seventy the tightrope walker Karl Wallenda crossed the gorge on a wire — doing two headstands along the way!
_shared.3cc03534e7d1: Spanish Florida. Today: Florida, US state. Spain claimed “La Florida” in the fifteen hundreds and made Saint Augustine its capital; Georgia was founded as a buffer against it. The United States got Florida from Spain by a treaty in eighteen nineteen, and it became a state in eighteen forty-five.
_shared.8bacbcb7364d: Jiajin Mountain. Over four thousand meters high with thin air and snow. Many soldiers in thin clothes froze on the way up.
_shared.a0a95bffe439: Sutter’s Mill. Today: Coloma, California. On January twenty-fourth, eighteen forty-eight, James Marshall spotted shiny flakes in the ditch below the sawmill he was building for John Sutter — gold! The Gold Rush brought about three hundred thousand people to California, and for California’s Native peoples it brought disaster.
_shared.ac2fed6d298b: Dubai. A city of skyscrapers in the United Arab Emirates, built in the desert with money from oil and trade. Its Burj Khalifa is the tallest building in the world, at eight hundred twenty-eight meters.
_shared.3a176d4ee6a4: Fort Cass. Today: Charleston, Tennessee. Thousands of Cherokee were held in crowded camps around Fort Cass in the hot summer of eighteen thirty-eight, and many died of disease. Chief John Ross won the right for the Cherokee to lead their own removal, and most groups set out from here in the fall.
_shared.a0c25ef66d49: Saint Marys River. It flows out of the Okefenokee Swamp and loops around to the Atlantic, forming the border between Georgia and Florida. It became Georgia’s southern border in seventeen sixty-three.
_shared.eee24b590f03: Charleston, Tennessee. This small town on the Hiwassee River grew up around Fort Cass, the center of the eighteen thirty-eight removal camps. Thousands of Cherokee waited here through a hot, sickly summer before the long walk west.
_shared.e6e6d5dd19b9: Harlem. A neighborhood in northern Manhattan that became the heart of Black culture in the nineteen twenties Harlem Renaissance — poet Langston Hughes, writer Zora Neale Hurston and jazz stars like Duke Ellington and Louis Armstrong. The Apollo Theater still holds its famous Amateur Night.
_shared.ac707fa59678: Wusong. Today: Baoshan District, Shanghai. In eighteen seventy-six a British company opened China’s first railway, a line of about fifteen kilometers from Shanghai to Wusong at the mouth of the Huangpu River. The Qing government bought it the next year — and tore it up.
_shared.22d1e33adfd0: National Constitution Center. A museum about the Constitution on Independence Mall in Philadelphia, opened in two thousand three. In Signers’ Hall you can stand among life-size bronze statues of forty-two delegates of the seventeen eighty-seven Convention.
_shared.6550ffe87b66: Wangxia. Today: Macao. In eighteen forty-four China and the United States signed their first treaty in this village, the Treaty of Wangxia; it was one of the unequal treaties forced on China after the Opium War. It was signed at the Kun Iam Temple, where a round stone table from that day is still kept.
_shared.9f89a155deb5: Chesapeake Bay. On September fifth, seventeen eighty-one, a French fleet under Admiral de Grasse drove off the British navy at the mouth of this bay, so no ships could rescue Cornwallis at Yorktown. The Chesapeake is the largest estuary in the United States.
_shared.1f820a23262e: Nanchang. The Nanchang Uprising fired the first shot of armed resistance against the Nationalists. August first is now the founding day of the People’s Liberation Army.
_shared.83327ddeb637: Bohai Sea. Almost surrounded by Liaoning, Hebei, Tianjin and Shandong. It is shallow — only about eighteen meters deep on average — and parts freeze in winter.
_shared.fa1eac161824: Savannah. Oglethorpe laid Savannah out in seventeen thirty-three as neighborhoods around shady squares — twenty-two of those squares are still there. Sherman’s March to the Sea ended here in eighteen sixty-four, and today it has one of the busiest container ports in the country.
_shared.338c78dc2537: Grand Canyon. About four hundred forty-six kilometers long and up to one point eight kilometers deep. Its walls show rock layers almost two billion years old, like pages in a history book.
_shared.80a898148359: Maryland. Lord Baltimore founded it in sixteen thirty-four as a refuge for Catholics, and its Toleration Act of sixteen forty-nine protected Christians of different churches. In the Civil War it was a slave state that stayed in the Union, and Lee’s first invasion of the North was stopped here at Antietam.
_shared.56f0ffc06df9: Castle Garden. Today: Castle Clinton National Monument, Battery Park, New York. Before Ellis Island, about eight million immigrants entered America through this round stone fort at the tip of Manhattan. Built as a fort before the War of eighteen twelve, it later became a concert hall and even an aquarium — today it is Castle Clinton, where you buy ferry tickets to the Statue of Liberty.
_shared.32f92614c16c: Marathon. Athenian soldiers beat a much bigger Persian army on this plain. The story of a runner carrying the news forty kilometers to Athens gave us the marathon race.
_shared.96409df300c9: Louisville. Named for King Louis the Sixteenth of France, who had helped America win independence. In seventeen ninety-six the legislature publicly burned the papers of the corrupt Yazoo land sale here — legend says the fire was lit with a magnifying glass and sunlight.
_shared.b00636ff7a0e: Glynn County. Home of Brunswick and most of the Golden Isles on Georgia’s coast. Its old nineteen oh seven courthouse sits in a park shaded by huge live oaks draped with Spanish moss.
_shared.795be573071c: Sanya. Sanya is about eighteen degrees north — but China’s southernmost point, Zengmu Ansha, is much farther south.
_shared.342496c7c6f8: Saint Paul. Minnesota’s capital, on the Mississippi River. From here James J. Hill’s Great Northern Railway reached all the way to Seattle in eighteen ninety-three — built without the free government land the other transcontinental lines got.
_shared.20c0e4b865e2: Kitty Hawk. The Wright brothers picked these windy sand dunes on North Carolina’s Outer Banks for steady winds and soft landings. On December seventeenth, nineteen oh three, Orville flew one hundred twenty feet in twelve seconds — shorter than the wingspan of a jumbo jet. A granite monument now crowns Big Kill Devil Hill.
_shared.75b381e05fed: Three Gorges Dam. Today: Sandouping, Yichang, Hubei. The dam is two thousand three hundred thirty-five meters long and one hundred eighty-one meters high. It controls floods, makes clean electricity and lets big ships sail to Chongqing.
_shared.2797244400df: Dallas. A big city in north Texas, one of the cities in the lesson’s missile-range calculator: Soviet missiles in Cuba could have reached it. In nineteen sixty-three President Kennedy was assassinated here.
_shared.bef9ddbce0df: Oconee River. It flows from the hills near Athens south past Milledgeville and joins the Ocmulgee to form the Altamaha. After the treaties of seventeen eighty-three and seventeen ninety it was the border between Georgia’s settlers and the Creek Nation.
_shared.f517aa41920f: Mount Langya. Today: southwest of Chuzhou, Anhui. Wooded hills just southwest of Chuzhou — “蔚然而深秀者, 琅琊也”. The Niang Spring and the Old Drunkard’s Pavilion are in its valleys.
_shared.e5797fe9abbe: Fort McAllister. This fort of earth and sand on the Ogeechee River had beaten off Union warships, but on December thirteenth, eighteen sixty-four, Hazen’s soldiers stormed it in about fifteen minutes. That opened a link to the Union fleet, and Savannah fell days later.
_shared.ddc954ed2266: Arabian Peninsula. The world’s largest peninsula, mostly desert. Around six ten Muhammad began preaching Islam in Mecca here.
_shared.256bc0953a4b: Thomas Edison National Historical Park. In eighteen eighty-seven Edison moved to a much bigger laboratory in West Orange, New Jersey, where his team built movie cameras and better phonographs. Visitors can see his lab, his huge library and a copy of the “Black Maria”, the first movie studio.
_shared.5b14c8f35ca8: Kowloon. Today: Kowloon, Hong Kong. The peninsula across the harbour from Hong Kong Island. Britain took its southern tip in eighteen sixty; China resumed sovereignty over all of Hong Kong in nineteen ninety-seven.
_shared.be8854bd085f: New England. Rocky soil and long winters made farming hard, so New Englanders fished, cut timber and built ships; most towns were founded by Puritans who wanted to worship in their own way. From eighteen seventy-two, one hundred twenty Chinese boys came here to study.
_shared.6bd2a9419e00: Missouri. Missouri joined the Union as a slave state in the Missouri Compromise of eighteen twenty, and its towns were the starting points of the Oregon and Santa Fe trails. In the winter of eighteen thirty-nine Trail of Tears groups crossed it, and in the Civil War it was a border slave state that stayed in the Union.
_shared.fed31c075039: Vidalia. This small Coastal Plain town gave its name to Vidalia onions, so sweet that some people bite into them like apples. By law, only onions grown in about twenty counties around Vidalia may carry the name.
_shared.f2d187d54c76: Trent. Today: Trento, Italy. Catholic bishops met here on and off for eighteen years to answer the Protestants and reform their own Church.
_shared.71851ffbd2c4: Russell-Brasstown Scenic Byway. A forty-one-mile scenic loop road through the Chattahoochee National Forest in the Blue Ridge Mountains. It passes the road up to Brasstown Bald, Georgia’s highest point, and is especially colorful in fall.
_shared.f11384475d14: UCLA. On October twenty-ninth, nineteen sixty-nine, a student in Leonard Kleinrock’s lab tried to type “L O G I N” to a computer at SRI — the system crashed after “L O”, so the first message on ARPANET, the internet’s ancestor, was “L O”. The room, three four two zero Boelter Hall, is now a small museum.
_shared.75cc6cb63cf1: New Netherland. Today: New York and New Jersey. The Dutch built fur-trading posts along the Hudson River and the town of New Amsterdam on Manhattan. In sixteen sixty-four English warships sailed in, the Dutch gave up without a fight, and New Amsterdam became New York.
_shared.c64d34edb2d0: Hoover Dam. Thousands of workers desperate for Depression-era jobs built this seven hundred twenty-six-foot concrete dam across the Colorado River, between Nevada and Arizona; it was begun under President Hoover and finished in nineteen thirty-six under FDR. It holds back Lake Mead and makes electricity for millions of people.
_shared.964c3448bed1: Tuskegee Institute. Today: Tuskegee University, Alabama. Booker T. Washington led this school for Black students, and from eighteen ninety-six George Washington Carver taught farmers here to rotate crops like peanuts and sweet potatoes. From nineteen forty-one the Tuskegee Airmen, the first Black military pilots, learned to fly at nearby Moton Field, where the old hangars are now a national historic site.
_shared.2d1d49f7a635: Terracotta Army. Today: Lintong, Xi’an, Shaanxi. About eight thousand life-size clay soldiers, each with a different face, stand in battle order one point five kilometers east of the tomb. Farmers found them in nineteen seventy-four.
_shared.d2b514b1b787: Franklin County. Land the Cherokee were made to give up in seventeen eighty-three became Franklin County, handed out free to white settlers as “headrights.” It was named after Benjamin Franklin.
_shared.5c42da4aff56: Swift Creek site. A Woodland-period village site beside Swift Creek near Macon, dug by archaeologists in the nineteen thirties. It gave its name to Swift Creek pottery, made by pressing carved wooden paddles into wet clay.
_shared.0bde316a0def: Amicalola Falls. At seven hundred twenty-nine feet, Georgia’s tallest waterfall tumbles down a Blue Ridge mountainside; its Cherokee name means “tumbling waters.” A staircase of about six hundred steps climbs beside it, and a trail from here leads to Springer Mountain.
_shared.77e19f616b95: Ruijin. Today: Ruijin, Jiangxi. Called the “Red Capital”. In October nineteen thirty-four the Red Army set out from Ruijin and Yudu on the Long March.
_shared.5415783e819f: Muscogee County. Home of Columbus on the Chattahoochee River, across from Alabama; the county is named for the Muscogee, Creek, people who lived here. In nineteen seventy-one Columbus and Muscogee County became the first in Georgia to join into one combined government.
_shared.8890468f3574: World of Coca-Cola. Coca-Cola was invented by an Atlanta pharmacist in eighteen eighty-six, and the company still has its headquarters in the city. At this museum beside Centennial Olympic Park you can see the vault that holds the secret formula and taste drinks from around the world.
_shared.8e5f2b04988c: Caracas. Capital of Venezuela, in a cool mountain valley about nine hundred meters up, just inland from the Caribbean coast.
_shared.1c6625e26167: Haojing. Today: southwest of Xi’an, Shaanxi. King Wu set out from Haojing to defeat the Shang at Muye, about ten forty-six B C E.
_shared.746c1a0f151f: Apalachee. Today: Tallahassee area, Florida. The land of the Apalachee people, skilled corn farmers in the Florida panhandle. De Soto spent the winter of fifteen thirty-nine to fifteen forty at their main town, Anhaica, in today’s Tallahassee, then marched north into Georgia on March third, fifteen forty.
_shared.068558027c38: Daqin, Roman Empire. Today: Rome, Italy. Silk reached Rome along the Silk Road and Roman nobles loved it. In ninety-seven C E Gan Ying set out for Daqin but turned back at the Persian Gulf.
_shared.8c34b6fc1263: Great Pyramid of Giza. Built about four thousand five hundred years ago for the pharaoh Khufu, it was the tallest building on Earth for almost four thousand years.
_shared.cdd5a651d8dd: Hexi Corridor. A one thousand-kilometer strip of oases between the Qilian Mountains and the desert, west of the Yellow River — the main road of the Silk Road.
_shared.6e04161b7a2f: West Lake. Today: Hangzhou, Zhejiang. Bai Juyi and Su Shi both governed Hangzhou, wrote poems about the lake and built dykes — the Bai and Su Causeways carry their names. Bai Juyi governed there from eight twenty-two to eight twenty-four, and Su Shi from ten eighty-nine to ten ninety-one.
_shared.9deddb35a571: Suez Canal. A one hundred ninety-three-kilometer canal joining the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, so ships between Europe and Asia need not sail around Africa. In twenty twenty-one one stuck ship held up about four hundred others.
_shared.54e79dba8c24: Taxila. A city where roads from Persia, Central Asia and India met, famous for its teachers. Chinese pilgrims called it 呾叉始罗.
_shared.246577518889: Hall County. Made in eighteen eighteen on land the Cherokee gave up in eighteen seventeen to eighteen nineteen, and named for Lyman Hall, a signer of the Declaration of Independence. Its county seat, Gainesville, calls itself the “Poultry Capital of the World,” and Lake Lanier covers a big part of the county.
_shared.50722cc1b528: The Alamo. Today: San Antonio, Texas. In eighteen thirty-six about two hundred defenders, including Davy Crockett, Jim Bowie and several Tejanos, Mexican Texans, held this old mission church for thirteen days before Mexico’s army stormed it. “Remember the Alamo!” became the Texans’ battle cry.
_shared.c75ddd8f4c2b: Milledgeville. Laid out in eighteen oh three and named for Governor John Milledge, it was Georgia’s capital for sixty years. Here the secession convention voted to leave the Union in January eighteen sixty-one, and in November eighteen sixty-four Union officers held a mock session in the statehouse to “repeal” secession.
_shared.0a380ad3a8ab: River Thames. London’s river. The city grew up here because ships could sail in from the North Sea; Tower Bridge has crossed it since eighteen ninety-four.
_shared.d1ec2a572fe1: Royal Observatory, Greenwich. Longitude zero degrees — the prime meridian — runs through this observatory in London. World time, UTC, is counted from here.
_shared.1ee7336f931d: Rhode Island. Roger Williams founded it in sixteen thirty-six as a place where the government could not force anyone’s religion. It was so independent that it skipped the Constitutional Convention and ratified last, by just thirty-four votes to thirty-two, in seventeen ninety.
_shared.4decf46dbcbd: Rock Eagle effigy mound. A giant bird with spread wings, made of thousands of white quartz rocks piled on the ground — one hundred two feet from head to tail. Nobody knows exactly who built it or why; the best view is from the stone tower beside it.
_shared.47c860f0d294: Fort Laramie. Tired emigrants rested at this trading post and fort; goods cost three times Missouri prices, so many families left heavy furniture behind here. In eighteen fifty-one and eighteen sixty-eight the US signed treaties with the Lakota and other nations here — promises it later broke.
_shared.1e3f2157e660: Peking University. Today: Beijing, the “Red Building” at Shatan; the university moved to Haidian in nineteen fifty-two. The Imperial University was the one reform of eighteen ninety-eight that survived. Twenty years later, as Peking University, it was a centre of the New Culture and May Fourth Movements.
_shared.92b566907d71: Xianyang. Today: northeast of today’s Xianyang, Shaanxi, near Xi’an. From Xianyang the First Emperor ruled a united China after two hundred twenty-one B C E. The city was burned down when the Qin fell.
_shared.b9a809f9b039: Fort Kearny. An army post built in eighteen forty-eight beside the Platte River to protect travelers, about three hundred twenty miles along the trail. Emigrants could pick up mail, buy supplies and fix wagons here.
_shared.fe86ec2ec305: Bengal. Today: Bangladesh and West Bengal, India. In fourteen fourteen envoys from Bengal brought a giraffe from Africa to the Ming emperor — people in Beijing thought it was a qilin!
_shared.e0305ffb42c2: Taizicheng. Today: Chongli, Zhangjiakou, Hebei. A station in the snowy hills of Chongli, where skiing events of the twenty twenty-two Winter Olympics were held. Trains from Beijing take about an hour.
_shared.add1567e1d49: Tainan. Today: Tainan, Taiwan Province. Zheng Chenggong landed here in sixteen sixty-one and drove out the Dutch from Fort Zeelandia. Tainan was Taiwan’s main city for more than two hundred years.
_shared.04bcf51b576a: Sparta. Today: Sparti, Greece. Boys left home at seven to train as soldiers. Sparta had almost no city walls — its soldiers were its walls.
_shared.df2de83d7612: Shanksville. On the eleventh of September, two thousand one, the passengers and crew of United Flight ninety-three fought back against the hijackers, and the plane crashed in a field near this Pennsylvania village instead of reaching Washington. The memorial’s Tower of Voices holds forty wind chimes, one for each person on board.
_shared.a9c37033a19c: Hartwell. The county seat of Hart County, also named for Nancy Hart. Huge Lake Hartwell, made by damming the Savannah River in the early nineteen sixties, lies right next to the town.
_shared.1c58d737501b: Alabama. Georgia’s neighbor to the west — the Chattahoochee River forms much of the border. Much of it was Creek and Cherokee land until the forced removals of the eighteen thirties; later Montgomery, Selma and Birmingham became famous places of the civil rights movement.
_shared.3a61590316a8: Liangzhu. Today: Yuhang, Hangzhou, Zhejiang. A walled city with palaces, dams and fine jade, about five thousand years old — proof of more than five thousand years of Chinese civilization.
_shared.8609fbce4edc: Irwin County. A small farming county in south Georgia whose county seat is Ocilla. Jefferson Davis, the Confederate president, was captured at his camp near Irwinville here in May eighteen sixty-five.
_shared.d9d53bc12af1: Paris. Notre-Dame cathedral was begun here in eleven sixty-three and its university grew around twelve hundred. In seventeen eighty-nine Parisians stormed the Bastille fortress.
_shared.2639b9d4734f: Ohio Valley. Britain and France both claimed this rich land along the Ohio River, home to the Shawnee, Lenape and other Native nations. In seventeen fifty-four a twenty-two-year-old George Washington fired some of the first shots here, starting the French and Indian War.
_shared.d2d6863c2f2a: Edmund Pettus Bridge. On the seventh of March, nineteen sixty-five, state troopers beat peaceful voting-rights marchers led by John Lewis and Hosea Williams on this bridge in Selma — “Bloody Sunday”. Two weeks later thousands crossed it again on the march to Montgomery, and the Voting Rights Act followed that August.
_shared.8768fe25831e: Omaha Beach. One of five Allied landing beaches in Normandy, France, on D-Day; American troops met the fiercest fighting here and suffered heavy losses. On the cliff above, the Normandy American Cemetery holds more than nine thousand white marble crosses and Stars of David.
_shared.8fdffd2d9a5e: Saint Lawrence River. It carries water from the Great Lakes about one thousand two hundred kilometers to the Atlantic. Ships use it as a water highway into the middle of North America.
_shared.d3d85537ac73: Isthmus of Panama. A narrow strip of land, only about fifty kilometers wide at its narrowest, joining North and South America. The Panama Canal cuts through it.
_shared.9e7f4cf1dd6d: Springer Mountain. The Appalachian Trail begins on top of this three thousand seven hundred eighty-foot Blue Ridge mountain. A bronze plaque on a rock marks the start of the roughly two thousand two hundred-mile walk to Maine.
_shared.7f73278facb1: Kuala Lumpur. Capital of Malaysia, near the Strait of Malacca, with the four hundred fifty-two-meter Petronas Twin Towers.
_shared.7720f705cfda: Columbia River. The great river of the Pacific Northwest cuts a deep gorge through the Cascade Mountains. Lewis and Clark canoed down it to the Pacific in eighteen oh five; later, emigrants on rafts risked its rapids below The Dalles.
_shared.c1f746b42e69: Bayan Har Mountains. Today: Qinghai. The Yellow River begins on the northern slopes of these mountains, about four thousand five hundred meters high on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.
_shared.42610ffdeb97: CERN. Europe’s particle-physics laboratory sits on the French-Swiss border near Geneva. Here Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web and put the first website online — and CERN gave the Web to everyone for free. Deep underground runs the Large Hadron Collider, a ring twenty-seven kilometers around.
_shared.eb401af55a3b: Houston. About two point three million people live in Houston today — more than lived in all thirteen colonies in seventeen seventy. NASA’s Mission Control here guided the astronauts; the first words from the Moon in nineteen sixty-nine were “Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.”
_shared.f25a2050aba1: Point Comfort. Today: Fort Monroe, Hampton, Virginia. In late August sixteen nineteen an English ship, the White Lion, brought “twenty and odd” Africans here, captured from a Portuguese slave ship — the first recorded Africans in English America. Today the spot is part of Fort Monroe National Monument.
_shared.7a800907006d: Vermont. Vermont was not one of the thirteen colonies: New York and New Hampshire both claimed it, so in seventeen seventy-seven it declared itself an independent republic — and its constitution was the first in America to ban adult slavery. It joined the United States as the fourteenth state in seventeen ninety-one.
_shared.f4f245fb0306: Dongjiaominxiang. Today: Dongcheng, Beijing. After nineteen oh one this street was a walled-off quarter for foreign embassies, guarded by foreign soldiers, where Chinese people were not allowed to live.
_shared.366a8a3b2a14: Little Kennesaw Mountain. The smaller peak just southwest of Kennesaw Mountain. In June eighteen sixty-four Confederate cannons sat on its top, and soldiers dug trenches that you can still follow on the hiking trail.
_shared.d5395d4ddea1: Beijing Ancient Observatory. Built in fourteen forty-two on top of the city wall, it was used for almost five hundred years. Huge bronze instruments still stand on its platform.
_shared.d350d7793e6f: Kansas. After eighteen fifty-four settlers could vote on slavery, so people for and against it rushed in and fought — about fifty-five people were killed in “Bleeding Kansas”. It joined the Union as a free state in January eighteen sixty-one; later Topeka’s school case, Brown versus Board, ended legal school segregation.
_shared.85e52e119fda: Gwinnett County. Created in eighteen eighteen on land the Creek were forced to give up, and named for Button Gwinnett, a signer of the Declaration of Independence. Once farmland, today it is one of the most diverse counties in the Southeast, with about a million people.
_shared.a61cf624dc04: Richmond. Richmond, Virginia, was the Confederate capital, only about one hundred miles from Washington, so both armies fought for years to protect or take it. When it fell in April eighteen sixty-five, fires burned much of the city and Jefferson Davis fled south.
_shared.07ec507f995b: Techwood Homes. Today: replaced by Centennial Place, nineteen nineties. During the Great Depression the government cleared a run-down neighborhood near Georgia Tech and built the first federal public housing in the US, with brick apartments for low-income families. It was for white families only; it was torn down before the nineteen ninety-six Olympics.
_shared.58597bc6ddf8: Thomson. Small-town home of Tom Watson, the fiery Populist who fought for poor farmers in the eighteen nineties and won free mail delivery to rural homes, Rural Free Delivery. His home, Hickory Hill, still stands in Thomson.
_shared.3c460558f408: Aydingkol Lake. A salty lake in the Turpan Basin, lying about one hundred fifty-four meters below sea level.
_shared.f178dc527d1f: New Echota. Today: Near Calhoun, Georgia. The Cherokee built their capital here, with a council house, a supreme court and a print shop that printed the Cherokee Phoenix in English and Cherokee from eighteen twenty-eight. The eighteen thirty-five Treaty of New Echota, signed by a small group without the Nation’s consent, led to the eighteen thirty-eight roundup — today you can walk among rebuilt buildings and the old Vann’s Tavern.
_shared.ec45ef2e5239: New Mexico. Most of it came from Mexico in eighteen forty-eight and its southern strip in the Gadsden Purchase of eighteen fifty-three; it became a state in nineteen twelve, and part of the Navajo Nation lies here. Scientists at Los Alamos built the first atomic bomb, tested at Trinity in nineteen forty-five, and Microsoft was founded in Albuquerque in nineteen seventy-five.
_shared.bc0ca1ee8c03: University Homes. Today: demolished, two thousand nine. Built near Atlanta University with New Deal money and opened in nineteen thirty-seven, it was among the first public housing in the US for Black families. Because of segregation, white families lived at Techwood Homes and Black families here.
_shared.f431233f2270: Zhang Fei Temple. Today: Yunyang, Chongqing. To save it from the rising water, the whole temple was taken apart and rebuilt thirty-two kilometers upstream.
_shared.4a302a47a3f5: Tokyo. Today: Tokyo, Japan. The capital of Japan. Many Chinese students studied there around nineteen hundred, and in nineteen oh five Sun Yat-sen founded the Chinese Revolutionary Alliance, Tongmenghui, in Tokyo.
_shared.4aa247a57d20: Missouri River. North America’s longest river, flowing about two thousand three hundred forty miles from Montana to the Mississippi. The railroad from Chicago reached its bank at Council Bluffs, across from Omaha, in eighteen sixty-seven.
_shared.9d729fbdd42c: Qutang Gorge. Its entrance, Kuimen, is so famous that it is printed on the back of the ten-yuan note.
_shared.af98368676a7: Nanjing. Nanjing has been a capital for many dynasties. In December nineteen thirty-seven Japanese troops murdered about three hundred thousand Chinese people here, the Nanjing Massacre. It was liberated on the twenty-third of April, nineteen forty-nine.
_shared.280c8e2b05af: Dublin. A Coastal Plain city on the Oconee River, only about two hundred twenty feet above sea level. Named after Dublin, Ireland, it throws a big Saint Patrick’s Day festival every March.
_shared.f608a8d6cac1: Mexico City. Capital of Mexico, built on the old Aztec capital Tenochtitlan, two thousand two hundred forty meters up in a mountain valley. About twenty-two million people live in its metro area.
