_shared.9b0b1af2f805: Cape Canaveral. Explorer One, Alan Shepard, John Glenn and Apollo Eleven all lifted off from this stretch of the Florida coast. Moon rockets were stacked in the Vehicle Assembly Building, whose doors — four hundred fifty-six feet high — are the tallest in the world.
_shared.08f03347bbed: Ichisi. Today: Near Macon, Georgia. A chiefdom on the Ocmulgee River, probably centered at the Lamar mounds near Macon. De Soto’s army arrived in late March fifteen forty — the first Europeans its people had ever seen.
_shared.af8fc5ef07dd: Dujiangyan. Today: Dujiangyan, Sichuan. The Fish Mouth splits the Min River in two, the Feisha Weir spills floods, and the Bottle-Neck Channel lets water onto the Chengdu Plain — still working after two thousand two hundred years.
_shared.ea48c4a7833d: Fort Jackson. Today: Near Wetumpka, Alabama. After the Creek War, Andrew Jackson forced the eighteen fourteen Treaty of Fort Jackson here, taking about twenty-three million acres — even from Creek towns that had fought on his side. Today the site is Fort Toulouse-Fort Jackson Park, with rebuilt forts and a riverside arboretum.
_shared.fde34a62fb19: Cairo. Saladin built its Citadel on a hill in the eleven seventies. In the Middle Ages it was one of the biggest trading cities in the world.
_shared.f9cc3366b572: Providence. Roger Williams, banished from Massachusetts for his ideas, founded it in sixteen thirty-six on land he got from the Narragansett people. He named it for God’s “providence”, care; today it is the capital of Rhode Island.
_shared.6fd08481c49c: Federal Hall. On the thirtieth of April, seventeen eighty-nine, George Washington took the oath as the first President on a balcony here, when New York was the nation’s capital. Today’s building stands on the same spot on Wall Street, with a big statue of Washington on its steps. The building dates to eighteen forty-two.
_shared.1ca4942bda0e: Yizhou. Today: Taiwan. In two hundred thirty Sun Quan sent Wei Wen with a fleet of ten thousand soldiers across the sea to Yizhou — the earliest record of mainland people reaching Taiwan in large numbers.
_shared.df4d9586fac8: Appalachian Mountains. A one thousand five hundred-mile chain of very old, worn-down mountains that ends in north Georgia, where the Appalachian Trail starts at Springer Mountain. The Proclamation of seventeen sixty-three banned colonists from settling west of them — one of the complaints that led to the Revolution.
_shared.6df5dc2823ad: Matterhorn. A sharp pyramid-shaped peak in the Alps on the Swiss-Italian border. The peak is four thousand four hundred seventy-eight meters high.
_shared.2afcbdd9164a: China-Laos Railway. One thousand thirty-five kilometers from Kunming in China to Vientiane, capital of Laos, through one hundred sixty-seven tunnels. It gives land-locked Laos a fast link to ports and markets.
_shared.917a332bebfd: Babylon. Today: near Hillah, Iraq. Hammurabi ruled from here and set up his law code. Around six hundred B C E it was the biggest city in the world, entered through the blue Ishtar Gate.
_shared.ceb65a434d46: Yellowstone National Park. Today: Wyoming, USA. The world’s first national park, eighteen seventy-two, famous for geysers and hot springs. At Mammoth Hot Springs, warm water builds terraces of travertine.
_shared.4b9b13f6fa91: Trail of Tears State Park. In the bitter winter of eighteen thirty-eight to eighteen thirty-nine, Cherokee families on the forced removal waited for weeks to cross the ice-choked Mississippi River here. Many died of cold and sickness; the park in Missouri remembers them.
_shared.e54956d89867: Independence Rock. A huge granite dome where emigrants carved or painted their names — more than five thousand can still be found. Wagon trains tried to reach it by the Fourth of July so they would cross the mountains before the snow.
_shared.f3f8cadd58d3: Quebec. Samuel de Champlain founded it in sixteen oh eight on cliffs above the Saint Lawrence River, and it became the capital of New France. It is the only city north of Mexico that still has its old city walls, and most people there speak French.
_shared.74a2036defb0: Independence Hall. The Declaration of Independence was signed here in seventeen seventy-six, and the Constitution was written here in the summer of seventeen eighty-seven — both in the same Assembly Room. George Washington’s “rising sun” chair still stands at the front of the room.
_shared.2ebbffd32ee3: James River. In sixteen oh seven three English ships sailed up this river, named for King James the First, and the colonists built Jamestown on its bank. Later, tobacco plantations worked by enslaved people lined its shores.
_shared.ffb60b097a33: Blue Ridge Mountains. Part of the old, worn-down Appalachians. In north Georgia they hold the state’s highest point, Brasstown Bald, one thousand four hundred fifty-eight meters.
_shared.89c404508b65: Pyrenees. A mountain wall about four hundred thirty kilometers long between France and Spain. The tiny country of Andorra sits high in its valleys.
_shared.ded46b51aab2: Northwest Territory. Today: Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, part of Minnesota. The Northwest Ordinance of seventeen eighty-seven banned slavery here and promised that new states made from it would be equal to the old ones; five states came from it. The Shawnee, Miami and other nations fought hard to keep their lands but lost their British allies after the War of eighteen twelve.
_shared.59ad651319a3: Changning County. A county in Baoshan, western Yunnan. Its museum keeps a nineteen fifty-four certificate for a deputy elected to the Yunnan Provincial People’s Congress.
_shared.90cb8bb349b2: Liujiagang. Today: Liuhe, Taicang, Jiangsu. Zheng He’s great fleet of over two hundred ships and twenty-seven thousand men gathered here before sailing.
_shared.7ddb715a6bac: Seattle. A port city on Puget Sound, at the western end of James J. Hill’s Great Northern Railway, eighteen ninety-three. Its Space Needle was built for the nineteen sixty-two World’s Fair, and on clear days snowy Mount Rainier looms behind the city.
_shared.7bf210465c61: Lin’an. Today: Hangzhou, Zhejiang. After eleven twenty-seven the Song court moved south to Lin’an. Its West Lake has inspired poets for more than a thousand years.
_shared.9ef217921297: Acre. Today: Akko, Israel. The Crusaders’ main port and last big stronghold in the Holy Land. When it fell in twelve ninety-one, the Crusades in the East were over.
_shared.6fe64dfaaa50: Mount Zion Baptist Church. Today: part of the Albany Civil Rights Institute. In nineteen sixty-one to nineteen sixty-two the Albany Movement held its packed mass meetings in this small church, where people sang freedom songs and Martin Luther King Junior spoke. The old church is now part of the Albany Civil Rights Institute.
_shared.f5ab6f5d1000: New Hampshire. Its giant white pines were so valuable that the king’s men marked the best ones as masts for the Royal Navy. On the twenty-first of June, seventeen eighty-eight, it became the ninth state to approve the Constitution — exactly the number needed for it to take effect.
_shared.cc98e5a68c2f: Chartres Cathedral. It still has most of its original stained-glass windows from the twelve hundreds — Bible stories in coloured light for people who could not read.
_shared.c9dd61294d9f: Baltimore. To win trade with the West, Baltimore began building the Baltimore and Ohio in eighteen twenty-eight, one of America’s first railroads; by eighteen fifty-seven it reached Saint Louis. Its old roundhouse is now the B and O Railroad Museum, full of historic locomotives.
_shared.1e11d9c8f07b: Athens. Home of the University of Georgia, where classes began in eighteen oh one; the founders named the town after ancient Athens, a famous center of learning. Today it is also known for music — bands like R.E.M. got their start here.
_shared.401969adae3d: Yamacraw Bluff. Today: Riverfront of downtown Savannah. A forty-foot bluff above the Savannah River where Tomochichi’s Yamacraw people lived. Here they welcomed Oglethorpe and about one hundred fourteen settlers in February seventeen thirty-three, and Savannah was laid out on top.
_shared.990242a0ae73: Uruk. Today: Warka, Iraq. Around three thousand B C E perhaps forty thousand people lived inside its walls. Some of the oldest writing ever found comes from its temples.
_shared.099c3cdb2b31: Rio Grande. In eighteen forty-six US and Mexican soldiers clashed near this river, starting the Mexican-American War. Today it forms the border between Texas and Mexico for about one thousand two hundred fifty miles; in Mexico it is called the Río Bravo.
_shared.a52417fa285c: Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon. The deepest canyon on Earth, over five thousand meters in places, where the Yarlung Zangbo River bends around Namcha Barwa peak in Xizang.
_shared.09d280fa14fe: Okefenokee Swamp. North America’s largest blackwater swamp covers about four hundred thirty-eight thousand acres; its name is often said to mean “trembling earth,” because floating peat islands shake when you step on them. Alligators, cranes and black bears live here, and it feeds the Suwannee and Saint Marys rivers.
_shared.195afb5b401f: Yan’an. Today: Yan’an, Shaanxi. From Yan’an the Party led the War of Resistance. The Seventh National Congress was held here in nineteen forty-five. Its pagoda on the hill is a symbol of the revolution.
_shared.3bbc62bc2243: Delaware. Swedes, then the Dutch, then the English ruled it. On the seventh of December, seventeen eighty-seven, it became the first state to ratify the Constitution — every vote was yes — so it calls itself “The First State”; in the Civil War it was a slave state that stayed in the Union.
_shared.4e1128d05e41: Chimney Rock. This clay-and-sandstone spire rises about three hundred feet above the plains of western Nebraska and could be seen for days before emigrants reached it. More travelers wrote about it in their diaries than about any other landmark on the trail.
_shared.5bc374e438f9: Chuzhou. Today: Chuzhou, Anhui. “环滁皆山也” — the city is ringed by hills. Ouyang Xiu, demoted here at about forty, called himself the Old Drunkard and shared his joy with the people.
_shared.c317e2f181a6: Jordan River. A short river that flows south into the Dead Sea, the lowest place on land, about four hundred thirty meters below sea level. Several countries share its scarce water.
_shared.40022a32bc8f: Fort Hall. A fur-trading post on the Snake River, built in eighteen thirty-four. Nearby, Shoshone and Bannock people traded dried salmon with emigrants — most meetings on the trail were peaceful; today the area is part of the Fort Hall Reservation.
_shared.4107d0a6548f: Quitman County. A small county on the Chattahoochee River and the Alabama line, with only about two thousand people; its county seat is Georgetown. Under the county unit system its few voters had as much say as tens of thousands in Atlanta.
_shared.34a70e04fdaa: Sixteenth Street Baptist Church. This Birmingham church was a meeting place for civil rights marchers. On a Sunday morning in September nineteen sixty-three, a bomb planted by Ku Klux Klan members killed four girls — Addie Mae Collins, Cynthia Wesley, Carole Robertson and Carol Denise McNair — and the nation’s shock helped push Congress to pass the Civil Rights Act.
_shared.0ef79958629e: Mariana Trench. The deepest place in the ocean, in the western Pacific — deep enough to swallow Mount Everest with more than two kilometers to spare.
_shared.a3db33d75944: Chaeronea. Philip the Second of Macedon and his eighteen-year-old son Alexander won here, ending the independence of the Greek city-states. A stone lion marks the battlefield.
_shared.44fcfe403ad0: Louisiana Purchase. Today: central United States, from the Mississippi to the Rockies. In eighteen oh three the United States bought this huge land from Napoleon’s France for fifteen million dollars — about three cents an acre — and roughly doubled in size. Parts of fifteen of today’s states were carved from it, though Native nations still lived on the land and had never sold it.
_shared.d4bb44f0e021: Iguazu Falls. About two hundred seventy-five waterfalls on the border between Brazil and Argentina. The biggest drop is called the “Devil’s Throat”.
_shared.a723a9e45efb: Bethesda orphan house. The preacher George Whitefield founded this orphan house near Savannah in seventeen forty and raised money for it with his famous outdoor sermons. It is one of the oldest children’s homes in America that is still running.
_shared.07fb1662fd03: Jamestown. In May sixteen oh seven, one hundred four English men and boys built James Fort here — the first permanent English settlement in America. In the “starving time” winter of sixteen oh nine to sixteen ten most of the settlers died; archaeologists found the real fort’s remains in nineteen ninety-four.
_shared.4a27e4485e84: Cowpens. On the seventeenth of January, seventeen eighty-one, Daniel Morgan set a clever trap in this open cattle pasture: his militia fired two shots and fell back, and the charging British ran straight into his steady regulars. Nearly the whole British force was killed or captured.
_shared.7afd9663497b: Yongdingmen. The southern start of Beijing’s seven point eight-kilometer Central Axis. The gate was pulled down in nineteen fifty-seven and rebuilt in two thousand four to two thousand five from old drawings and photos.
_shared.8ed5ea9b4012: Ogeechee River. A dark “blackwater” river that flows about two hundred ninety miles from the Piedmont to the sea just south of Savannah. The seventeen sixty-three Treaty of Augusta took the land between it and the Savannah River from the Creek, and in eighteen sixty-four Sherman’s army stormed Fort McAllister at its mouth.
_shared.78b65f80457a: Yudu. Today: Yudu, Jiangxi. Over eighty thousand Red Army soldiers crossed the Yudu River here on pontoon bridges at night to begin the Long March.
_shared.208dcedc9613: Fort Wilkinson. Today: Near Milledgeville, Georgia. At this frontier fort on the Oconee River, Creek leaders signed the eighteen oh two Treaty of Fort Wilkinson, giving up the land between the Oconee and Ocmulgee rivers. Nothing of the fort stands today — only a historical marker.
_shared.b6239c80f09d: Stork Tower. Today: Yongji, Shanxi. A tower by the Yellow River where storks used to nest. From the top Wang Zhihuan saw “白日依山尽, 黄河入海流”; the old tower was lost in war and rebuilt in two thousand two.
_shared.bda92c6407ff: Huiyan Peak, Hengyang. Today: Hengyang, Hunan. The first of the seventy-two peaks of Mount Heng. Legend says wild geese flying south go no further — so in 衡阳雁去 the geese go home, but the soldiers cannot.
_shared.3294b8fbd21d: Xi’an. Thirteen dynasties had their capital here. In the Xi’an Incident of December nineteen thirty-six, Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng forced Chiang Kai-shek to stop the civil war and fight Japan.
